title: Try a pronunciation scoring tool on recorded practice sentences
body: Run the same ten sentences through =Speechace= and see if the score actually tracks improvement.

body: Not everything on the NAS matters equally, and I've never actually written down which files do.

title: Compare open-source TTS models on quality latency and licence
body: Every project stalls on picking a voice, so fix the comparison once. Run the same paragraph through three open models, log latency and licence terms, and mark the *licence* that actually allows commercial reuse.

title: Read the collected lyrics in Spanish, one song an evening
body: I dance to these songs every week and could not tell you what half of them say beyond the title. There is a collected lyrics book on the shelf that I have barely opened. Read one lyric each evening in the original, out loud once, and underline the lunfardo words I do not know instead of reaching for a translation straight away. Keep a running list of the words that come back in several songs, since those are the ones worth learning first. After a month, go back and see whether the /voseo/ forms still trip me up when I hear them sung, because that is the real test of whether it worked.

title: Swap one evening of subtitled Netflix for raw Spanish YouTube
body:
Queue a whole evening of unscripted Spanish YouTube instead of subtitled Netflix. [[obsidian:Spanish media list]]
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comprehensible_input

title: Finally start using daily SPF50 sunscreen every single morning
body: Finally add *daily SPF50* to the morning routine instead of only on holiday.

title: Read the C++ concepts and constexpr chapters properly, with a compiler open
body: Most of my templates still rely on SFINAE tricks that concepts now replace with readable errors. Rewrite one old =enable_if= helper as a concept, then make a small lookup table build entirely at compile time and confirm it with a static_assert.

title: Go through the installed editor plugins and cut the dead weight
body: The plugin list has grown for years and I could not say what half of them do. Some were installed for a single project and never removed, and startup feels slower than it used to. Open the list, disable everything I cannot justify in one sentence, and live with that for a week to see what I actually miss. For the survivors, look for whether a newer or better maintained alternative exists, especially for linting, bracket handling and the file tree. Keep a short note of what was removed and why, so that when something breaks I know what to re-enable rather than reinstalling blindly. Do not start trying new plugins until the cleanup is finished.

title: Get clear on how diffusion policy differs from behaviour cloning
body: Robot arms that act multimodally are hard for plain regression, and diffusion over action chunks is the fix everyone cites. Read the Diffusion Policy paper and note how action horizon and receding-horizon control fit together. [[obsidian:Robot Learning Notes]]

title: Practise estimating ad-serving capacity on the back of an envelope
body: I can size a web service but freeze when the question is how many requests per second a ranking model can take. Pick ten million daily active users, assume a request count per user, a peak-to-average ratio and a per-candidate model cost, and work out cores needed. Do it in five minutes, then redo it with different assumptions and see what dominates.

title: Read the GRPO paper next to a practitioner write-up
body: The paper says the critic can be dropped by normalising rewards within a group, but I suspect it skips details like length effects and std division. Read both, then list three things the paper does not say.

title: Settle the 400 versus 422 versus 409 argument I keep having
body:
Decide when I reach for =422= over =400= or =409= in my own endpoints and write the rule down.
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Status

title: Add a statistics page with graphs to the habit app
body: The habit app just logs raw numbers right now, and I never look at them because there is no trend to see. Add a stats page with weekly and monthly graphs, starting with the streak counter and sleep hours.

title: Drill tensor indexing with gather, scatter and advanced indexing puzzles
body: Twenty puzzles, no looking things up, redo the ones I got wrong.

title: Package the agenda app as a standalone desktop build
body: The agenda only runs through the sync server right now, which means no offline laptop use during travel. Bundle it with PyInstaller into a single binary that reads the local =tasks.db= file directly, no network calls at all.

title: Compare batch norm, layer norm and no norm on one small net
body:
Use the same small convnet and seed for each, and change only the normalization layer.
- Plot training loss and the activation mean and std per layer
- Repeat with a learning rate ten times higher to see which variant *tolerates the larger step* best
- Try batch size 8 as well, since batch norm should suffer there

title: Plan a longer loop that avoids the same three streets
body: Every run defaults to the same three streets because that's the route my legs know without thinking. Sketch a longer loop on the map tonight, one with an actual hill, and run it once before deciding whether it sticks.

title: Book flights for the family reunion before prices climb
body: *Book now* — fares only go up the closer it gets to the actual weekend.

title: Read about sequential recommenders and metrics beyond the next click
body: Start with SASRec, then look for papers on long-term value and retention.

title: Draft questions to ask interviewers, split by their *role*
body: Separate lists for the recruiter, an engineer, a manager and a senior researcher, since the same question lands differently on each.

title: Start the code-first applied causal inference book and do the exercises
body: I read causal material passively and then cannot write the estimator when a real question turns up. Pick one code-first applied textbook, run every notebook myself, and do the exercises. *Do not move on from a chapter until I can state its identification assumption in a sentence.*

title: Reject ungrounded answers in the personal notes assistant
body: Right now the assistant answers even when nothing in my notes supports it, and that is worse than saying nothing. Add a gate to the harness: if fewer than all claims are traced to a retrieved passage, return "not in your notes" and log the case for review.

title: Write a custom iterator class and compare it to a generator
Fix the wrong join order in my Polars cheat sheet
body: The =lazy_frame= example in the note actually eager-evaluates and never gets fixed.

title: Follow up on the unresolved action item from last standup
body: Nobody claimed the flaky test fix from Tuesday's standup and it's still failing the build. Ping the channel directly rather than waiting for it to resurface next week.

title: Book the flu jab at the usual pharmacy
Book the skin check before summer sun makes it worse
body: The mole on my shoulder looks *slightly darker* than last year's photo. Call the GP surgery tomorrow and ask for a skin check referral rather than waiting for the next routine visit.

title: Start a running work log for experiment results and abandoned ideas
body: One dated line per result, decision or dropped experiment, with the reason it was dropped.

title: Build a searchable index of the offline drive shelf
body: Six drives sit in a shoebox and finding one photo means plugging in each until I get lucky. Write a script that walks every drive and dumps filenames plus checksums into a single =index.csv=, then I can grep instead of guess.

title: Build a nightly pipeline that fetches new papers, filters, and mails a digest
body:
Small project, on purpose: a scheduled job that pulls new items from a feed of preprints, drops anything that does not match a short keyword and author list, stores what survives in SQLite, and emits one plain-text digest each morning. The temptation is to start with the ranking model; do not. Version one is fetch, dedupe by ID, filter by keywords, write a row, print a digest. That alone will show whether the feed is worth reading.

Decisions to make up front: cron or a systemd timer, where the state lives so a missed night does not lose items, and how the digest is delivered (email to myself is fine). Log every run with counts of fetched, kept and dropped, because the silent failure mode of these things is a filter that quietly matches nothing for three weeks and I never notice.

Only after a fortnight of real digests, look at whether embeddings or a small classifier would beat the keyword list. [[obsidian:Paper Digest Pipeline Design]]

title: Read Thinking, Fast and Slow and mark which claims survived replication
body: The priming chapter is the one everyone now says fell apart, and I have been repeating half of this book at dinner without knowing which half is still standing. Get a chapter-by-chapter summary first, then read only the chapters on anchoring and loss aversion in full. Keep a two-column note: the claim, and whether it replicated. Finish with a short paragraph on which =Kahneman= claims I would still defend in an argument.

title: Study C++20 coroutines conceptually before writing any
body: The promise type, awaiter and handle machinery looks baffling from the code alone. Read a good explainer on what the compiler does with a coroutine frame, and sketch the lifecycle on paper. Only then decide whether a small generator is worth writing.

title: Sort out the causal inference vocabulary I keep mixing up
body:
The terms blur together whenever I read a paper, so a short glossary with one example each should fix it.
- Difference between ATE, ATT and CATE
- What ignorability and positivity each actually require
- Where propensity scores help and where they blow up
- One line on instrumental variables versus adjustment

title: Decide what safety kit goes in the pack for solo day hikes
body: I walk alone more often now and my kit is a plaster and optimism. The decision is what is actually worth carrying on a day route with patchy signal: a proper foil bivvy rather than a blanket, a whistle, a small headtorch, a paper map and compass I can use, and a charged power bank. A personal locator beacon costs more but is the only item that works with no signal at all, so price one against how often I really go beyond coverage. Also leave a route and return time with someone every time. Pack the kit once, weigh it, and check the batteries on the first of each month. [[obsidian:Hiking safety kit]]

title: Learn how Python =logging= handlers and levels really propagate
body: Replace the scattered print calls in the ingest scripts with one configured logger.

title: Read at least ten pages before checking my phone
body: Read ten pages first thing, before the phone gets picked up at all.

title: Work out what a provider model update would look like in my logs
body: The vendor can swap the underlying model under a pinned alias and nobody tells me until users complain. Pick three cheap signals, such as output length, refusal rate and a weekly replay of the golden set, and chart them by day so a step change shows up as a step.

title: Merge the three scattered photo folders into one year-month structure
body: Photos are split between the NAS, an old laptop export and the phone backup, with overlaps everywhere. Pick a single tree of year then month, copy everything in without deleting sources, and run a duplicate finder before touching anything. Only remove the old folders after a spot check.

title: Learn the modes by ear instead of memorising formulas
body: Naming modes from a parent scale is easy but useless at the keyboard, because I still can't hear the difference between Dorian and Aeolian in real time. Start with one mode a week: play it over a static drone, sing the characteristic note, then improvise short phrases that lean on it. The goal is *recognising the sound*, not reciting which scale degree is flattened, so no writing anything down until the ear already knows the answer.

title: Answer "describe a conflict with a colleague" in two minutes flat
body: Use one real story and make sure the *outcome and what I changed afterwards* is the last thing said.

title: Add a whistle and space blanket to the day pack
body: Cheap insurance for a twisted ankle miles from the car park.

title: Study speaker diarization on hour-long recordings, not clean clips
body: Every demo I have seen uses two-minute clips with clean audio, and language lessons and tutoring calls run an hour with crosstalk. Read how pyannote segments and clusters speakers, then run one =55 minute= tutoring recording through it and check where the speaker turns drift.

title: Draw the line between assistant memory and the daily plan
body: Memory keeps standing facts; the plan file keeps anything with a date attached. Next step: move every dated item out of memory this week. [[obsidian:Notes vs Plans Boundary]]

title: Write the design pattern note for deterministic authority in agents
body: Agent designs blur who decides what. Write one page in the notes: the model proposes, plain code holds authority, and each tool gets a *narrow scope granted per task, never per session*. Include one worked example with a file-writing tool.

title: Add Mandarin Chinese as the first non-European language
body: European languages share the Latin script and mostly regular tokenization, so the app currently assumes both. Chinese breaks that in word segmentation, pinyin display and stroke-order lookups. Next step is picking a segmentation library and running it against a small sample list before touching the schema.

title: Learn what bf16, fp16 and FP8 each break in practice
body: I keep picking a dtype by folklore, and the loss spikes I hit last month were probably a range problem rather than a precision one. Go through exponent and mantissa widths for each format, then when loss scaling is needed and why fp16 needs it while bf16 mostly does not. Then look at FP8 scaling factors per tensor, and the 4-bit microscaled formats with shared block exponents. Write down one concrete failure mode for each so I can recognise it in a loss curve. Notes go in [[obsidian:Mixed precision pitfalls]]

title: Map the whole post-training stack before reading any single paper
body: Draw the stages end to end first, so each algorithm has a slot to sit in.

title: Build a table matching the level guide to real work done
body: The level document lists things like 'drives technical direction across the team' in language vague enough to mean almost anything, which is exactly how I end up unsure whether I'm actually there. Copy each bullet from the guide into one column, then next to it list the specific project, decision, or piece of work that demonstrates it, or leave it blank if nothing fits yet. The blanks are the useful part — they're the actual list of what to go do next quarter, not a mystery.

title: Compare free GPU tiers and cheap spot instances for weekend experiments
body: Make a table of hourly price, GPU type, session limits and storage for each option before signing up for anything.

title: Read the BEIR paper before reading group and recheck the BM25 baseline
body:
Sparse retrieval gains often vanish against a well-tuned BM25, so note which BEIR datasets each claim rests on.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08663

title: Decide whether a display calibrator is worth buying
body:
Before spending anything, work out what the monitor already does out of the box and what a print would need.
- Check the panel's factory report and its sRGB coverage
- Compare a test print against the screen under daylight
- Price a used calibrator against borrowing one for an afternoon
[[obsidian:Colour Management Workflow]]

title: Read the case against attention as explanation and pick a side
Learn what point clouds and meshes do that voxels could not
Pit a time series foundation model against ETS and seasonal naive
body:
The zero-shot claims for pretrained forecasting models are impressive on the papers' own benchmarks, and I have no idea whether they survive on the weekly series I actually care about. Most published comparisons use short horizons and a tuned deep baseline rather than the boring things that usually win, so the interesting question is whether the gap to a properly configured ETS or theta model is real.

Plan: pick twenty of my own series with at least three years of history, hold out the last season, and run seasonal naive, ETS, theta and one pretrained model such as Chronos or TimesFM without fine-tuning. Score with MASE so series of different scale are comparable, and also record wall-clock time per series because that is part of the honest cost. Then look at where the pretrained model loses; I expect short, spiky series. Finish with a one-paragraph verdict: is it worth the dependency, or is ETS enough.

title: Curate a scored QA set from an open corpus and measure lift
body: Take a slice of an open question-answer corpus, score each example for quality with a cheap heuristic plus a small model judge, and keep only the top third. Then fine-tune the same small model twice, once on the full slice and once on the curated third, with matched compute and seeds. Report the difference on a held-out set that neither run has seen. If curation gives no lift, that is worth writing up too, because it means the scoring is measuring the wrong thing.

title: Pick the randomization unit for the checkout-page test and defend it
body: Randomizing by session would let one customer see both versions across visits, which muddies the effect and looks unprofessional. Randomizing by user is the obvious fix, but shared household accounts and the referral feature could create interference between arms. Write a half-page memo comparing user, household and region as units, say which contamination each one allows, and state the sample size cost of the coarser choice. Add stratification by past spend tier, and decide up front what would make me discard the result.

title: Look into whether zone 2 training is worth the slog
body: Every running podcast has spent the last year insisting on more zone 2 and less speed work, and I have ignored it because slow running feels like wasted time. But the actual argument is about aerobic base, not about virtue, and my recent times have plateaued in a way that speed work alone has not fixed. Read through the actual physiology rather than the podcast summary, work out what heart rate range counts as zone 2 for me specifically rather than a generic formula, and commit to four weeks of mostly easy running before judging whether it does anything at all.

title: Read the Stan prior choice recommendations with a small regression in mind
body:
Skim the page and note which default priors I would actually use for a small regression.
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

body: The README still describes command-line flags from before the config file rewrite, so anyone cloning it now hits a wall of errors that have nothing to do with real bugs. I should add a short usage example with real output, explain what the cache directory actually does, and note the one dependency that only installs cleanly with a specific Python version. Screenshots would help too, since half the value is the formatted output, not the raw JSON underneath. body: Half of them haven't been opened in over a year and just add to the scroll.

title: Check which Thinking, Fast and Slow claims still replicate
body: Half the priming studies in that book failed to replicate, so I keep citing junk. Make a short list of the big claims, cross-check each against the replication literature, and only keep what still holds.

body: I write Python daily but only know the parts I stumbled into, so *read it selectively for the data model and iterators* chapters.

title: Work out what the compact's lens is /really/ in full-frame terms
body: Convert focal length and aperture to full-frame equivalents for each camera and put them in one small table.

title: Start a running list of *RL failure symptoms* and their causes
body: RL bugs look the same from outside: flat reward, no clue why. Open a note today and add each symptom with its confirmed cause, starting with the last two runs.

title: Find out when multi-agent setups lose to a single agent
body: Most demos I see use several agents by default, and I have started to suspect that a lot of them would work at least as well as one agent with good tools. Collect the evidence: read the recent write-ups and papers on multi-agent failure modes, such as coordination overhead, error compounding, context loss between hand-offs and cost blowup. For each one, note what task was tested, what the single-agent baseline was and how fairly it was tuned. Then pick one workflow I actually care about, probably the research assistant, and write down whether splitting it would help by my reading of the evidence. The output is one page with a clear recommendation, not a literature review, and it should say what result would change my mind.

title: Sketch a one-page map of interpretability methods by question answered
body: Split into intrinsic vs post-hoc and local vs global, and put =SHAP= and LIME in the right boxes.

title: Read up on cross-embodiment policies like RT-X and Octo
body: Note what data mixing across different robots actually bought them over single-robot training.

title: Learn what a vector database actually replaces before comparing products
body: Understand the nearest-neighbour problem first, then look at Pinecone, Qdrant and pgvector.

title: Work out how to enforce business rules on top of the ranker
body: Merchandising wants sponsored items in slots 1 and 4 and a cap of two per brand, and I suspect naive re-sorting quietly wrecks relevance. Read up on constrained re-ranking, then take one toy query set and measure NDCG before and after the rules.

title: Back up phone photos somewhere that is not just the phone
body: All the photos from the last two years live only on the phone, and one drop would lose them for good. Set up an automatic backup to a second location this weekend and confirm it actually ran. Notes on which service and folder structure go in [[obsidian:Photo backup setup]].

title: Redesign the settings dialog in the habit tracker app
body: Right now every toggle lives in one long scroll and nobody, including me, can find the export option without hunting. Group things into three tabs — habits, reminders, and data — and put the *export/import buttons* somewhere permanent instead of buried at the bottom. Mock it up in a plain sketch first, since the last time I jumped straight to code I spent an evening moving buttons two pixels at a time instead of thinking about grouping.

body: Cover feature schema, export step, and the runtime call, starting from the =ranker_v3= model I remember best.

body: Log into the router admin page and install the pending firmware update tonight.

title: Work out how to report RL results without fooling myself
body: Every learning curve I have plotted so far is one lucky run with a smoothed line, and I know that is not evidence. Read the Agarwal et al. paper on statistical precipice and then rerun my small CartPole and Acrobot comparisons with at least ten seeds each. Report interquartile mean with bootstrap confidence intervals instead of the best seed, and write down how many seeds I would need before a difference is believable. Keep the plotting script so the next comparison reuses it rather than starting from scratch.

title: Fix a monthly board game night instead of ad hoc ones
body: Games only happen when someone spontaneously suggests it, which means the newer, heavier boxes never get played because nobody wants to explain rules on the fly. Pick a fixed date, first Friday of the month, and send the invite now so it actually recurs.

body: I can recite the definition but could not explain *why the aggregate rate reverses once you split by department* without the table in front of me. Load the classic admissions counts into a notebook, compute both views, and write two sentences on which one answers a causal question.

title: Set up interpretability tooling and find the open sparse autoencoder resources

title: Check what the free cloud tiers can actually host
body: Several providers advertise a free tier, but the limits differ in ways that only show up after deployment: idle spin-down, monthly compute hours, outbound bandwidth, whether a small database is included, and whether a card is needed at signup. Make one comparison table for four or five of them and be honest about what a small Python web tool needs. Then pick the one that fits and deploy the smallest useful thing I have, probably the note search script behind a simple page, so I learn the deploy flow end to end. *Check what happens when the free quota runs out* — a surprise bill is the failure I want to rule out first.

title: Set up a weekly error-analysis routine for the ranking model
body: Right now I look at a few bad examples, feel bad, and change nothing. Sample fifty failures at random each week, tag each with one category from a small taxonomy, count them, and pick the biggest bucket to turn into one concrete fix or data request.

title: Learn what goes wrong with two-way fixed effects in staggered rollouts
body: Most of the difference-in-differences I have seen is plain two-way fixed effects, and apparently it can give the wrong sign when treatment timing varies. Read the Goodman-Bacon decomposition first, then the Callaway and Sant'Anna estimator. *Older estimators fail when already-treated units act as controls,* and I want to see that on simulated data.

title: Plan a fifteen-minute daily routine for the small travel keyboard
body: Unweighted keys mean no touch practice, so spend the time on chord shapes and ear work.

title: Decide whether daily sunscreen on face and neck earns its place
body: Weigh the evidence and the cost, then either buy a plain SPF 30 or drop it. [[obsidian:Skin and sun notes]]

title: Match last month's card statement against the actual receipts
body: Two charges on the statement don't match anything in my memory, which usually means a subscription renewed quietly or a duplicate charge slipped through. Go line by line against receipts and flag anything unexplained; the *goal* is zero unexplained lines by Sunday.

title: Compare Brier score and log score on the same set of forecasts
body: Both are proper but they punish confident mistakes very differently. Take last quarter's forecasts, compute both scores, and note which model changes rank between them and why.

title: Understand hybrid sparse and dense retrieval with reciprocal rank fusion
body: Compare BM25, vectors and a fused ranking on a few real queries. [[obsidian:Hybrid Retrieval Notes]]

title: Refresh the standard *NP-complete* reductions before interviews resume
body: I can name NP-complete problems but freeze when asked to actually reduce one live. Pick five classics — SAT, vertex cover, subset sum, knapsack, and bin packing — and practice sketching the reduction on paper in under five minutes each. The real interview question is never 'is this NP-complete', it is 'given that it is, what do you actually propose' — approximation, heuristics, or restricting the input size — and that answer is the part I have never rehearsed.

title: Renew the two library books before the due date
body: Renew both library books online tonight before the automatic late fee kicks in tomorrow.

title: Email the shelter coordinator about the holiday schedule
body: Confirm which weeks still need drivers before I commit to any dates.

title: Work out a realistic itinerary for the Lisbon long weekend
body: Four days is not enough for everything the guidebooks list, so the real task is cutting rather than adding. Pick one neighbourhood to wander without a plan, one day trip by train, and leave the rest loose enough to follow whatever the weather does. Check which museums close on Mondays before building around them, and note the tram routes that actually run on the days we are there rather than the timetable in general. Better to arrive with three anchors than a full schedule I abandon by the second morning.

title: Figure out the equivalent aperture between full frame and crop
body: f/2.8 on the crop body has never matched what f/2.8 gives on the full-frame one for background blur, and I keep forgetting the multiplier. Work out the actual equivalent using the =1.5x= factor and write it down before the next portrait session.

title: List the next batch of features for the nutrition app
body:
The nutrition app needs another round of small features before it feels finished.
- micronutrient breakdown beyond just macros
- smart scale sync for weight and body fat
- weekly trend graphs instead of daily-only view
- quick-add for repeated meals

title: Design exceptions in Python with chaining and exception groups
body:
My current habit is catching Exception near the top and logging a string, which throws away exactly the information I would want later. Learn the alternatives properly. First, a small hierarchy for one project: a base error for the package and two or three specific subclasses, with a clear rule for when to create a new class and when an existing built-in is right.

Second, chaining. Understand the difference between raise X from e, which marks an explicit cause, and raising inside an except block without from, which sets the implicit context, and what raise X from None hides. Write the same failure three ways and read the traceback of each so I can see which one I would want at 2am.

Third, exception groups and except* from Python 3.11. Build a toy example with several tasks failing at once under asyncio.TaskGroup, and see how except* splits the group by type, and why an ordinary except does not match the members. Also add a note with add_note and see where it appears in the traceback. The goal is a short set of rules I can apply, not a survey of every feature.

title: Claim the switching cashback and note when it should actually land
body: The new energy supplier's offer is a cash payment after the switch, but the small print says I must *claim it through the emailed link within the window, not just wait for it*. Find the email, submit the bank details, screenshot the confirmation, and put the stated payout timeframe in the calendar. If nothing arrives by the day after that, chase them with the confirmation reference rather than starting from scratch.

title: Summarise double descent precisely without hand-waving
body: Write a three-line summary of double descent that says *the test error peak sits at the interpolation threshold*, not at some vague point of high complexity.

title: Work out what the agent's shell tool should be allowed to touch
body: Right now the shell tool can read the whole home directory, which is far more than any task needs. Write down a capability list per tool, then try a read-only mount of the project dir as the first step. Notes in [[obsidian:Agent permissions sketch]].

title: Review which apps still have location access turned on
body: Half of these were granted access years ago for a single feature I no longer use, and *always-on location* for a shopping app has no good reason to exist. Go through the permissions list app by app and switch anything non-essential to 'while using' or off entirely.

title: Read the Mamba paper and work out where it actually beats attention
Compare plain RAG against a query-decomposition loop on multi-hop questions
body: Single-shot retrieval keeps missing the second half of questions that need two documents. Take a few hundred questions from HotpotQA, run one pipeline with a single retrieval call and one that splits the question into sub-queries, retrieves for each and merges the evidence before answering. Keep the retriever, the chunk size and the generator identical so the only variable is the loop. *Report answer accuracy and the number of retrieval calls side by side*, because a gain that costs four times the latency is a different conclusion from a free one. Finish with a short written comparison that includes three failure cases from each side.

title: Fix the retention rule for dashcam footage before disk fills
body: Keep dashcam clips =30 days= unless marked, then loop-overwrite automatically.

title: Renew the running club membership before the early-bird discount ends
body: The fifteen percent discount only works through the affiliate portal, not the direct site. [[obsidian:Running Club Renewal]]

title: Budget the fine-tuning run before pressing go
body: Last time the job died at hour nine with a full disk and an unexpected bill. Estimate tokens times epochs, throughput per GPU from a short pilot, checkpoint size and storage, then add a *thirty percent margin* on both time and cost before booking the cluster.

title: Look into a capture clip for the camera strap
body: A belt clip would beat digging the camera out of the bag for quick shots.

title: Add *PII redaction* to the text ingestion step before anything is stored
body: Run a detector over a sample of real-looking logs and count what it misses.

title: Apply the sight-reading chapter to five minutes of practice
body: The chapter's whole argument is that sight-reading badly and often beats reading nothing new, which is the opposite of my instinct to only ever play pieces I already half-know. Pick something two grades below my level, read through once without stopping no matter how many wrong notes, and do that for five minutes before the real practice block starts, every day this week. [[obsidian:Piano practice]]

title: Understand *mean pooling* versus CLS pooling for sentence embeddings
body: Read the pooling section of the sentence-transformers docs and test both on one toy set.

title: Version prompt, tools and model as one agent artifact
body: Work out a single manifest that pins all three so a rollback restores the whole thing. [[obsidian:Agent Release Manifest Ideas]]

title: Compare a small ViT and a ResNet on shrinking data
body: The claim that ViTs need far more data than convnets is easy to repeat and hard to feel. Train both on CIFAR-10 at 100%, 25% and 5% of the training set, and see *where the gap flips*. Keep parameter counts roughly matched and use the same augmentation recipe.

title: Explain aleatoric versus epistemic uncertainty with a shrinking-data experiment
body: Show that **epistemic uncertainty falls with more data and aleatoric does not**, using an ensemble on noisy sine data.

title: Study context isolation for long-running agents using sub-agents
body: Long agent runs rot because the context fills with old tool output. Read how isolating work into sub-agents with clean windows helps, then sketch where I would split a =research-then-write= task.

title: Train a small classifier on a public spoken-digit dataset
body: Pick a small dataset like Free Spoken Digit and build the smallest classifier that actually generalises rather than memorising ten speakers. Extract MFCCs, train a plain logistic regression as the baseline before touching anything deep, and only then try a small CNN. The point isn't accuracy, it's the *confusion matrix* — which digits get mixed up and whether that matches the phonetic similarity I'd expect, like six and seven under noise.

title: Sketch a side project ranking short finance news headlines
body: A small ranking model over finance headlines would double as both a project and a demo.

title: Finally shred three years of old bank statements in the drawer
body: The drawer is stuffed and /nobody/ needs paper statements from 2022 anymore.

title: Learn how to test nondeterministic LLM systems and support audits
body: Get clear on evals, seeded runs and audit logs for regulated use. [[obsidian:Testing nondeterministic systems]]

title: Write down the four judge biases and one cheap mitigation for each
body: I keep half-remembering that judges prefer longer answers and prefer whichever answer comes first, but I could not say what to actually do about it. Make a short table: position bias (swap the order and only count verdicts that survive), verbosity bias (add a length-matched control or penalise length in the rubric), self-preference (do not let a model grade its own family), and language bias (test the same answers translated). Then pick the two that matter for my setup and add a check for them to the harness rather than just knowing they exist.

title: Derive the =logistic regression= MLE gradient and check it numerically
body: Write the log-likelihood, get the gradient as X^T(y - p), then compare against finite differences in a few lines of numpy.

title: Rerun the nearest-neighbour benchmark using our real =query log= sample
body: Synthetic random queries flatter the index, so recall and latency should be measured on actual traffic.

title: Book a *coronary calcium score* scan before turning forty-five
body: Resting on 'no symptoms' is not much reassurance given the family history of early heart disease, and a calcium score is one of the few tests that gives an actual number rather than a risk category built on averages. It's not straightforward to get without a specific referral pathway, but private imaging clinics run it for a fixed price and the scan itself takes under fifteen minutes. Book it through a centre that reports an Agatston score directly rather than a vague summary letter, and take the result to the GP alongside the lipid panel already booked, not instead of it.

title: Use Cracking the Coding Interview only for the recursion chapter
body: I don't need the whole book, just a refresher on recursion before Thursday's practice problems. Skip straight to that chapter, work the /three/ examples by hand, then close it again.

title: Learn how feature stores and model serving fit together in one design
body: I have used pieces of this, a batch job here and an endpoint there, but never drawn the full path from raw events to a prediction and back to a training set. The parts that keep causing trouble are the ones between the boxes: point-in-time correctness, training-serving skew, and how a model version gets rolled out and rolled back. Read the Feast documentation and one public write-up of a production serving architecture, then sketch the whole flow on a single page with the failure points marked. Choose one failure point, probably skew, and think about how I would detect it cheaply. [[obsidian:ML Platform Architecture]]

title: Work out the cheapest way to run personal ML experiments
body: Right now I either burn evenings waiting on the laptop or leave a rented instance running overnight by accident. Compare three routes for a typical experiment of one to three hours: local machine with a small runtime, a spot instance on a smaller GPU cloud, and a free notebook tier. For each, record the price per run, the setup time from nothing, and what gets lost when the session ends. Then choose a default and write a two-line launch script for it, so starting a run costs no more thought than starting a local one. Add an auto-shutdown to whichever paid route wins.

title: List the ways a reward function gets gamed in simple gridworlds
body: Pull three or four textbook examples, like the boat-race loop, and note what signal would have caught each.

title: Write down the interview questions before they blur together
body: Half the panel's questions are already blurring together an hour later. [[obsidian:Interview question bank]]

title: Work out what the graph Laplacian actually says about a graph
body: Spectral methods keep getting name-dropped and I nod along without being able to derive anything. Start from D minus A, show why the quadratic form measures smoothness across edges, then connect the eigenvectors to Fourier modes on a path graph. Do the normalized version by hand on a five-node example and note where the eigenvalues are bounded. Finish by writing down how Laplacian eigenvectors get used as positional encodings and why their sign ambiguity is a nuisance.

title: Restock the spice drawer before the empty jars multiply
body:
Half the jars are down to dust and I keep reaching for them out of habit rather than checking first.
- Cumin, smoked paprika, and coriander seed
- *Refill the salt cellar*, it's been empty for a week
- Check whether the bay leaves are still any good

title: Try a split or ergonomic keyboard layout properly and count the strain
body: My right wrist aches by Thursday and I suspect the stretch to the modifier keys and the flat, tented-nowhere board. Read up on Colemak-DH and Dvorak against just remapping Caps Lock to Control, and on what actually helps: split halves, tenting, thumb clusters, shorter reach. Decide what is worth the two weeks of slow typing, and what can be done for free this week. Change one thing first, note the wrist for a fortnight, and only then buy anything, so that I know which change did the work.

title: Read the ANN-Benchmarks methodology page before trusting any vector index numbers
body:
Check what they hold fixed and what they plot, recall against queries per second.
https://ann-benchmarks.com

title: Meal-prep lunches for the busy week before the trip
body: Three days of back-to-back meetings starting Monday mean there is no time to cook, only time to reheat. Pick one grain, one protein, and two vegetables that can be recombined differently each day so lunch does not feel identical all week. *Portion everything into five containers on Sunday afternoon* rather than one big pot, because the pot never actually gets eaten from evenly and the last portion always goes off in the fridge unnoticed.

title: Break down one *blues* turnaround and try the substitutions
body: Take a plain twelve-bar and swap in tritone subs and passing diminished chords bar by bar.

title: Reread the PPO paper's clipping section with a pencil
body: Derive what the clip actually does to the gradient when the ratio leaves the trust region.

title: Browse a plotting library gallery and steal three diagnostics
body: My training plots are just a loss curve, and I miss problems until late. Spend an hour in the gallery of a visualization library, pick three diagnostics such as gradient histograms or confusion heatmaps, and add them to my template. Notes in [[obsidian:Training diagnostics toolkit]].

title: Check what hyperparameter transfer actually promises about learning rates
body: muP claims the best learning rate stops shifting with width if the parametrization is right. Read a summary, write the one-line rule for scaling init and rate, then test it on two widths of the toy MLP. [[obsidian:Scaling and transfer reading list]]

title: Cancel the direct debit for the now-unused broadband line
Run a fast fundamentals check to find remaining gaps
body: Twenty years since school theory and I don't know if I've forgotten key signatures or never really understood them. Spend one evening on a diagnostic quiz covering intervals, key signatures and scale degrees, then triage from what actually trips me up. [[obsidian:Music Theory Fundamentals Check]]

title: Read one travel photographer's blog for actual location ideas
body: Stop bookmarking galleries and read how they scouted the actual shot instead.

title: Review actor-critic and multi-agent RL and where it is /actually/ used
body: Read one overview of PPO and MADDPG and list two real applications each.

title: Explain PPO as a fix for the problems in vanilla policy gradient
body: I use the name constantly and could not derive the clipped objective on a whiteboard. Start from REINFORCE, then trust-region methods, and write out *why clipping stands in for the KL constraint* in half a page.

title: Understand Python closures and late binding before the next lambda-in-a-loop bug
body: Callbacks built in a loop all see the last value, and I fix it by trial each time. Read how closures capture variables rather than values, then write three short examples that fail and the default-argument fix for each.

title: Measure tokenizer fertility across the languages I care about
Read up on Kafka consumer lag as a *freshness* signal
body: Learn what lag means, how it is calculated, and *why lag in messages is not the same as lag in seconds*.

title: Learn how cold-start items get recommended without any interactions
body: New items have no clicks, so a pure collaborative model cannot rank them at all. Read one survey on hybrid and content-based approaches, then sketch how item text embeddings could seed a new item's vector until it collects data. **The key point is the fallback path**, not the model.

title: Read the YouTube deep neural network recommendation paper and extract the design decisions
body:
Read the 2016 YouTube paper on deep neural networks for recommendations and treat it as a case study, not a model to copy. The value is in the framing decisions, so pull those out in a short list rather than summarising the architecture.

Things to answer: why it is split into candidate generation and ranking, and what each stage optimises. Why the candidate model is trained as extreme multiclass classification over watch events. Why watch time is used for ranking instead of click-through, and how weighted logistic regression gets at it. What the example age feature is doing about the bias toward old videos. Why they hold out the most recent watch rather than a random one, which is the same leakage worry I have with my own offline evaluations.

Finish with two or three sentences on what I would say if asked in an interview why a two-stage system is used at all. The latency and catalogue-size argument is the one I tend to fumble, so write that one out in full and check the numbers against the paper.

title: Fix the password manager's health report instead of ignoring it
body: The health report has flagged forty reused passwords for months and I keep closing the tab instead of dealing with it. Pick ten a week, starting with anything tied to email or banking, and work through the list until it's actually clean.

title: Write down the termination conditions for my agent loop
body: Max steps, token budget, wall-clock limit and a no-progress check, all in one place.

title: Wire up an LLM call to suggest new vocabulary words
body: Manually spotting gaps in the word list is slow and I keep adding duplicates. The plan is a scheduled call that reads my *existing* word list per language and returns a short list of common words missing from it, which I then approve one by one before import.

title: Check whether the citations in RAG answers actually support the claims
body: Sample fifty answers and mark each citation as supported, partial or unrelated.

title: Renew the home insurance properly instead of letting it lapse
body:
The renewal notice arrived weeks ago and it's still sitting unopened in the pile, which is exactly how last year's cover briefly lapsed.
- Compare at least two other quotes before accepting the renewal price
- Check the *rebuild cost* is still accurate given recent work on the house
- Confirm the excess and flood cover haven't changed quietly
- Set the payment date a week before the actual deadline

title: Research a realistic hiking route along the Pembrokeshire coast
body: Every year the trip stays a vague idea until it is too late to book anywhere decent along the path. Compare the coast path sections for distance and tide times, check accommodation availability for spring, and settle on a fortnight before it slips again.

title: Skim the confident learning paper and try cleanlab on one dataset
body:
Start with a small text set I already know, and check /how many/ flagged labels are truly wrong.
https://github.com/cleanlab/cleanlab

title: Clean up the phone home screen and delete dead apps
body: The home screen has three banking apps I no longer use, two games I have not opened in a year, and a folder labelled misc that has quietly become a graveyard. Every time I need something quickly I scroll past all of it, which defeats the entire point of a phone. The plan is to delete anything untouched in the last ninety days, move the rest into four clearly named folders by function, and keep only genuinely daily apps on the first screen. I tried this once already and it drifted back within a month, so this time the folder names and the review date go into [[obsidian:Phone declutter routine]].

title: Add a dry-run flag to the photo renaming script
body: It should print the new names without touching any files.

title: Package the tracker app to run without any sync
body: The tracker only runs through the dev server right now, useless the moment I am off wifi on a trip. Bundle it with something like PyInstaller or Tauri, point it at a local SQLite file, and confirm it launches with no network at all.

title: Leave the overdue review for =Lakeview Cottage= rentals
body: It's been three months since that stay and the agency still deserves a rating.

title: Read the *survey* on neural information retrieval as an entry point
body:
Use it as a map of the field before diving into individual papers, then list the topics to follow up.
https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.01509

title: Prep search ranking design answers for a strict latency budget
body: Every practice answer so far ignores the /latency/ constraint until the interviewer forces it in at the end. Start the next three mocks by stating the budget upfront and design backward from it, cutting features before adding indexes.

title: Build a retraining job that only promotes better models
body: Right now retraining is manual and I promote whatever finished last, which is not a policy. Write a scheduled job that trains, scores on =holdout.parquet=, compares with the current model, and registers the new one only if the metric improves.

title: Understand stationarity properly before running another ARIMA on anything
body:
I keep differencing until the plot looks flat, which is not a test. Learn what *weak stationarity* actually requires and how ADF and KPSS disagree.
https://otexts.com/fpp3/stationarity.html

title: Chase the visa application before the appointment slots run out
body: The consulate only releases appointments six weeks ahead and the ones for late October are already thin. Book the earliest slot at =Consulate General= and gather the bank statements tonight so the form isn't the bottleneck tomorrow.

title: Read a few agent postmortems to see how tool-using loops actually break
body: Most of what I know about agent failure is from my own toy runs. Collect three published postmortems or eval writeups, pull out the failure categories, and check which ones my own agent code has no guard against yet.

title: Book: Speech and Language Processing by Jurafsky and Martin
body: The draft third edition is free online and keeps getting updated, which makes it a better reference than any paper-bound NLP text I could buy. Start with the chapters on n-grams, logistic regression and embeddings, then move to transformers. One chapter per sitting, with the exercises done rather than admired.

title: Check whether chain-of-thought hints are admitted in the answer
body: Rerun the hint-injection setup on =gsm8k_small.jsonl= and count how often the trace mentions the hint.

title: Look at the Coursera Reinforcement Learning specialization from the University of Alberta
body: Four courses, starts with bandits and ends with a capstone; check the audit option first.

title: Plot accuracy against reasoning tokens for one open reasoning model
body:
Sweep the budget from =256= to 8192 tokens and note where the curve flattens.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393

title: Try the aperture exercise from the photography book properly
body: The book has one exercise I've skipped three times: shoot the same subject at three different apertures from a tripod, nothing else changed, and actually compare the frames side by side instead of just reading the theory and nodding. Do it this weekend with the kitchen window as the subject, save the set as =aperture-test.org=, and write two lines on what actually changed versus what I expected.

title: Sketch a backfill and migration plan for switching embedding models
body: Changing the embedding model means every stored vector is stale and old and new vectors cannot be compared, which is the part that gets underestimated. Write down the plan before any code: dual-write into a second index, backfill in batches with a rate limit, shadow-query both indexes and compare overlap, then cut over with the old index kept for a week. Also decide what /drift/ metric I would watch afterwards, probably mean cosine of new queries to their top hit, plus the share of queries with no good match.

title: Get three handyman quotes for the deck railing repair
body: The back deck railing has wobbled since spring, and stepping near the corner post now gives a real sway that makes me not trust it with guests leaning on it. It might be a loose bolt or a rotted post base, and I cannot tell without someone underneath looking. Call three handymen, ask each to inspect the post before quoting, and get the price broken into labor and materials so the quotes are actually comparable instead of three unrelated lump sums.

title: Force a NaN on purpose and catch it with anomaly detection
body: Divide by a zeroed tensor in a toy net, turn on =detect_anomaly=, and read the traceback.

title: Use How to Measure Anything only as a lookup for one problem
body: I cannot put a number on how much time the weekly review saves. Look up only the chapter on calibrated estimates, do the =90% confidence= exercise, and leave the rest of the book alone.

title: Fit a scaling law to my own small runs without fooling myself
body:
I have a dozen training runs at different sizes and the curve looks like a clean power law on a log-log plot, which is exactly when I should be suspicious. Straight lines on log-log plots are forgiving, and a fit with three free parameters through eight points can look convincing and extrapolate badly.

First decide what is fitted and what is held out: fit on the smaller runs, predict the largest two, and report the miss. Include an irreducible-loss term and see how much the exponent changes when it is fixed at zero versus free. Fit with several random starts, since the optimiser is fussy here, and give a rough interval by bootstrapping over runs. If the interval on the exponent is wide enough that the extrapolation is meaningless, that is the result, and I should write it down as such instead of quietly dropping the plot.

title: Put family birthdays into a recurring calendar before October
body: Three birthdays already slipped past unnoticed this year because nothing reminded me in time.

title: Compare offset and cursor pagination on a table big enough to hurt
body: Offset paging feels fine on small tables and I have never seen where it breaks. Load a few million rows into SQLite, time page 1 against page 50,000, then rebuild it with a keyset cursor. [[obsidian:API Design Notes]]

title: Find out what constrained decoding costs in serving throughput
body: Check how grammar-guided JSON output changes tokens per second compared with free generation.

title: Study how a standard lakehouse platform is put together
body: Read up on Delta Lake or Iceberg, since *the transaction log* is what makes the rest of the platform make sense.

title: Compare BatchNorm and LayerNorm when the batch size shrinks
body: Train the same small convnet at batch size 2, 8 and 64 and note where =BatchNorm= starts to fall apart.

title: Generalize the last onsite's playbook before it goes stale
body: The playbook is still full of company jargon nobody else uses. [[obsidian:Interview Playbook Generic]]

title: Compare FSDP full-shard and =SHARD_GRAD_OP= on peak memory
body: Same small GPT, same batch, two strategies, then log peak allocated memory and step time for each.

title: Learn enough Emacs Lisp to write my own small editor commands
body: Begin with one command that *inserts the current date heading* into my notes, then grow from there.

title: Buy a foldable water bottle before the flight next month
body: Carrying an empty bottle through security beats buying another plastic one airside.

title: Sketch max-entropy RL and what the temperature buys in practice
Work out how score-based models and the SDE view fit together
body: I can recite the DDPM training loss and still could not explain why it is the same thing as score matching, which means I have memorised a recipe rather than understood it. Read Song's score-based SDE paper slowly, with the forward noising process, the reverse-time SDE and the probability flow ODE written out by hand on one page. The point is to see why the same trained network can be sampled either stochastically or deterministically, and where the choice of noise schedule comes in. Then reread the DDIM update and check that it drops out as a special case. Only after that is it worth touching any code, otherwise I will just copy a sampler loop again and not know why the step sizes look the way they do.

title: Find a tutor for tones through a lesson marketplace
body: Self-study never fixes tone errors because I can't hear my own mistakes. Book a trial lesson on a marketplace this week, aim for someone who drills *tones* specifically, not general conversation.

title: Decide on a heart rate monitor instead of guessing effort
body: Every session so far has been judged by feel, which is fine for noticing a bad day but useless for telling whether the easy runs are actually easy. A chest strap is more accurate than a wrist sensor but less comfortable, and the *whole point* is that I will actually wear it, so comfort probably wins over the last few percent of accuracy. Read two or three comparisons rather than the marketing pages, buy the chest strap anyway if the numbers are close, and give it three weeks before deciding it was a waste of money. Three weeks is enough to know if a habit sticks.

title: Read Designing Machine Learning Systems and check it against my own pipelines
body: I have shipped a few models by now, but mostly by copying what the previous team did, so I could not say which of my habits are sound and which are just inherited. Chip Huyen's book covers exactly the ground I have been walking blind: data drift, monitoring, deployment patterns, feature stores. Read a chapter at a time and, at the end of each, write three lines: what I already do, what I do differently and why, and what I have never thought about. The third list is the useful one. If it turns out I have been skipping something basic like shadow deployment, better to find out from a book than from an incident.

title: Work through the GPU programming lecture series alongside real kernel code
body:
The lectures cover the basics well, but I retain far more when I open a production kernel straight after each one and find the same ideas in it. Pick one lecture per week, then read a matching piece of a real codebase: a fused attention kernel, a layernorm, a quantised matmul. *The goal is to be able to read a kernel I did not write and say what each block of threads is doing.* Keep a short file with one paragraph per lecture and a link to the code I read, so the reading turns into reference material and not a pile of open tabs. Skip the exercises that need hardware I do not have and use a rented GPU for the rest.
https://github.com/gpu-mode/lectures

title: Give agenda tasks small icons instead of plain checkboxes
body: Small icons per task type would make the agenda scannable at a glance. [[obsidian:Agenda Icon Set Ideas]]

title: Sort *fifty failures by hand* before choosing any metric
body: Read fifty bad outputs and name the failure types first.

title: Compare Paxos and Raft trade-offs for a replicated log
body: Focus on what each gives up in understandability, leader handling and availability under partition. [[obsidian:Distributed systems trade-offs]]

title: Read the original HNSW paper before touching any index parameters
body:
I keep setting =efConstruction= by copying defaults and want to know what it actually trades away.
https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320

title: Write a bootstrap from scratch and find where it fails
body:
The bootstrap feels like magic, which usually means I do not understand when it stops working. Implement percentile bootstrap for a mean and a median with plain numpy, compare against the analytic interval, then try it on the maximum of a uniform sample and on a tiny n of eight. The max case is the famous failure, and I want to see the resampled distribution pile up on one value. Also build a permutation test for a difference in means and check it agrees with the t-test on nice data. Write down what each method assumes.

[[obsidian:Resampling methods notes]]

title: Drill the sliding window pattern until it's automatic
body: Every sliding-window problem still takes me five minutes to set up the invariant, which is too slow under time pressure. Redo the classic ten from LeetCode's tag list cold, no hints, then write the invariant first. [[obsidian:Sliding window cheat sheet]]

title: Read a book chapter bridging BM25 and neural retrieval
body: I use dense retrieval without understanding what it replaced. Pick a survey or textbook chapter that connects term weighting, BM25 and learned rankers, read it over a weekend, and write down what a dense model still cannot do that BM25 handles.

title: Buy a collapsible water bottle from the sports shop
body: The =HydraPak= one folds flat and fits the day pack side pocket.

title: Send a first real patch to a library I use every week
body: I lean on the same HTTP client library almost daily and have never given anything back, even though I have hit three papercuts in its docs. Read CONTRIBUTING, pick one small documentation or error-message fix from the issue tracker, and open the pull request. Start with the issue about =retry backoff= wording.

title: Record this week's demo talk and review the playback
body: Watch the recording back and fix only the *two* worst habits, not everything.

title: Build a location-scouting checklist before each planned shoot
body: Every outing so far has been decided on the day, which means half the good light gets missed while I stand around deciding what to point the camera at. Before the next one, write down for each spot: sun angle at the time I expect to arrive, cloud forecast for that hour, and the shot I actually expect to come home with. Then go, take it, and afterward compare the real frame against what I wrote down beforehand. If the gap is mostly light I failed to predict, the checklist needs a better weather source, one that tells me about haze and not just whether it will rain.

title: File the leftover reading items into the right topic notes
body: There are about six saved links on offline evaluation and bandits sitting in the inbox with no home. Open each one, write a one-line summary, and move it into the matching topic note in the knowledge base. Delete the ones I know I will not read.

title: Check what is actually filling up the phone storage
body: Screenshots and three podcast app caches, not photos, turned out to be the real problem.

title: Profile the slow feature script instead of guessing where time goes
body: Run cProfile and then py-spy on the real input and rank the hot spots before changing anything.

title: Finish the free Stanford CS231n lecture series and assignments
body: Do the lectures in order and at least the first two assignments; notes are at =cs231n.github.io=.

title: Apply to the data analyst opening before it expires
body:
The *deadline* is Friday, so no more rereading the description for reassurance.
https://www.linkedin.com/jobs/

title: Queue the CS25 Transformers United lectures with the guest speakers
Work out a latency budget for one full voice agent turn
body:
Everyone quotes "under a second" without saying where the time goes, so I want a budget I can actually check against.
- Split a turn into stages: capture, network, endpointing wait, ASR final, LLM first token, TTS first audio, playback
- Read up on the roughly 200–300 ms gap people leave between turns in conversation, and what happens to /perceived/ quality past 800 ms
- Note which stages can overlap by streaming and which are hard serial
- Put the whole thing in a small table with a target and a worst case per stage

title: Turn odds ratios into a worked example a colleague could follow
body: Coefficients from the churn model keep getting read as probabilities, which they are not. Take one fitted logistic model, exponentiate two coefficients, and write the sentence for each. **An odds ratio is not a change in probability**, so add the baseline-risk case that shows the difference.

title: Write down what offline RL distribution shift looks like in one plot
body: Show a Q-function extrapolating badly on actions absent from the logged data.

title: Add a rule to the agent file about never spinning up paid cloud resources
body: One line in the instruction file: ask first before creating anything that bills by the hour.

title: Free up phone storage by checking what is actually using it
body: The phone keeps warning about storage but I have never actually looked at the breakdown, just deleted photos at random. Check settings for the actual usage by app first, since it is probably one bloated messaging cache rather than the camera roll.

title: Try regression discontinuity on the =free-shipping-threshold= change
body: Orders just under and just over the cutoff should be near-identical, which makes it a cleaner comparison than any before-and-after.

title: Plan one photography outing around the city, with a route
body: I only ever photograph the city by accident, on the way to something else. Choose one morning, pick three spots within walking distance of each other, and write the route down. **Decide the subject for each spot before leaving**, so I am not just wandering with the camera in the bag.

title: Compare sparse, dense and multi-vector retrieval for the design doc
body: One table of index size, latency, tail-query behaviour and ops burden, so the doc argues from trade-offs instead of fashion.

title: Try one round of structured brainstorming on the flaky deploy problem
body: I always default to the first fix that occurs to me. Run =brainwriting= for ten minutes on the flaky deploy pipeline: six ideas written silently, then rotate them into worse and weirder variants. Note afterwards whether anything came out that I would not have reached otherwise.

title: Look into consumer rights before returning the faulty blender
body: It stopped working after six weeks, well inside the reversal period under the Consumer Rights Act, but I only half remember how that works in practice. Check the exact wording, draft the return email accordingly, and log the details in [[obsidian:Consumer rights notes]].

title: Work through the ML interview book by attempting every problem cold
body: Reading solutions feels like learning and mostly is not. Take the interview-prep book, set a twenty-minute timer per problem, write my answer on paper, and only then open the solution. Mark the ones I got wrong so I can redo them a week later.

title: Work out equivalent focal length between the two camera bodies
body: Switching between the full-frame body and the smaller travel camera means the same lens gives a completely different framing, and I keep composing for the wrong one out of habit. Work through the actual crop factor for the second body and produce a short table converting the handful of focal lengths I actually use, from wide to short telephoto, so that on location I can glance at it instead of doing the multiplication in my head and getting it wrong under time pressure. Print it small enough to tape inside the camera bag lid.

title: Rebuild the monthly budget categories around how I actually spend
body: The current categories were set up years ago and no longer match anything — half of spending falls into 'miscellaneous' now, which tells me nothing useful. Redo the categories to match the last six months of real transactions. [[obsidian:Budget categories rework]]

title: Write the public landscape of emergence claims in language models
body: There are plenty of scattered posts on whether emergent abilities are real or a metric artefact, but no single place lays the arguments side by side. Draft an outline with the main papers, the strongest objection to each and the open questions, then publish it as a short page on my site.

title: Post the old driving licence back to the licensing agency
body: The replacement arrived weeks ago and the old paper counterpart should be returned.

title: Try Caps Lock as Escape and Control on the laptop keyboard
body: Remap it so a tap gives Escape and a hold gives Control, and give it *one full week* before judging.

title: Resolve the conflicting advice on caffeine and sleep into one protocol
body:
Every source says something different: cut off at noon, cut off eight hours before bed, or it does not matter if you fall asleep fine. I drink coffee until mid-afternoon and sleep badly often enough that I should stop shrugging and settle it.

Get a summary of four or five sources, ideally a sleep researcher, a sports-nutrition review and one sceptical piece, and put their claims side by side with the reasoning each gives. Where they disagree, work out whether it is about half-life, individual variation or just different definitions of good sleep. Then write *one protocol* with a specific cutoff time, and run it for three weeks while noting how long it takes me to fall asleep. If nothing changes, I get my afternoon coffee back with a clear conscience.

title: Understand difference-in-differences and the parallel trends assumption properly
body: I can write the two-by-two estimator but could not defend it to a sceptical reviewer. title: Learn how to be a well-behaved client of a rate-limited API

My scripts currently retry in a tight loop and then fall over, which is unkind to the provider and to my own results. Cover the following:

- A client-side token bucket so I stay under the limit instead of bouncing off it
- A cap on concurrent requests, and what to do when the queue grows faster than it drains

Call the surgery reception, *confirm the referral was actually submitted*, and ask for the reference number so I can chase the hospital directly if it stalls again. title: Read the main preference optimization papers in order
body:
The aim is to understand why DPO-style methods drift toward long, agreeable answers and what people do about it.

- Find a study of *sycophancy* induced by preference data

title: Build the nightly job that fetches, filters and digests new postings
body: Right now I check three feeds by hand and lose track of what I have already looked at. Make it a small scheduled pipeline: fetch new items once a night, drop anything that fails a keyword and age filter, store the survivors in SQLite keyed on URL so nothing appears twice, and write a plain-text digest of the day's new rows. Keep it boring — one script, one cron line, one table. The dedup key is the part to get right first; the filter rules can be wrong for a while and be fixed later. Notes on the schema and filter rules go in [[obsidian:Feed digest pipeline]].

title: Write the review for the rental agency before I forget
body: Be fair and specific: the *deposit was returned promptly* but the maintenance requests took weeks to get answered.

title: Give the agent a scoped tool set for the notes vault
body: Before I let an agent near my notes, define exactly which tools it gets. Start with read-only access to =~/notes/projects= and a single append-only tool for the inbox file. No delete, no shell. Run one task with only these and write down which missing permission I actually wanted.

title: Log this month's running total before the numbers blur
body: Add September's total to =running-log.org= before I lose track of which weeks I actually ran.

title: Understand streaming ASR properly, not just as a websocket that returns text
body:
Right now I treat streaming recognition as a black box that sends partial transcripts, and that is exactly why I cannot explain why some vendors feel faster than others. Work out what a chunked streaming model actually does: chunk size, lookahead, how partials get revised, and what the difference is between a partial and a final result.

Then pin down the metrics that matter and how each is measured: time to first partial, finalisation delay after end of speech, real-time factor, and word error rate on partials versus finals. Do the same for TTS, where time to first byte and the gap between audio chunks decide whether speech sounds continuous. Finish with a one-page comparison table for two ASR and two TTS providers, filled in from my own test calls rather than marketing pages, since claimed latency and measured latency are rarely the same number.

title: Form an actual opinion on where type annotations pay off
body: I keep adding types out of habit rather than judgment, and it shows in modules where the annotations are pure noise. Pick one messy module, add strict types end to end, and time how long it took versus what it actually caught before deciding this is worth doing everywhere.

title: Sort generated code into three piles by how much scrutiny
body: Reading every line of generated code does not scale, and reading none of it is how a subtle bug reaches the billing path. Sort my requests into three piles: throwaway scripts, glue code with clear tests, and anything touching money, auth or concurrency. The first gets run and skimmed, the second gets a type check plus a test I wrote /before/ seeing the code, and the third gets read line by line however green the tests are. Write the piles as a half-page note and try it for a week.

title: Reproduce the sparse autoencoder feature result on a small model
body: Everyone cites SAE features as evidence that interpretability works, and I have never run one end to end. Train a small one on a GPT-2 layer, check how many features are dead, and write up whatever comes out, including a negative result.

title: Go through the mechanism design lecture series properly, not in fragments
body: I have watched isolated lectures on Myerson and revenue equivalence and each time the thread is lost by the next sitting. Pick one full series, commit to two lectures a week, and do the problem sets for at least the first four weeks. The point is to get the virtual value and optimal reserve price argument to the stage where I can rebuild it on a whiteboard without notes. Keep a running sheet of results and the assumptions each one quietly needs, since interview follow-ups nearly always attack the assumptions rather than the result. After the single-item material is solid, move on to multi-slot position auctions and see where the clean theory starts to break.

title: Check whether my writing reads as *AI-generated* and whether it matters
body: A colleague hinted that my longer posts sound machine-written. Run three of them through a couple of detectors, and ask two friends to guess blind. Then decide if it changes how I write or if it is just noise, since detectors are known to be unreliable.

title: Drill numpy broadcasting shape rules until I stop guessing
body: Do twenty shape puzzles by hand first, and check each answer with *the rule of aligning shapes from the right*.

title: Survey recent click-through-rate model variants beyond DeepFM
body: List four or five, note what each changes about feature interactions, and which ones are worth a trial.

title: Add automatic backups to the personal finance scraper
body: The scraper overwrites =ledger.db= on every run, so one bad pull wipes out months of categorized transactions with no way back. I want a simple rotation instead: copy the database to a dated file before each run, keep the last thirty copies, and prune anything older automatically so the backup folder does not grow forever. The categorization rules took the longest to get right, and they live only inside that one file, which is exactly why losing it would be so annoying. Half an hour of scripting now beats redoing weeks of manual tagging later, so this should not keep getting bumped down the list.

title: Use the last failed training run to practise diagnosing overfitting
body: The run from last week had validation loss turning upward at epoch six while training accuracy kept climbing, and I just added dropout at random. Reopen the logs, plot both curves, and check for label leakage or near-duplicate images between splits before changing any hyperparameter. Write the diagnosis in two sentences.

title: Add paired bootstrap intervals to every model comparison I run
body: Comparing two models on the same prompts with raw accuracy alone is *not evidence of a real difference*, so report a paired interval every time.

title: Implement an LRU cache from scratch without checking editorial
body: I have seen this problem enough times to fake familiarity, which is exactly the trap. Close every tab, implement the *doubly-linked-list* version cold, then only afterward compare against the accepted solution for edge cases I missed.

title: Delete the sync conflict files piling up in the =Documents= folder
body: Sort them by date, diff each against the original, keep the newer one and remove the rest.

body: Want to see what changed between versions and why latent imagination beats pixel prediction. [[obsidian:World models reading list]]

body: One page with each loss, what it optimises, and where it disagrees with NDCG.

title: Rotate the password manager master password before it gets stale
body: It has been unchanged since I first set up the vault years ago, and that's the *single point of failure* for everything else. Generate a new long passphrase, update it in the app, and store the old one nowhere at all.

Pick up the reserved book from the library desk
Learn a structured checklist for monitoring an ML model in production
body: Accuracy dropping is the last thing to show up, and by then the damage is done. I want a framework that separates data drift, prediction drift and label-delayed performance so I know what to watch first. Take one existing model, fill in a table with =model-monitoring.org= as the file, one row per signal, and mark which ones are actually collected today.

title: Decide build, buy or managed for each layer of the stack
body: The small product has about five layers, namely inference, vector store, auth, observability and the eval harness, and I keep treating the choice as one global stance. It is not one. Inference is probably managed while the model is not my differentiator, but the eval harness is the one thing I should build, since it encodes what good means here.
