Then mark each layer build, buy or managed, and revisit only if one of those numbers moves.

title: Fit a partial pooling model for the twelve small regional stores
body: Each store has a few months of sales, so the per-store averages are noisy and the pooled average hides real differences. Fit a varying-intercept model on =stores_q3.csv= with a weakly informative prior on the group standard deviation, then plot raw means against the shrunken estimates. The stores with the fewest rows should move the most, and if they do not I have a bug or a prior that is too tight. Finish with one sentence a manager could act on, such as which store is genuinely above average and which just had a lucky month.

title: Turn the last onsite's system design notes into a reusable playbook
body: Strip out the company name and keep only the reusable tradeoff framework underneath.

title: Write down what each coding benchmark really tests and where it leaks

For each one, write a short entry covering the task format, how the answers are checked, whether the test suite is weak enough to pass wrong code, and whether the problems have been public long enough to be in training data. Mark HumanEval as saturated, and note that =LiveCodeBench= tries to dodge contamination by using date-stamped problems. Finish with one line on which I would trust for a model released this year.

title: Work out what a good ML postmortem looks like versus a normal one
Read a full regression summary line by line and diagnose the multicollinearity
body:
I can fit an OLS model in a line of code but the summary table still reads like a wall of numbers, and I skip straight to the R-squared and the p-values. Fix that by generating data where two predictors are strongly correlated, say correlation 0.95 with the true effect split between them, and fitting the model with both, then with one at a time.

Go through the output row by row and write next to each number what it is for: coefficient, standard error, t, p, the confidence interval, the condition number warning at the bottom, the Durbin-Watson and Omnibus lines. Then compute the variance inflation factors by hand and check they match the library. The thing to see is that *the overall fit stays excellent while individual coefficients become wide and unstable*, and that refitting on fresh samples flips their signs. Repeat five hundred times and plot the coefficient estimates as a scatter, which should show a long diagonal cloud. Save the annotated summary as a one-page note for later reference.

title: Deploy the sentiment model on kind and reach it through a Service

title: Curate a short list of photographers worth following
body: Half the appeal of good photography is seeing enough of it that my own eye gets better, and social media is the wrong tool for that because it optimises for engagement rather than for teaching me anything. Start a small file, =photo-inspo.org=, with five or six photographers whose composition or light I want to absorb, one line each on what specifically I'm learning from them, and revisit it monthly instead of letting a feed decide what I look at.

The book is free, runs in notebooks, and has PyTorch versions of everything, which is why I keep opening it and then only executing cells. That is not reading. The plan is to go through it in order, starting with the preliminaries and linear networks, and to write a short paragraph after each chapter in my own words before running anything. body: Right now I have three ways of pulling skills out of job descriptions and no evidence about which one is any good: a keyword match against a taxonomy, an embedding similarity approach, and an LLM prompt with a fixed output schema. body: Take the three-level Shape-style hierarchy from the old side project and rebuild it from small parts.

title: Read the paper on how language models learn facts and write down the takeaways
body:
There is a paper on how language models acquire factual knowledge during pretraining that I have seen quoted in several threads and never opened. Everyone paraphrases its conclusion in a slightly different way, which is a good sign that I should read the source instead of the paraphrases.

Read it once through for the shape of the argument, then a second time with a pen. What I want from it is *three or four takeaways I could state in one sentence each*: what the models learn quickly, what they forget, and how the frequency of a fact in the training data affects whether it sticks. Then note which claims rest on small controlled experiments and which rest on large-scale observations, because those deserve different levels of trust.

I do not need to reproduce the experiments or follow every appendix. If the methods section is dense, skim it and come back only if a conclusion looks surprising. Put the takeaways in a note the same day, while I still remember what the paper said versus what I assumed it said. Then check whether any of it should change how I think about fine-tuning a model on new facts, which is the practical reason I am reading it at all.

title: Decide build, buy or managed for each layer of the small stack

title: Work through a full Bayesian workflow with =PyMC= on one small dataset
body: Most of what I have read jumps straight to the posterior and skips the parts that actually catch mistakes. Pick a small dataset, maybe weekly sales for one shop, and go in order: choose weakly informative priors, run prior predictive checks, fit, look at R-hat, ESS and divergences, then posterior predictive checks. Only after that compare two candidate models. Write a one-line note at each stage on what would make me stop and change the model. The point is to have a checklist I trust, not another notebook that ends at a pretty trace plot.

title: Sort the broken blender return before the warranty ends
body: The blender started smelling of burning plastic on the second run, which is not a case for troubleshooting, just paperwork. title: Check the evidence for role prompting and multi-turn degradation
body: Two folk beliefs I keep repeating: that telling a model it is an expert improves answers, and that quality drops as a conversation gets longer. I would like to know what the studies actually measured. Collect two or three papers on persona or role prompting and see whether the gains hold across tasks or vanish on factual questions. Then find the work on multi-turn degradation and check whether it is about long context, underspecified instructions, or something else. Keep the notes in =prompting-evidence.org=, with one line each for the setup, the effect size and whether the result was replicated. If the evidence is thin, I should stop giving advice on it.

title: Write scaled dot-product attention from scratch before touching a library
body: I keep using attention layers as a black box and could not explain the scaling factor if asked. Implement it in plain PyTorch on tensors of shape =(B, H, T, D)=, add the causal mask, and check the output against the built-in function to within a small tolerance.

title: Practise probability puzzles by writing ten-line simulations
body:
Whenever a probability question shows up, I try to reason it out and then doubt the answer. Better habit: write the quick simulation first, look at the number, then work out why. Start with the classics, since they are famous for fooling intuition: Monty Hall, the birthday problem with 23 people, two children where one is a girl, and the expected number of rolls to see all six faces of a die. Each should be a short function, one million trials, printed with a rough standard error so I know how many digits to trust.

Keep them all in one notebook, one cell per puzzle, with a comment stating my gut guess before running. *The gap between the gut guess and the simulated answer is the useful output*, so keep a running tally of where I was wrong and what the pattern was. If conditional probability keeps tripping me up, that tells me what to study next. Once ten puzzles are done, pick three and derive the exact answer on paper to check the simulation.

title: Work out why exchangeability is all split conformal really needs
body: Write the coverage proof out by hand, rank argument and all. [[obsidian:Conformal prediction notes]]

title: Count push-ups from the webcam using pose estimation
body: Once the pose model runs on still images, the natural next exercise is a repetition counter. The idea is simple: track the elbow angle from shoulder, elbow and wrist keypoints, and count one rep each time it goes below a low threshold and then comes back above a high one. Two thresholds rather than one is what stops jitter from being counted as reps, a /hysteresis/ trick I should be able to explain afterwards. Test it on a recorded clip before going live, because debugging in front of a webcam while doing push-ups is a poor use of anyone's arms. Log the count and the clip length to the console first, and only then think about a UI.

title: Survey what a multi-turn agentic RL environment needs beyond a single prompt
body: Single-turn RLVR is easy to picture: prompt, completion, checker. An agentic loop adds tool calls, state that persists between turns, sandboxes that have to be reset, and rollouts of very different lengths that stall the batch. Read through how one open framework such as =verl= or OpenRLHF handles the rollout and learner split, and write down where the environment lives, how a trajectory is masked so tool outputs are not trained on, and what happens when a sandbox times out mid-episode.

title: Add micronutrient tracking to the nutrition app's meal log
body: Macros are logged but iron, B12 and vitamin D are invisible, which matters since I eat mostly plant-based. Extend the meal schema with a micronutrient table and pull values from a food database on entry. [[obsidian:Nutrition tracking]]

title: Arrange the cat-sitter for the week we're away in October
Learn how codebooks in a VQ-VAE go wrong and collapse
body: I have used the term codebook collapse without being able to explain it properly. Read the original VQ-VAE paper, then train a tiny one on MNIST and log how many codes are actually used per epoch, trying a dead-code reset to see the difference.

title: Book a dentist that will actually take a panoramic X-ray
body: The last panoramic X-ray was years ago, before the wisdom teeth started shifting, and the gum line on the lower left has receded enough that I notice it flossing. General checkups keep skipping the imaging because nothing actually hurts. Book with =Riverside Dental= and specifically ask for an OPG rather than the usual four bitewings — it shows bone loss and impacted roots, not just cavities between teeth.

title: Derive ridge and lasso as MAP estimates under Gaussian and Laplace priors
body: Do it on paper once, start to finish, so the penalty-prior link is something I can reproduce.

title: Tighten the CV's whitespace so it reads at a glance
body: Cut the margins and line spacing so the whole thing fits without feeling cramped.

title: Write a two-layer MLP with manual backprop in plain NumPy
body: No autograd, no trainer, just gradients derived on paper and checked numerically.

title: Work out if compression bags are worth the suitcase space
body: Every trip ends with the case half-unpacked on the floor because nothing keeps its shape once it's opened, and cubes never survive past the first repack. Compression bags might actually solve the volume problem for the bulky stuff — jackets and towels — rather than the tidiness problem cubes solve. *The real question is whether the extra folding time is worth it for a five-day trip*, not whether they work at all. Buy one set, test on the next weekend trip before committing to a full set.

title: Compare in-batch, hard and mined negatives for embedding models
body: Random in-batch negatives are cheap but easy, hard negatives help until they turn out to be false negatives. Read two papers on negative mining for dense retrieval and write down what each does about false negatives. The aim is a rule of thumb for picking a strategy, not a survey.

title: Do the Sutton and Barto exercises for chapter =3=
body: I read the RL book passively last year and remember almost none of the maths. Redo the MDP chapter with pen and paper, do the exercises that have no published solutions first, and only then look up answers.

title: Compare three dentists on price and *recall interval* before booking
body: Ring three local practices, ask the price of a scale and polish and how they set check-up intervals, then pick one.

title: Turn the one-company interview playbook into a generic one
body: Strip out the product names and keep the =four-round= structure, so the same file works for the next loop.

title: Prepare talking points for the promotion conversation early
body: Waiting until the manager asks 'so what do you want next' means answering on the spot with whatever comes to mind, which is never the strongest version of the case. Write out the target level, three pieces of evidence for each stated expectation, and the timeline that feels realistic, then read it back a week later once the initial enthusiasm has worn off. Bring the written version to the one-to-one instead of trying to reconstruct it live, and treat any pushback as information about which piece of evidence needs to be stronger, not as a verdict to accept quietly.

title: Get =ollama= running locally and see what fits in 16 GB
body: I keep paying for API calls on experiments that a small local model could handle. Install the runtime, pull one 7B and one 3B quantised model, and note tokens per second and memory use for each in a scratch file so I know the real ceiling of this machine.

title: Generate synthetic queries for a retriever with no labelled data
body: Prompt an LLM for three questions per document chunk, filter by round-trip retrieval, then train on the survivors.

title: Skim the SimCLR paper again for the negatives-versus-batch-size argument
body:
Re-read the section tying batch size to =InfoNCE= quality, with notes on why more negatives helped.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05709

title: Check passport expiry before booking anything for the autumn trip
body:
Six months validity is the usual rule and mine is cutting it close this year.
https://www.gov.uk/renew-adult-passport

title: Split my interviewer questions into lists by their role
Write down what idempotency keys should look like for agent tool calls
body: Every side-effecting tool needs a key derived from run and step, not a random one. [[obsidian:Idempotency notes for agent tools]]

title: Find out where the FP8 formats break down
body: Compare E4M3 and E5M2 ranges and note that *per-tensor scaling* is what keeps activations from saturating.

title: Work out when threads beat processes for my preprocessing scripts
body: Time the same tokenising job under threads, processes and plain serial before deciding anything.

title: Write the per-company routine that predicts likely design prompts
Fine-tune a pretrained ViT on the leaf disease photos and read the curves
body: Training from scratch on a few thousand images taught me nothing except how fast a small network memorises. Take a pretrained backbone from timm, freeze it for two epochs, then unfreeze, and plot train against validation loss each run. *The gap between the two curves is the thing to learn to read*, since it separates overfitting from a labelling problem in the data.

title: Try a split or ergonomic keyboard layout trial for *two weeks*
body: Pick one alternative layout, commit to it long enough to judge, and note wrist strain daily.

title: Try target encoding against hashing on one high-cardinality column
body: Pick a user-id-like feature and compare both on the same held-out split.

title: Check where my chess rating actually stands this year
body: Look up the rating history on =chess.com= before claiming I've improved without evidence.

title: Turn the half-knitted scarf into something actually finished
body: The scarf has sat at the same length since spring because starting something new is more fun than finishing something old. Pick it back up tonight, knit two rows before doing anything else, and keep it visible on the sofa arm as a nudge.

title: Write a short review of The Selfish Gene in my own words
body: I read it years ago and only remember the slogan, so a review is a good way to find out what stuck. Reread the first and last chapters, write half a page, and *mark the two ideas I actually disagree with* instead of nodding along to all of it.

title: Write down the actual process for disputing the council tax band
body:
The house next door is in a lower band despite being nearly identical in size, and I've been meaning to challenge ours for over a year without ever finding the actual procedure. It's not a single form — first check the banding on the valuation office website, then look at comparable properties on the same street, and only then submit a formal challenge with evidence attached rather than just a complaint.

Last time I tried this from memory and gave up after twenty minutes because I couldn't remember which site handles appeals versus which one handles the original valuation. Write the steps down properly this time: gather at least four comparable addresses with their bands, note the valuation date the whole street was assessed against, and keep a copy of everything submitted in case it needs escalating to a tribunal. Set a reminder to follow up if there's no response within eight weeks, since these things tend to go quiet without a nudge.

title: Browse sparse autoencoder features in a small model with =Neuronpedia=
body: Pick ten features, read their top activating examples, and note which look genuinely monosemantic.

title: Learn how postings lists get compressed and why it makes queries faster
body: The claim that smaller indexes are also faster still sounds backwards to me, so I want to see it properly. Start with delta encoding of document IDs, then variable-byte, then the block-based schemes like PForDelta and Elias-Fano, and note what each one costs in decode speed and what it gives in space. Then look at skip pointers and how block-max metadata lets WAND or MaxScore skip whole blocks without decoding them. Finish by writing a toy postings list in Python, compressing it two ways and timing intersections on a few thousand terms.

title: Learn the essential keyboard shortcuts for the new laptop
body:
*Stop reaching for the mouse for basic window and tab switching* and drill the shortcuts weekly.
https://support.apple.com/en-us/102650

title: Buy a small waterproof rechargeable headlamp for trips
Recreate the reference clip shot for shot with the =X-T30=
body: Match framing, lens length and cut timing for the first ten shots, then list where mine differs most from the original.

title: Compare provider batch APIs against a self-run queue for overnight jobs
body: Decide at what volume the *discounted batch endpoint* stops beating my own queue on a rented GPU.

title: Work through the OWASP Top 10 as bug classes, not a checklist
body:
I can recite the list and still could not spot most of it in a pull request, which means I know the names and not the mechanisms. Take each category down to the underlying flaw: broken access control is a missing ownership check, injection is data crossing into code, and so on. For every one, write a five-line vulnerable snippet, then the fix, then how a test would catch it. Do them two per week with a deliberately vulnerable practice app, and stop treating the year-stamped ranking as the thing to memorise. The classes outlast the list.

https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/

title: Buy my niece a proper tenth birthday present this time
body: Last year's gift was a rushed card-shop purchase bought on the way over, and it showed. Ask her mother for size and interests now, order online with time to spare. [[obsidian:Family gift ideas]]

title: Add a =CronJob= that logs drift metrics for the deployed model
body: Without a scheduled check I only learn the model has drifted when someone complains. Write a Kubernetes CronJob that computes a simple input drift score daily and writes it to a table, then run it once by hand first.

title: Service the lawnmower before it sits idle all winter long
body: Running it dry with old fuel left in the tank is exactly what seized the last one over winter storage. Drain the tank, run the carburetor dry, change the oil, and sharpen the blade before it goes into the shed for the season.

title: Work out how =top-k= gating picks experts per token
body: Read the Shazeer sparse gating paper and write the softmax-then-top-k steps in my own words.

title: Read the Chinchilla paper and redo its compute-optimal split by hand
body: The point is to see how a fixed compute budget divides between parameters and tokens.

title: Ask for a full lipid panel and Lp(a) test once
body: Lipoprotein(a) is largely genetic, does not change with diet, and only needs measuring *once in a lifetime* to be informative. With my father's early heart trouble, that is worth knowing. Ring the GP, ask for a lipid panel plus Lp(a), and book the fasting slot.

title: Buy a small quick-charge power bank for flights
body: Carry-on power banks need to be under 100 Wh, so check the rating before buying.

title: Pick one daily Spanish app and stop shopping for a better one
body: Duolingo's streak is shallow, but the habit matters more than the method, so accept the flaw and start.

title: Learn what a query understanding layer should output before retrieval
body: We pass the raw string straight to the index, which throws away intent, language, entities and filters that could be extracted first. List the fields a query understanding step could emit, such as intent class, detected entities and corrected text, and mark which ones we could add cheaply this quarter.

title: Find out how specification gaming gets detected during training
body: Look for cases where the /proxy reward rose/ while the true objective quietly fell, and what monitoring caught it.

title: Apply SHAP to a gradient-boosted model on the =adult= census data
body: Check that the attributions sum to the prediction minus the baseline, then compare with plain feature importance.

title: Sort out the blood pressure prescription before it runs out
body: Three days of pills left and the pharmacy needs at least a week to process a repeat through the surgery, which I keep forgetting until I'm counting tablets on a Sunday night. Ring the surgery in the morning, confirm the dose hasn't changed since the last review, and ask them to send the request straight to the usual pharmacy rather than leaving it for me to collect and drop off in person like last time.

title: Hook the nutrition app up to the smart scale
body: The scale already records weight and body fat in its own app, and I retype the number into mine every morning, when I remember. Check first whether the scale exports through a health platform or only through its own cloud, because that decides the whole approach. If there is an export, write a small importer that reads it once a day and stores weight with a timestamp, ignoring duplicates. If there is not, a manual CSV import is acceptable for now. Do not attempt anything with body fat percentages until I have looked at how noisy they are from day to day.

title: Add a =BatchNorm= versus LayerNorm run to the small net
body: Same net, same seed, only the normalization changed; plot loss and gradient norm together.

title: Write a short checklist of what I look for in code review
body: Keep it to one page and stick it in the team notes.

title: Set up seeding and deterministic training and record what still drifts
body:
Goal is a training script where the same seed gives the same curve on the same machine, and a written list of the reasons it will not do so elsewhere. Seed Python, NumPy and torch, set the cuBLAS workspace variable, turn on deterministic algorithms, and make the dataloader workers derive their seeds from the base seed instead of the clock.

Then run the same config twice and diff the loss logs line by line. I expect the first divergence to come from something like an atomic-add kernel or a nondeterministic op in the environment, not from my own code, and the point of the exercise is to find which. Put the result in =repro-notes.org= with the exact versions of torch, CUDA and the driver next to it, because bitwise equality across hardware or library versions is not something I should promise anyone, including myself. If the runs are identical for 1000 steps but diverge after that, note the step count rather than calling it fixed.

title: Build a design-doc template library sorted by problem archetype
body: Most design prompts fall into a handful of shapes: ranking a feed, retrieval plus rerank, classification with a cost of error, anomaly detection, and batch versus online scoring. Write one template per archetype with the same skeleton: goal, constraints, data, baseline, model, evaluation, rollout, failure modes. Each template should fit on a single page and carry one worked example, so that when a new prompt arrives I pick the nearest archetype and adapt rather than starting from a blank page. Keep the archetype list short and add a new one only when two real prompts refuse to fit.

title: Watch Hans Rosling's bubble chart talk again with notes this time
body: I've watched it twice and never written anything down, which defeats the point. Watch it once more, pause every time the axes change, and note the three tricks he uses to make four variables readable at once.

title: Derive why *ridge* and lasso are just Gaussian and Laplace priors
body:
Do the MAP algebra once by hand so the penalty-prior link stops being a slogan.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regularized_least_squares

title: Train a small VAE on MNIST and look at the blur
body: Latent size =2= first, so the digit manifold can be plotted directly.

title: Compare free GPU notebook tiers against paid hourly rentals
body: Write down session limits, disk persistence and queue times for each before committing any money.

title: Work through the Google SRE book chapters on monitoring
body: I keep building dashboards from whatever metrics are easy to export, and then nobody looks at them. The monitoring chapters give a vocabulary for what to alert on and why. Read the four golden signals chapter and the one on alerting philosophy, then compare against what we currently page on.

title: Work out where the takeaway money actually goes each month
body: The card statement shows another string of small takeaway orders that add up to more than the grocery bill, and I only notice when the balance surprises me. Pull the last three months into the spreadsheet and total by category before changing anything.

title: Find out where gensim and NLTK stand today and what replaced them
Test *in-body* stabilisation against a tripod at export size
body: Handheld with IBIS on feels steadier through the viewfinder, but that is not the same as sharper in the file. Shoot the same low-light scene three ways: tripod, IBIS off handheld, IBIS on handheld, all at the same shutter speed, then export each to 2000px wide and view at actual pixels on the laptop screen only. If the IBIS shot cannot be told apart from the tripod shot at that size, stop worrying about it for anything I post online.

title: Explain nDCG properly instead of half-remembering the formula
body: I can say *nDCG* exists but not derive it from first principles.

title: Work through stationarity and differencing on a real monthly series
body: Every forecasting tutorial assumes I know what stationary means and I only half do. Take one monthly series, run an ADF test, difference it, and plot the ACF before and after. *The goal is to see why differencing changes what the model can learn,* not to memorise the test.

title: Work through the statistical learning course, Python edition first, R later
Work through the sliding window problems on the Blind 75 list
body:
Do the three window ones first, and note which needed a hint; =Minimum Window Substring= is the likely culprit.
https://neetcode.io/practice

title: Find out why binary quantization needs rescoring more than int8 does
body: Write a two-line explanation and check it against a recall run.

title: Set up currency and cash before the trip to Osaka
body: Airport exchange counters are always the worst rate, and I fall for the convenience every time I forget to plan ahead. *Order the currency online this week instead of at the gate.* Keep a cash buffer and put the rest on the no-fee card.

title: Design structured logging and telemetry for an LLM product
body:
Plain text logs are fine for a web handler and nearly useless for an LLM feature, where the interesting question is always "what exactly did the model see and say, and what did it cost?" Without a schema decided up front, every incident turns into grepping free text and guessing which prompt version was live.

Sketch the event schema first, on paper, before touching any library. Each request should carry a trace id, prompt template name and version, model name and pinned version, token counts in and out, latency split into queue, retrieval and generation, tool calls with their outcomes, and a coarse outcome label such as answered, refused, or fell back. *The key decision is what to redact or hash at write time, because prompts contain user data and you cannot un-log it later.* Then look at how OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions name these fields so I am not inventing a private vocabulary, and decide what gets sampled versus kept in full. Deliverable: a one-page schema plus a list of the five dashboard questions it must answer on a bad night, such as which prompt version started the refusal spike.
https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/

title: Derive ridge and lasso as MAP estimates under Gaussian and Laplace priors
body: Two short derivations on paper, and the point is that *the penalty is the negative log prior* rather than a trick.

title: Skim the FlashAttention paper for the memory-traffic argument
body:
Focus on the IO-complexity section, and the tiling figure with =SRAM= sizes.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.14135

title: Compare paged KV cache allocation with naive per-request preallocation
body: Work out the memory waste numbers from the vLLM paper. [[obsidian:LLM serving notes]]

title: Order a matching keycap set for the new switches
body: The stock keycaps look mismatched now that half the switches are new.

title: Note which layers are most sensitive to *low-bit* quantization
body: Look up why the embedding and output layers are often kept at higher precision.

title: Browse sparse autoencoder features in a small model with =SAELens=
body: Load one pretrained SAE and read the top-activating examples for twenty features.

title: Compare three local GP practices before switching from the current one
body:
The current GP practice takes three weeks for a routine appointment, so it's worth comparing alternatives properly instead of just switching to whichever is closest.
- Call each practice and ask for the actual wait time for a non-urgent slot
- Check the CQC rating and read the last inspection report, not just the star score
- Compare whether blood tests are done on-site or require a separate booking
- *Weigh convenience against quality* before registering anywhere new

title: Measure threads against processes on a CPU-bound Python job
body: Time the same hash-heavy function under threading and multiprocessing and write down which wins.

title: Set custom buttons and memory recall for street versus tripod work
body: Two memory banks now: one for handheld street, one for tripod landscapes. [[obsidian:Camera custom settings]]

title: Compare Parquet and ORC on a sample table for size and scan speed
body: Same table, both formats, note file size and time to read three columns.

title: Write a design-doc template for each problem archetype
body: Ranking, retrieval, feed, fraud and batch pipeline each need their own skeleton. [[obsidian:Design Doc Templates]]

title: Learn what a good CLI tool schema looks like for agents
body: Read a few public tool-schema examples and note what makes parameter names and error messages easy for a model to use.

title: Build a nightly job that fetches new papers and mails a digest
body: Fetch, keyword-filter, store in SQLite, then send one short digest each morning instead of a feed I never open.

title: Tear down every leftover cloud resource from the last experiments
Chase the dental reimbursement that never actually came through
body:
The insurer's portal still shows the claim as processed, but the money never landed in the account, and it has now been long enough that I have stopped trusting the timeline they gave me. This is the second time this year a claim has gone quiet after the initial confirmation email, and both times it turned out to be a missing reference number on their end rather than anything wrong with the paperwork I sent.

Call during their stated quiet hours rather than emailing again, since the last email sat unanswered for two weeks, and ask specifically for the claim reference and the payment batch date rather than a general status update. If they cannot give an actual date, ask them to email written confirmation of the amount and expected payment window, because a phone reassurance with nothing in writing is exactly what happened last time before it dragged on for another month. Keep a note of who I spoke to and when, and if there is no payment within ten working days after that call, escalate to a formal complaint rather than calling a third time and getting the same non-answer.

title: Explore the Seaborn and Plotly galleries for training diagnostics
body: Pick three plot types, like ridge plots for activations, that I would actually reuse in every experiment.

title: Take the implicit bias test cold before reading the book
body: Do it /before/ opening the book, so the result isn't primed by the chapter.

title: Decide the email setup: one main address plus aliases
body:
Right now I have four addresses and no rule for which one goes where. Before migrating anything I need to settle the architecture: one paid provider with a custom domain, or stay free and lean on plus-addressing? Aliases per category (shopping, travel, newsletters) would make later unsubscribing trivial and let me see who leaks my address. Pick the provider, write the alias scheme in three lines, and only then start moving accounts, once, in a single pass instead of drifting.
[[obsidian:Email Architecture Decision]]

title: Book the train tickets before the early fare tier closes
body: The cheap advance fares vanish about six weeks out, so today is the day.

title: Start Bayesian Methods for Hackers with PyMC open beside it
body: I read statistics as prose and it never sticks; a book that gets to the posterior by computing it fits me better. Set up a fresh environment, run the first two chapters as notebooks, and change every prior once to see what moves. Keep a list of the sampler warnings I do not understand yet.

title: Read a book chapter bridging BM25 and neural retrieval
body: Aim to understand where sparse and dense scores complement each other before building a hybrid.

title: Learn GCN, GraphSAGE and GAT as three aggregation choices
body:
Same message-passing skeleton, but the aggregator decides what the model can /distinguish/. Write each update rule side by side.
https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02907

title: Work out why two-way fixed effects breaks with staggered treatment timing
body: Read the Goodman-Bacon decomposition and note where already-treated units end up as *bad controls* in the comparison.

title: Chase the visa application that has gone quiet for weeks
body: Submitted the renewal application over six weeks ago and the tracking portal still shows the same status it did on day one, with no email and no reference to anything changing. Before assuming it's just slow, call the processing centre directly, have the application number and payment reference ready, and ask specifically whether anything is missing from the file rather than just when it will be done. If travel dates are close, it's worth asking about expedited processing too, since that option tends to disappear once a trip gets nearer.

title: Build a location-scouting routine, then compare it with the result
body:
Good light at a location is mostly a matter of homework, and I have been doing the homework in my head, which means I forget it by the time I arrive. Make a short template, one entry per place: where the sun will be at the hour I plan to be there, what the weather forecast says for that day, and the shot I expect to get, described in a sentence or a rough sketch.

The useful step is the last one. After the outing, put the actual frame next to the prediction and write two lines on what differed: the light came from another angle, the cloud did something unexpected, the composition I imagined was blocked by a fence. After five or six entries I should see which part of my planning is consistently wrong, and that is the part to fix. Start with one place I already know well, so the comparison is about the method and not about an unfamiliar spot.

title: Fit a scaling law on three small model sizes and see what breaks
body: Everyone quotes power-law exponents, but I have never fitted one myself and I suspect the error bars would be embarrassing. Train three tiny models on =tinyshakespeare=, fit loss against parameters with an irreducible term, and report the fit with a bootstrap interval, not a single line.

title: Do a proper pass through old email attachments and downloads
body:
The downloads folder has become a dumping ground for every PDF, installer, and screenshot from the last three years, and the email account is worse — attachments going back a decade that I will never open again but that are quietly eating storage quota. Neither problem is urgent on its own, which is exactly why it has been ignored this long.

Start with the folder, since it is the smaller job: sort by size, delete anything obviously disposable like old installers, and move anything worth keeping into a proper archive rather than leaving it loose. For email, search by attachment size rather than trying to go through messages one at a time, and work through the largest first. One folder, =Receipts-2019=, alone accounts for several hundred megabytes of scanned paperwork that could just as easily live as a single zipped file elsewhere. Budget an evening for this rather than trying to do it in a spare ten minutes, because half-finished cleanups just create a second mess on top of the first one.

title: Refresh Unix pipelines with awk, sed and xargs drills
body: Redo the log-wrangling exercises without reaching for Python this time. [[obsidian:Shell One-Liners Cheatsheet]]

title: Build an actual pedalboard instead of the drawer of pedals
body: The pedals live in a drawer, tangled, and every practice session starts with five minutes of untangling cables before I've played a note. That five minutes is enough friction that I skip practice more often than I'd like to admit. Buy a cheap board and a strip of velcro, lay out the signal chain on paper first, then mount and label each cable so a pedal can be swapped without unplugging the whole chain. Do it in one evening, not across three weekends, or it will join the guitar case as another unfinished intention.

title: Order replacement switches for the custom keyboard
body: Six or seven keys on the board have started to chatter, mostly the space bar neighbours and one of the vowels, which makes typing a minor annoyance every day. Count how many I actually need, add a few extra as spares, and make sure they match the existing type and the pin style, since the board is hot-swappable and I don't want to solder. Also pick up a switch puller if the old one is still missing. Order in one go so I don't pay shipping twice. Switch model, lube notes and the layout are in [[obsidian:Keyboard build log]].

title: Trace one recommender paper from the reading list into a small experiment
body: Reading alone does not stick for me. Choose one paper on two-tower retrieval, then reproduce its main *baseline comparison* on a small public dataset like MovieLens, even if the numbers are lower than reported. Note the gap and guess at reasons.

title: Compare response-level, on-policy and self-distillation and when each wins
body: The choice hinges on whether the student's *own mistakes* show up in the training data.

title: Wrap the existing churn classifier in split conformal prediction sets
body: Hold out =calib.parquet= as the calibration set and check empirical coverage at alpha 0.1.

title: Consider a small air purifier for long train journeys
body: Hotel air always feels stale, so a compact purifier might be worth packing.

title: Work out how filtered vector search hurts recall and latency
body: Test a tight filter against a =HNSW= index at 1% selectivity and write down what happens to recall.

title: Write down the conditions under which I would actually leave this job
body: Right now "I'll know when it's time" is the whole policy, which means I will rationalise anything. Write four or five explicit criteria in =leave-criteria.org=, each with a threshold, and set a quarterly reminder to check them honestly.

title: Work through Build a Large Language Model From Scratch
body: Do one chapter per week and keep the notebooks running, not just read.

title: Work out when rebase is right and when merge is
body: Pick a rule for feature branches and write it in one paragraph.

title: Rebuild the two-pointer pattern from scratch on paper
body: I keep reaching for a two-pointer solution without proving termination, and it shows in interviews when asked why it stops. Redo five classic problems by hand, writing the loop invariant before any code, then implement without looking back.

title: Renew the cycling club membership through the discount portal
body:
The member-only renewal link takes about a tenner off, but only if I go through =the members' area=, not the main site.
https://www.cyclinguk.org

title: Rewrite the three interview stories using the STAR structure
body:
Turn the vague war stories into situation, task, action, result before the next round.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Situation,_task,_action,_result

title: Learn how to behave as a client of a rate-limited API
body: My scripts currently retry in a tight loop and get throttled harder each time. Read up on exponential backoff with jitter, honouring the retry-after header, and a client-side token bucket, then rewrite the one wrapper all my scripts share so it queues instead of hammering.

title: Write up a one-page checklist for putting a ranking model into production
body: Include feature parity between training and serving, and *log the scores* on live traffic for later comparison.

title: Pay the final gas and electric bill to the old supplier
body: The switch went through last month and the old supplier has now issued a closing statement. Pay it by bank transfer before the due date, quoting the account number on the letter, so it doesn't turn into a debt-collection letter later.

title: Pick one encryption policy and finally apply it everywhere
body: Cold drives are encrypted, travel drives are not, and cloud is a coin flip — *fix that with one rule*.

title: Read the main scaling-law papers and note where the power law bends
body:
Aim is a one-page summary, not a reading list.
- Kaplan et al. and the Chinchilla revision: what changed in the compute-optimal split between parameters and tokens
- Whether the same exponents show up for vision or recommendation models, or only for language
- *Where the fit breaks down*: data repetition, irreducible loss floors and the small-scale extrapolation problem

title: Book the annual eye test before the old glasses give up
body: The *headaches* only started once I stopped wearing them for reading.

title: Build a tiny labelled fixture set to score two retrievers in the repo
body: Right now I compare the retrievers by feel, which does not survive a code review. Hand-label 40 queries with relevant documents, commit them as fixtures, and write one script that prints recall@10 and MRR for both methods.

title: Put auth, per-tenant limits and rate limiting in front of the inference endpoint
Derive the policy gradient theorem by hand, sourcing every step
body: Every write-up I have read jumps from the gradient of the expected return to the neat expectation of grad log pi times return, and I nod along without being able to redo it. Do it on paper from scratch: write the trajectory probability, move the gradient inside the sum, apply the log-derivative trick, then show the transition dynamics drop out because they do not depend on theta. Next to each line note which identity or assumption it uses. Then do the reward-to-go step separately, since that is where causality gets quietly slipped in. If any line cannot be justified in a sentence, that is the gap to chase, not something to skip.

title: Work through the SIGIR tutorial on unbiased learning to rank
body: The tutorial slides are the fastest route to the propensity-weighting story without reading ten papers in the wrong order. Go through it once with the notebook open, and note where the click model assumptions are actually stated versus hidden. [[obsidian:Unbiased LTR reading list]]

title: Learn how phone calls reach a voice agent
body: Telephony is the part I understand least, and it hides real latency and audio quality limits. Read up on SIP, PSTN trunks and 8 kHz mu-law audio, then sketch the path of one inbound call into my agent and mark each hop.

title: Study why LSTMs lost to transformers, and what it teaches
body:
Parallel training, not accuracy alone, decided it; also check what state-space models revive.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_short-term_memory

title: Try slow practice from The Musician's Way on one hard bar
body: The left-hand shift in bar nine of the etude still breaks every run. Apply the book's slow-then-gradual-speedup method for ten minutes a day for a week and log the metronome marking each time. [[obsidian:Practice Log Guitar]]

title: Rehearse the promotion pitch until it sounds like fact
body: *Say the strongest evidence first*, then let the rest support it.

title: Plan one deliberate Milky Way shot before autumn ends
body:
Only ever caught stars by accident, never once planned the core position or the site on purpose. Do it properly, before the season closes for the year.
- Pick a Bortle class three or darker site within two hours' drive
- Check the core's rise time and azimuth for the chosen date
- Bring a headlamp with a red mode and spare batteries
[[obsidian:Night sky photography]]

title: Check which browser extensions are actually still needed
Book the dilated eye exam I keep postponing
body: Glaucoma is silent early, so a dilated check is the /only/ way to catch it; ring the optician this week.

title: Pick one habit from Atomic Habits and *test it for ten days*
body: Choose the one that costs nothing to try, log it daily, then decide.

title: Actually take the Sunday rest day off from everything
body: Sunday is a *rest day*, not a day for an easy jog that turns into a tempo run.

title: Decide whether lock-free queues and Bayesian optimization are worth it
body: I keep reaching for clever techniques because they are interesting, and lock-free queues are the worst offender. Before building one, write down what the mutex version costs at the contention I actually have: measure it with a realistic thread count and see whether the lock even shows up in a profile. If it is under a few percent of runtime, the answer is no and the note says so. Do the same exercise for Bayesian optimization on the tuning job: count evaluations, how long each takes, and whether a plain random search with the same budget gets within noise of the best result.

title: Reduce food waste with a proper *use-first* shelf
body:
Things go off at the back of the fridge because nothing marks them as urgent.
- Put a shelf for anything expiring within three days
- Move leftovers there first thing after cooking
- Check it before deciding what to cook next

title: Measure tokenizer fertility on my target languages before picking a model
body: Every language-learning idea I have involves text that is not English, and I keep assuming the tokenizer handles it fine. It may not: a language that splits into three times as many tokens costs three times as much and fits a third of the context. Take 500 sentences each of Polish, Turkish and Thai, count tokens per word for two or three tokenizers, and put the numbers in a small table in =fertility.csv=. Then read up on training a domain tokenizer, and decide whether it is ever worth it over just switching models. Fertility is a measurement; my hunch about which language is worst is not.

title: Settle which status codes my little API should actually return
body: Mine returns 200 for nearly everything, including errors, which leaves clients guessing. Read the status code sections of RFC 9110, then rewrite the handlers in the side project so that 201, 204, 404, 409 and 422 each mean one specific thing.

title: Book: Alan Turing: The Enigma by Andrew Hodges
body:
Long, but the standard biography and the mathematics is not skipped over. Read it a hundred pages at a time on trains, not in one push.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Turing:_The_Enigma

title: Log micronutrients not just calories in the tracker
body: Calories alone hide the iron and B12 gaps that actually matter to me.

title: Compute MFU for our last training run without flattering it
body: The dashboard shows high GPU utilization while the run is plainly slow, which is the classic illusion: the metric only says a kernel was resident, not that the tensor cores were busy. Count the model FLOPs per token honestly, exclude recomputation, divide by peak dense throughput, and write down the real percentage.

title: Build a template library keyed to system design archetypes
body: Every design interview reduces to the same handful of shapes — feed ranking, notification fanout, /search/ — so a template per archetype beats starting blank each time; draft the feed-ranking template first since it recurs most.

title: Try synthetic control on the regional pricing change
body: The price change went live in one region only, so a simple before-and-after comparison will mix in seasonality and everything else that happened that quarter. Build a donor pool from the untouched regions, fit weights on the pre-period so the synthetic region tracks the real one closely, then compare the post-period gap. Run placebo fits on each donor region and see whether the real gap stands out from those. If pre-period fit is poor, say so and stop rather than forcing a story out of it.

title: Fix one consistent name per figure using the glossary book
body: Pick the glossary's term for each figure and rename the clashing notes to match. [[obsidian:Tango Figure Glossary Naming]]

body: Do it in plain PyTorch with an explicit mask and check shapes against the built-in version. [[obsidian:Transformer internals notes]]

body: Train on ten keywords, then read the confusion matrix. [[obsidian:Speech Commands Baseline Notes]]

Write the sparse versus dense versus multi-vector comparison for the design doc
body: The team keeps arguing from anecdotes, and a table would end it. Compare BM25-style sparse, single-vector dense and ColBERT-style multi-vector on index size, latency, exact-match behaviour and out-of-domain robustness, then add a recommendation paragraph with the caveats stated plainly.

title: Request the two days off around the public holiday
body: Submit the time-off request early since that week always fills up fast.

body: The current doc is basically *one company's* loop with names filed off.

body: Cashback lands about sixty days after switching; check status in [[obsidian:Household bills 2026]].

Pick the flaky deploy pipeline and use one technique properly, then write down what it did or did not produce.

body: Nobody organizes it if I don't start the thread first. [[obsidian:Family reunion planning]]

title: Design the rebuild and reindex strategy for the vector index
body: Embedding model upgrades mean the whole vector index has to be rebuilt, and right now I have no plan for doing that without hurting search quality or freezing writes. Write down the approach: build the new index in parallel under a versioned name such as =docs_v2=, dual-write new documents to both, backfill in batches with a throttle, compare recall and latency on a fixed query set, then flip the alias and keep the old index for a week for rollback. Also note the storage and compute cost of holding two copies, since that is the part managers will ask about first.

title: Work through censoring properly before touching a survival library
body: I keep using the words right-censored and time-to-event without being able to say why dropping censored rows biases the answer. Write a tiny simulation where some subjects are lost before the event, compute the naive mean time and the Kaplan-Meier estimate, and see how far apart they are.

title: Work out why recall matters more early in the cascade
body: An early stage cannot recover an item it has already dropped, so it is judged on /recall at a cutoff/ rather than precision. Check this against a real two-stage example and write the one-line metric for each stage next to the candidate counts.

title: Write a reference design for serving a ranker via ONNX
body: Sketch the export, versioning and runtime path for a tree-based ranker. [[obsidian:Ranking serving reference design]]

title: Plot the PPO clipped objective against the ratio for both advantage signs
body: Two panels, epsilon 0.2, and mark where the gradient goes to zero on each side.

title: Read the composition chapter of the photography book and shoot one exercise
body: I own a book on how to see like a photographer that I have only ever skimmed for the pictures. Read just the chapter on framing and negative space, and pick one idea from it. Then a small exercise: walk the same street for thirty minutes with a single prime lens and take twelve frames that use only that idea. Delete all but three, and write one line on each about why it works or does not. No gear shopping until that is done.

title: Set up a modern Python project with one config file, linter and formatter
body: Everything in a single pyproject, with ruff doing both jobs and nothing else to keep in sync.

title: Set up a two-stage search with quantized scan and rescoring
body: Full-precision vectors in memory are what make the current index expensive, and I keep reading that a compressed first pass plus a small rescore recovers most of the recall. Take one embedding set of about a million vectors, build a binary or int8 scan that returns the top few hundred candidates, then rescore those with the original floats. Measure recall at 10 against brute force for three oversampling factors, and note memory and query time next to each. The oversampling factor is the knob I do not yet have a feel for, so the table matters more than any single number.

title: Write a one-page results summary to give my manager before calibration
body:
Calibration happens in a room I am not in, so whatever my manager says about me is limited to what they remember and what I have made easy to repeat. Right now that is probably the last six weeks and one incident. A one-page summary handed over ahead of time fixes the recency problem, and it also forces me to find out whether I can actually state my year in five sentences.

Structure it as four or five results, each with the same three parts: what the problem was, what I did specifically (not what the team did), and the evidence, meaning a number, a design doc, a before-and-after, or a person who would confirm it. Leave out effort and busyness entirely; nobody in calibration scores hours. Include one result that was messy or only partly successful and say what I learned, because a page with no rough edges reads as unreliable. Keep it to one side of paper so it can be pasted into an email without being trimmed.

Then ask for fifteen minutes with my manager a week before the deadline, not the day before, and ask two questions: is anything here likely to be disputed, and what would they add? Their answers matter more than the page. Adjust the summary after that conversation and not before it.

title: Stop hardcoding the Spanish dictionary and make the lookup language-agnostic
body: Every lookup in the app currently assumes the headword is Spanish: the parser expects one particular entry format, the accent stripping is baked in, and the sort order is Spanish too. That was fine while it was the only language, but adding a second one now means copying half the module. Pull the language out into a config object with its own source, normalisation rules and sort key, and have the lookup take that as an argument. Start with what the Spanish code actually depends on, list those assumptions in one place, and only then decide what the interface needs. Doing it before the Chinese work saves me from building the wrong abstraction twice.

title: Fine-tune a small embedding model on our support tickets
body: Off-the-shelf embeddings keep ranking generic help-centre pages above the ticket that actually solved the problem. Take a small sentence-transformers model, build a few thousand query and ticket pairs, train with in-batch negatives for one epoch, and compare recall at 10 against the untouched baseline.

title: Reseal the shower grout before the bathroom leak returns
body: Water is seeping through a hairline crack in the grout again near the drain corner.

title: Sketch a collider example where conditioning creates a fake correlation
Put auth and a rate limit in front of the inference endpoint
body: Right now anyone who finds the URL can run the model and burn the quota. Add per-key authentication and a request limit, then test with two fake tenants to confirm that one cannot see the other's requests or logs. Leave the /simple/ version first and tighten later.

title: Work through the *OWASP Top 10* by vulnerability class, not by list
body: The list is a ranking of symptoms, and I keep memorising the headings without knowing what the underlying bug looks like in code. Better to go class by class: injection, broken access control, insecure deserialization, SSRF, and write one small vulnerable Flask handler for each, then the fix next to it. Broken access control is the one I suspect I have actually shipped, since it hides in "the user is logged in, so it's fine" checks. Use a deliberately broken practice app so nothing real gets attacked, and keep the notes as a table of class, root cause, one-line fix.

title: Understand why Nesterov momentum converges faster on smooth convex problems
body: I use the momentum flag all the time and cannot explain what the look-ahead gradient actually buys, beyond "it is a bit better". Minimise an ill-conditioned quadratic with a condition number around =100=, in plain gradient descent, heavy-ball and Nesterov, and plot loss against iteration on a log axis. Then look up the =O(1/k^2)= rate versus =O(1/k)= and check that the slopes on my plot roughly agree with it. Finish with a paragraph in my own words on what changes if the problem is stochastic or non-convex, since that is where the guarantee quietly stops applying and where most of the folk wisdom comes from.

title: Compare an agent framework against a hand-written loop for my own use
Watch the same couple dance three different orchestras
body: I have a habit of admiring a couple's dancing without noticing how much of it is /the music/ steering them. Find three clips of the same couple, each to a different orchestra, and note how their walking, pauses and embellishments change with the phrasing. Write what I see into the couple's page in the archive, then try one of the ideas at the next practica and see whether it survives contact with a real partner and a crowded floor.

title: Implement BPE and WordPiece from scratch on a tiny corpus
body: I use tokenizers daily and cannot say how the merge rules are chosen or why WordPiece scores pairs differently from BPE. Write a small BPE trainer in Python on a few thousand words, print the first twenty merges, then change the pair score to the WordPiece likelihood criterion and compare the vocabularies.

title: Decide whether spot capacity is safe for the batch summarisation jobs
body: Check that the jobs checkpoint and are idempotent enough to survive a reclaimed instance before moving them.

title: Read the GraphGPS paper on graph transformers and positional encodings
Build the eval harness with latency tables before training anything
body: Get per-request latency percentiles and an error breakdown by category running on the baseline first, then touch the model.

title: Work out the difference between reset, restore and revert
Clean up the career notes folder and make a real preparation hub
body: The folder has one stub called =career.org= and a pile of loose files beside it. Move everything under it, link the question bank, stories and company notes from the stub, and delete whatever I have not opened in a year.

title: Get =BIRD= dev running with schema linking before touching the prompt
body: Prune the schema to relevant tables and columns first, then compare execution accuracy with and without it.

title: Read up on how BPE and WordPiece build their vocabularies
body: Train a toy BPE on =corpus.txt= by hand and compare the merge choice with WordPiece's likelihood criterion.

title: Get a separate AI coding session to generate topic answer files
body: Writing every answer file by hand is why the folder stalls at five. Give a fresh coding session the template plus the topic list in =topics.csv= and have it produce one draft file per topic. Then I only review and correct them, which is the part I actually learn from.

title: Add a semantic cache experiment to the support bot
body: Measure the hit rate on a week of logged prompts at a similarity cutoff of =0.92=.

title: Reorganize the phone's home screens around actual habits
body:
The current layout is whatever order apps got installed in, not what I reach for. Sort by how the day actually goes:
- morning: weather, calendar, transit
- work: notes, mail, timer
- evening: reading, music, maps
Full folder scheme and icon pack notes in [[obsidian:Phone setup]].

title: Check how the =Perceiver= conditions on audio inputs
Compress a photo with truncated SVD and watch quality against rank
body: Try ranks 5, 20 and 50 on a grayscale image and plot the singular value decay. [[obsidian:SVD Notes]]

title: Revisit the assumptions and geometry behind linear discriminant analysis
body: I use LDA as a black box and cannot say when it breaks. Go back to the setup: Gaussian classes sharing one covariance matrix, which is what makes the decision boundary linear. Sketch the two-class case in 2D, showing how the boundary depends on the inverse covariance and the class means, and how it turns quadratic once the covariances are allowed to differ (QDA). Then try it on a dataset where the shared covariance assumption is clearly false and see what happens to the boundary and to the error rate.

title: Record the sharpest aperture for every lens in one file
body: Stop guessing at f/8 by default; *f/5.6 is the sharpest stop* on the 35mm.

body: Watching Japanese videos I fully understand teaches me nothing new each day.

body: Live with it for a week on the laptop before deciding whether to keep it.

body:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mean_reciprocal_rank

body: Short read on the race for DNA structure; worth it for the =Rosalind Franklin= portrayal debate.

body: A release should fail when the golden set score drops, so *no prompt change ships without a passing run*.

body: Check the analytic answers against a few lines of code, then change the rules and see what moves.

body: Fit a small model, then check whether the *global importance ranking* matches permutation importance.

body: Idempotency is the *key point* of retries, so I should be able to explain it without looking it up.

title: Get back to daily sketching instead of occasional bursts
body: Sketching happens in bursts of enthusiasm that fade within a week, and nothing ever gets past a rough outline. Set a *ten-minute daily minimum*, one small object, no erasing, starting tomorrow morning before the excuses arrive.

title: Turn on automatic OS updates instead of postponing every prompt
body: Enable automatic updates in =Settings > Software Update= and stop clicking Later.

title: Train a small VAE on MNIST and look at the blur
body: Sample from the prior and compare against reconstructions to see where the blur comes from.

title: Work out a sustainable recurring shift at the shelter
body: I keep saying yes to one-off shifts whenever someone messages, which means my week is unpredictable and the shelter never has a hole they can plan around. Better to pick one weekly slot and stick to it, even if it is shorter than what I have been doing lately. *Commit to Tuesday evenings only* and tell the coordinator that is the standing arrangement, so trades are the exception instead of the default and everyone stops guessing which weeks I show up.

title: Map out a study plan for the December proficiency exam
body:
The exam is in December and so far my preparation has been vague reassurance that I am 'roughly B2', which is not a plan, it is a feeling. The DELE has four sections with separate pass thresholds, and I have never actually timed myself on the listening section under exam conditions, which is the one where I tend to lose focus after the first few minutes and guess the rest.

Get the official past papers for the level and run one full timed section a week rather than doing scattered practice across all four whenever I feel like it. Score each attempt honestly against the published answer key, log the raw score by section rather than an overall impression, and pick the weakest section as the following week's actual focus instead of whichever felt more comfortable to redo. Book the exam date itself now, before the preparation feels complete, since the deadline is what will actually make the weekly timed sections happen instead of sliding to the following weekend.

title: Learn enough TypeScript to spot when the types are lying
body: Learn enough TypeScript to review generated code: generics, union types and where =any= leaks in. I don't need to write it fluently, only to notice when the types are lying. Work through the handbook chapters on narrowing and generics, then review one real diff.

title: Say the conflict-with-a-colleague story out loud, three times
body: Situation, what I did, what changed afterwards, and no blaming the other person in the first sentence. [[obsidian:Interview story bank]]

title: Write recall@k, MRR and nDCG from scratch in numpy
body: I keep calling library functions without knowing exactly what they do with ties and empty relevance lists. Implement all three in =metrics.py=, then check them against a hand-worked example of five queries so the edge cases are pinned down.

title: Work out a latency and cost budget for a multi-stage ranker
body:
A ranking stack only makes sense once each stage has a number attached to it, so sketch one on paper.
- Set a total latency target and split it across retrieval, light ranking and heavy ranking
- Estimate cost per thousand requests for each stage at a given candidate count
- Find which stage to shrink first when the budget is blown

body:

body: Make section headings clearly larger than job titles and cut the two-page layout's dense margins.

body: Notebook diffs are unreadable JSON noise, so every review turns into me eyeballing screenshots instead of code. Set up nbdime or jupytext pairing so plain-text diffs actually show what changed, then commit the paired script alongside the notebook.

body: Do the bias-corrected moments on a one-parameter quadratic and compare to a library run.

body: The current Spanish list is scraped junk; I need a *curated* five hundred word core list.

body: Work out what selectivity changes compared with plain S4, and why it kills the convolution trick.

title: Program custom buttons and memory recall on both cameras
body: Put street, portrait and low-light setups on C1 to C3 and mirror them where the bodies allow. [[obsidian:Camera Custom Modes]]

title: Work out when Raft is worth it and when a database will do
body: I keep reading Raft explained as if every service needs its own consensus layer, and I can recite leader election without being able to say when I would choose it. Write a one-page answer to the question: what problems actually need consensus, and which ones are solved by leaning on an existing store like etcd or a single Postgres primary. Cover what a network partition does to each option, what the cost is in write latency, and how many nodes I would really run. Then test it by picking two systems I use at work and saying which side of the line they fall on and why. If I cannot defend the answer out loud, the notes are not finished.

title: Compare Monte Carlo and temporal difference value estimates by bias and variance
Write a short threat model for the agent's sandbox and file access
body: List what an attacker controlling one tool result could read, write or reach from inside the sandbox, and which network egress is really needed.

title: Compare product, scalar and binary quantization for a vector index
body: I use these three names as if they were interchangeable and they are not. Scalar squeezes each dimension to a byte, binary keeps one bit per dimension and leans on Hamming distance, and product quantization splits the vector into sub-blocks with a learned codebook each. Write one page giving the memory per vector for a 768-dimension embedding under each scheme, what recall each tends to lose, and which ones need training data. Use =faiss= docs as the source for the product quantization part, and do not skip the section on asymmetric distance computation.

title: Study how to train GNNs on graphs too big for memory
Trace the all-to-all pattern in expert parallel training
body: Draw the dispatch and combine steps for one layer and mark where /communication volume/ scales with token count.

body: Call to confirm the booking at =Hotel Alvorada= since the email never replied.

body: Picked this over rereading Clean Code because the complexity argument matches what actually slows me down: modules that are individually tidy but leak decisions into every caller. Read a chapter a week, and for each one write the single idea I'd defend in an argument, filed under career notes. The point I most want to keep is that *comments should explain why, not restate what the code already says*, since that is the habit I slip on under deadline pressure.

body: Make a retried POST return the stored result instead of charging twice. [[obsidian:Idempotency Keys Sketch]]

title: Compare monitor prices properly before the next payday
body: Check three different retailers and the manufacturer site before deciding.

title: Learn when a custom CUDA kernel is actually worth writing
body: Most of my slow code is slow because of memory movement or Python overhead, not missing kernels. *Profile first, and only write a kernel when the profile names one op as the bottleneck.* Next step: profile one existing training loop and read the top five entries.

title: Rebuild the marathon plan around consistency, not peak long runs
body:
Every previous attempt at this has been the same shape: a plan downloaded from somewhere, followed faithfully for six weeks, then abandoned the first time work or weather knocks out a long run, because the plan has no room for a missed session without feeling like a failure. The long run becomes the only thing that matters and everything else gets treated as optional, which is backwards, since the weekly volume across easy runs is what actually builds the aerobic base the long run is supposed to test.

Build the next plan around a floor rather than a peak: a minimum number of easy running days per week that is genuinely protected, and let the long run and any speed work sit on top of that floor rather than in place of it. If a week goes wrong, the rule is to keep the floor and drop everything else, not the other way round. Pick a plan structure that states this explicitly rather than one that just lists distances by week, and be honest that eighteen weeks of steady training beats a heroic six weeks followed by a slow rebuild every single time.

title: Explain grokking precisely enough to stop saying it just generalizes late
body: The claim is that validation accuracy jumps long after training accuracy hits 100% on small algorithmic tasks. Read the original paper and write one paragraph on what /weight decay/ does to that story, with no hand-waving about phases.

title: Proofread the README for the feed-reader project before anyone sees it
body: I wrote it in one sitting months ago and it assumes /I/ already know how the config file works, which nobody else does. Read it top to bottom as a stranger, fix the install steps that skip a dependency, and add one screenshot.

title: Work out why word error rate misleads on noisy transcripts
body: Read up on WER pitfalls and what semantic or task-level scores replace it.

title: Decide on a =CBT= course for the flying fear at last
body:
The NHS overview backs structured exposure over one-off relaxation apps, so book it.
https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/talking-therapies-medicine-treatments/talking-therapies-and-counselling/cognitive-behavioural-therapy-cbt/overview/

title: Decide whether packing cubes or compression bags earn their place
body: Every trip I end up with one bag where nothing can be found and a second where everything is crushed. Cubes would help me sort by day or by type, compression bags would help mainly with the bulky jumper and the sleeping layer. Before buying either, pack the last trip's kit both ways at home and see which actually saves space, since compression bags often just make a dense, heavy brick. Note weight added, not only volume saved. Sizes and results go in [[obsidian:Travel packing system]].

title: Reproduce Simpson's paradox on the kidney stone data
body: Two tables, one reversed trend; write out which margin is the honest one.

title: Survey mixture-of-experts variants against a dense Transformer
body: Switch Transformer, GShard, Mixtral-style top-2 routing and the newer fine-grained expert designs all trade compute for parameters in different ways. Make a one-page comparison of routing rule, load-balancing loss, active versus total parameters and known failure modes such as expert collapse. Then state in one line when a dense model is still the better choice. [[obsidian:MoE architectures reading notes]]

title: Package the habit tracker as a standalone desktop app with no sync
body: Wrap it so it runs offline on the laptop with a local database file. [[obsidian:Habit tracker architecture]]

title: Check what the photo-backup subscription actually costs me now
body: The price went up twice and I only noticed because a friend mentioned it, /quietly/.

title: Read the book on tango endings and take proper notes
body: I can dance through a tanda but the last phrase always feels improvised and slightly panicked. Read the chapter on how the music signals a close, and write *what the final two bars tell the leader to do* into the vault, one note per ending type, before I go to practica on Thursday.

title: Study linear and integer programming well enough to frame a decision problem
body: The gap in my head is between knowing that a solver exists and being able to turn a plain-English constraint problem into variables, an objective and constraints. Start with linear programming: write a small production-planning example by hand, solve it graphically, then encode the same thing with =scipy.optimize.linprog= and check the answers agree. After that, add the requirement that quantities be whole numbers or that a choice be yes/no, and see what changes — why the problem stops being easy, and what branch and bound is doing at a high level. Finish with one knapsack-style model in PuLP or OR-Tools and note where the LP relaxation gives a fractional answer.

title: Pay the final bill from the old broadband provider
body: They sent one last invoice after the switch and I almost missed the due date.

title: Check the light at Riverside Park before Sunday's shoot
body: Walk =Riverside Park= at six once to see where the light actually falls.

title: Build one file for every insurance policy number and renewal date
body: Home, car and life insurance renewal dates are scattered across three inboxes and one paper folder, so I only ever notice a lapse after it's happened. Last year the car policy auto-renewed at a much higher rate simply because nobody compared it against new quotes in time. One note instead: insurer, policy number, renewal date, and the broker's direct line, updated every time a policy changes rather than once a year in a panic. [[obsidian:Insurance Policies]]

title: Design an evaluation harness for the browsing agent prototype
body: Final-answer accuracy alone says nothing about how the agent got there, and a lucky guess looks the same as a sound run. Log full trajectories, count steps and token cost per task, and add trajectory-level checks such as repeated tool calls or ignored errors. Then add an LLM judge, but *calibrate the judge against fifty hand-labelled runs* before I believe its scores.

title: Book a dilated eye exam that includes a glaucoma pressure check
body: Glaucoma is silent until the damage is done, so get the pressure and optic nerve checked.

body:
Look for the cleanest overview of consistency-style methods before picking one.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01469

title: Study prior art in self-hosted read-later tools and steal only the good parts
body: Several self-hosted bookmark and read-later projects already solve ingestion, tagging and full-text search, and I am about to reinvent half of it. Spend an evening skimming the READMEs and data models of three of them, and note only what is reusable: how they store the fetched page, how they dedupe URLs, how they queue fetches. Ignore the web UI and the user accounts entirely. The output is a one-page note in =prior-art.org= with a line per project saying what I would copy and what I would leave, and then I decide whether to build anything at all.

title: Write manual data parallelism before touching DistributedDataParallel again
body: I keep using the wrapper without being able to say what it does between backward and step. Write the loop by hand: broadcast the initial weights, all_reduce each gradient, divide by world size, then step. Run it on two ranks against a single-process baseline and check the losses match before comparing speed with the built-in wrapper.

title: Read the LIMA paper and note what to copy for tuning
body: Skim the LIMA paper and list which data-curation ideas are cheap enough to try on my own set.

body: Pick a spare disk, restore a random folder from last month's snapshot, and compare checksums against the live copy.
