body: Plant one fact at varying depths in a fixed prompt and plot recall by position.

title: Design a capability-scoped permission model for the agent's tools
body:
Currently every tool is available to every run, which is convenient and indefensible. Sketch the model on paper first:
- Split tools into read-only, reversible write, and irreversible, and give each class a different default
- Scope credentials per run, so a =calendar.write= token cannot also send mail
- Decide which calls need explicit approval and which are only logged
- Make deny the default when a tool is not listed

title: Work through altered dominants and common jazz substitutions
body: Every fake book I open has a tritone sub or an altered V7 I can hear but not name, which slows down any real analysis. Pick five standards, mark every substitution against the plain changes, and write out why each one still resolves.

title: Sort the saved coding-interview problem list into real tiers
Sort out time-to-first-token versus inter-token latency for real workloads
body: I keep quoting TTFT and inter-token latency as if they were interchangeable, and they are not: TTFT is dominated by queueing plus prefill, inter-token latency by decode batch size and memory bandwidth. A chat UI cares about both, a summarisation job cares about neither and only about total tokens per second. Pick the two workloads I actually run, decide which metric each one should be judged on, and note the percentile that matters (p95 rather than mean, since the tail is where users notice). Then run a small load test against a local vLLM instance, saved as =latency_sweep.py=, at three concurrency levels and plot how each metric moves as concurrency rises. The point is to see the trade-off in my own numbers rather than in a vendor chart.

title: Follow one instructor's video channel and file figure breakdowns into the move library
body: Subscribe, watch the last ten uploads, and write each figure breakdown into the library under its own entry.

title: Learn enough Emacs Lisp to stop copy-pasting other people's config

title: Decide how to notice when the provider silently updates the model
body: Pinned aliases still drift, and I would rather hear about it from a dashboard than from a user. Run the fixed canary prompts nightly, store outputs with a timestamp, and diff embedding distance and pass rate against the previous week's baseline.

title: Settle on one text-to-speech reader for long articles

title: Check whether the selfish-gene framing still holds up today

body: Start with the =skiplist.py= scratch file and time inserts at one million keys.

title: Decide how deeply to read the Bayesian data analysis book
body: It is huge and I have been treating it as either everything or nothing. Make a decision: read the first five chapters cover to cover for the basic workflow, then use the rest as a reference when a modelling problem calls for it. Check the free PDF from the author's site so I do not buy the paper copy yet. I will keep a running list in =bda-reading.org= of which chapters I have used for a real problem, and if that list is still empty in three months, the book stays on the shelf.

title: Trial time-blocking from Deep Work for two weeks properly
body:
Every time I've tried this before it lasted about a day and a half before a meeting request or a genuinely urgent email blew a hole in the calendar and I gave up rather than repair it. The book's actual claim isn't that the schedule is sacred, it's that unplanned time defaults to shallow work, so the fix for a broken block is to reschedule it the same day, not to abandon the whole experiment.

So the trial is two weeks, not a vague ongoing intention: block four two-hour deep sessions a week, protect them by declining anything non-urgent that lands inside one, and when a block does get destroyed, move it rather than skip it. The *only* thing I'm measuring is whether the number of protected sessions actually completed stays above three most weeks — not whether I feel more productive, which is not a number I trust myself to report honestly. Log it daily, review at day fourteen, and decide then whether it's a habit or just another highlighted chapter.

title: Book the overdue dentist checkup before it becomes urgent
body: The last cleaning was over *eighteen months* ago and the gums have started bleeding when I floss, which is exactly the warning sign the hygienist told me not to ignore. Call the practice this week, ask for the earliest slot even if it means a lunchtime gap, and mention the bleeding up front so they don't just do the routine polish and send me away. Also ask whether the old filling needs a look while I'm there.

title: Read up on overthinking and where extra reasoning tokens stop paying
Pick one language app for daily practice and stop shopping
Derive ridge and lasso as MAP estimates under Gaussian and Laplace priors
body: I keep quoting this equivalence without being able to write it out, so my intuition about why lasso gives exact zeros is borrowed. Do the derivation on paper from the log posterior, then note what the penalty strength corresponds to in terms of prior variance.

title: Explain NDCG properly, including the variants nobody mentions
body: I can recite the formula but stumble the moment someone asks why the log discount, or whether gain is linear or exponential in relevance. Write one page in my own words covering DCG, the ideal ordering, how ties and missing judgements are handled, and the @k cutoff, with a worked example of five results.

title: Explain how conformal prediction gets coverage and where it breaks
body: Write the split-conformal recipe and note that the guarantee is marginal, not conditional.

title: Map the path from seq2seq with attention to modern transformer choices
body:
I know the transformer as a finished object and not as the end of a chain of decisions. Rebuild the history in order: encoder-decoder RNNs with a fixed context vector, the bottleneck problem, additive attention, then multiplicative attention, then dropping recurrence entirely. After that, list the later choices that are now default and why: pre-norm over post-norm, rotary position embeddings instead of sinusoidal, decoder-only rather than encoder-decoder, grouped-query attention for cheaper inference, and gated MLP variants. For each one I want the problem it was fixing and the paper or report that made it stick, so it reads as a sequence of fixes and not a bag of tricks.

If it is clear enough by the end, write it as a single timeline in my notes and check it against the original papers rather than blog summaries.

title: Compare process rewards and outcome rewards on a maths task
body: Pick one small paper on each and note what *the outcome reward fails to penalise* on a correct answer reached by bad reasoning.

title: Reread Predictably Irrational and mark which experiments still hold
body:
I read this the first time uncritically, nodding along at every anchoring and decoy-effect study without once asking whether it had been replicated at scale or just in a single undergraduate sample. That's not reading, that's collecting anecdotes with a psychology professor's name attached. Go back through with a highlighter and a separate notebook, and for each headline claim — anchoring, the decoy effect, the endowment effect, zero-price framing — note whether it's held up in the replication literature or been substantially qualified since.

The *actual* point isn't to become a replication-crisis pedant about a decade-old pop-psych book; it's to work out which two or three ideas are solid enough to actually change a decision I make, like pricing something or structuring a choice for someone else. Everything else gets filed as 'plausible, use with caution' rather than repeated at dinner as settled science. Budget one evening for the reread and skim, not a full cover-to-cover pass — I've already read it once, this is an audit, not a revisit.

title: Pick one city block and photograph it properly
body: Stop wandering the whole city and commit to one street for an afternoon.

title: Work out why word error rate hides the errors that matter
body: Read up on cases where a =WER= of 8% still ruins the transcript because the misses are names and numbers.

title: Swap ReLU for GELU and plot gradient norms per layer

title: Read Sutton and Barto properly, but only the first third
body: The canonical reinforcement learning textbook is free and I keep citing it without having read past the bandit chapter. The introductory part is where the ideas actually live: bandits, MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo, temporal-difference learning. Past that it turns into a reference for when I need a specific method. Do chapters one to six in order, do the exercises that look hard rather than the ones that look pleasant, and write a paragraph per chapter from memory before moving on. If I cannot write the paragraph, I did not read the chapter.

List the task types, which datasets are saturated, and which overlap with common training data.

body: Pick one folder per leg, restore it somewhere else, and diff it against the original.

title: Keep a diary of the evening headaches and painkiller use
body: They cluster in the late afternoon most weekdays and I've been reaching for paracetamol without really tracking how often, which is its own problem if it tips into medication-overuse headache. Start a plain diary: time of onset, what I'd eaten, screen time that day, and what I took. *Two weeks of honest entries* is enough to show the GP a pattern instead of a vague complaint, and enough to catch it myself if the painkiller frequency is doing more harm than the headaches.

title: Draft a write policy for the research agent's memory
body: Right now the agent stores everything, which makes retrieval noisy. Write down what earns a write: stated preferences, decisions and corrections, but *not raw tool output or one-off chatter*. Then test the rules on five old transcripts and count what would have been kept.

title: Add a no-expensive-cloud-resources rule to the agent instructions file
body: Write one line telling the agent it must *ask before provisioning anything billable* in the cloud.

title: Find out which music fundamentals have actually gone rusty
body: Take a quick diagnostic on key signatures, intervals and scales to see what is left. [[obsidian:Theory Gap List]]

title: Ask an LLM for ten new words based on what I already know
body: The word list is big enough now that it has obvious gaps, and I never notice them myself. Send the current list, capped at a few hundred words, with a prompt asking for ten useful words at a similar level that are not on it, then review them by hand before anything is saved.

title: Understand precision, recall, and NDCG well enough to teach them
body: I can recite the precision and recall formulas but freeze when asked to derive NDCG from DCG or explain why /position/ matters more than raw relevance in ranking metrics. Write out the full derivation from first principles, work a five-item ranked list by hand comparing DCG, IDCG, and NDCG, and be ready to explain when precision@k is misleading versus recall@k, especially for imbalanced result sets where most items are irrelevant by construction.

title: Work out the latency budget for a three-stage ranking pipeline
body: Retrieval, first-pass ranking and re-ranking each eat into the same response time, and the expensive model only fits if the earlier stages cut hard. Sketch a budget with candidate counts per stage and *the cost per thousand candidates at each stage*, then see where it breaks.

title: Add micronutrient tracking to the nutrition app
body: Right now the app knows calories, protein, carbs and fat, and that is why I have no idea whether I get enough iron or vitamin D. Pull a small open food composition dataset and map my most frequent twenty foods to it by hand, rather than trying to cover everything and drowning in matching problems. Add four columns to start with: iron, calcium, vitamin D, and fibre. Show them as percent of daily reference on the day view, with a plain bar. Anything not mapped simply shows as unknown, not as zero, since a false zero would look like a deficiency and mislead me.

title: Decide between Elasticsearch, OpenSearch and Tantivy for the notes search project
body: The notes archive has outgrown grep and I keep drifting toward whichever engine I read about last. Fix that with one table: a row per candidate (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Typesense, Meilisearch, Tantivy), columns for licence, idle RAM, hosting cost on a small box, and support for BM25 tuning, filters and vectors. *Check the licence column first*, since it rules candidates out before any feature does. Then index the same 50k documents in the two survivors and pick the one I would still want to run in a year.

title: Explain why GRPO-style training collapses when the reward barely varies
body: When every sample in a group gets the same reward, the group-normalised advantage is zero or pure noise, and the gradient carries almost nothing except whatever the length and KL terms push on. That is the mechanism behind a lot of "training just stalled" runs on prompts that are too easy or too hard. Write a one-page note on it, then log the fraction of prompts with *zero advantage variance* per batch on a small run and see whether it predicts the plateau.

title: Sketch fallback order for when the main model API is down
body: Decide the chain of providers and a cached-answer last resort. [[obsidian:LLM Product Cost Levers]]

title: Learn the ten editor shortcuts I keep reaching for the mouse for
body: I still click for things like multi-cursor, go-to-file and toggling the terminal, and it slows everything down. Print a cheat sheet and *force myself to use keys only* for one week, adding a shortcut only when I catch myself clicking.

body: I forget the direction of the reduction every single time I need it.

title: Understand how Python exception chaining and exception groups actually behave
body: I keep writing bare except blocks that re-raise a new error and lose the original cause, and I have never used except* at all. Read up on raise from versus the implicit context, what __cause__ and __suppress_context__ do to the printed traceback, and when a custom exception hierarchy is worth having. Then work through ExceptionGroup and except* with a small asyncio example, so I know why it matches by type and can split a group instead of catching it whole. Write a few throwaway scripts and read the tracebacks carefully.

body: Pull the =L5= rubric next to the project list and mark every gap honestly.

title: Write the automatic rollback rule before the canary starts
body: The canary is the easy part; deciding in advance what counts as bad is the hard part. Pick two or three guard metrics, such as error rate, p95 latency and one quality proxy, set the threshold and the window for each, and get the rollback to fire without a human noticing first.

title: Practise cherry-pick on a scratch repo until conflicts stop scaring me
Do one exercise from the ear-training book before reading further
body: I bought it for interval recognition and have read forty pages without playing a note, which is backwards. Pick the first exercise on hearing a fifth against a fourth, do ten minutes a day at the piano for a week, and only continue if my hit rate improves. Refs: [[obsidian:Ear training practice log]]

title: Drill window functions until ROW_NUMBER and RANK are automatic
body: I still pause to recall the difference between RANK and DENSE_RANK.

title: Map what changed in C++ from C++11 to C++23 for my old habits
body:
My mental baseline is roughly C++11 with some C++14 sprinkled in, and I suspect I am writing around features that now exist. Make one table with a row per standard and only the changes I would realistically use, not the whole standards document.

For C++14 and 17 I want structured bindings, std::optional, std::variant, string_view, if with initialiser, fold expressions and guaranteed copy elision. For C++20, concepts, ranges, spans, three-way comparison and std::format, plus a note on coroutines that says whether I will ever need them or just need to recognise them. For C++23, std::expected as value-based error handling, since it is the one that could replace my exception habits, and std::print. Next to every row put the old idiom it replaces, so the table doubles as a list of things to stop writing.

After that, take one of my older small programs and modernise it using only what is in the table, then compare the two versions. If the result is not clearly shorter or clearer, the feature does not go on my regular list. Check what my compiler and standard library actually support before trusting the table, because support for the newer library features still lags behind the language ones.

title: Pick up the passport photos from the chemist
Learn Python decorators including functools.wraps and arguments
body: I copy decorator snippets without seeing why there are three nested functions once arguments appear. Write a /timing decorator/ with an optional argument, then inspect the function name and docstring with and without functools.wraps to see what gets lost.

The stock switches have gotten scratchy on the space bar and a few others after two years of daily typing.

[[obsidian:Keyboard build notes]]

body: I can explain the clipped objective but I have never written the whole loop, and the gaps show whenever I read RL code. Write a single-file PPO with GAE for CartPole, run five seeds, and overlay the return curve on the CleanRL reference until they agree within noise. [[obsidian:RL from scratch notes]]

title: Check which apps still have access to the old account
Work out what reflog actually keeps and for how long
body: I want to know the expiry defaults before I trust it as a safety net.

title: Find out what the caching allocator does with freed blocks
body: Read the PyTorch CUDA caching allocator notes and write three lines on block splitting.

title: Book the overdue haircut before the wedding next weekend
body: It's grown past *presentable* and the wedding is closing in fast.

title: Understand what a good ML postmortem looks like
body: Most postmortems I have read stop at "the model drifted" and never say why nobody noticed for a week. Read three public write-ups from big teams, then draft a one-page template of my own with sections for detection gap, blast radius and follow-up owners.

title: Understand delivery semantics in message queues before picking one for the feature pipeline
body:
I keep using the phrases at-least-once and exactly-once as if they were interchangeable with "reliable", and they are not. Start with what a broker can actually promise versus what the consumer has to do on its own: acknowledgements, redelivery after a timeout, consumer offsets, and why duplicates appear at all when a worker dies between processing and acking.

The key point to internalise is that *exactly-once is really at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing*, and the interesting design work is making the write side safe to repeat. Read how Kafka handles transactions and idempotent producers, then compare with a plain work queue like SQS or RabbitMQ where ordering and replay are much weaker. Also cover partitioning and ordering guarantees per key, consumer groups, backpressure, and dead-letter queues. End with a one-page comparison of log-style streams versus task queues, and a note on which one suits a stream of user events feeding features versus a stream of jobs to run.

title: Train a small VAE on MNIST and look at the blur
body: I keep repeating that VAEs give blurry samples without ever having seen why. Train a tiny one with a 2-d latent, plot the latent grid decode, then vary the KL weight and watch /what actually changes/ in sharpness and coverage.

title: Prepare properly for the second-round interview on Thursday
body: I got through the phone screen mostly on enthusiasm, but the technical round will ask about systems I've only used casually. Block out two evenings to review the actual documentation and write three questions of my own instead of turning up empty-handed.

title: Collect the cases where a plain A/B test beats a fancy bandit

title: Understand why bf16 is forgiving and fp16 is not
body: I keep hearing that bf16 just works and fp16 needs loss scaling, and I can repeat it without being able to explain it. Compare the exponent and mantissa bits, write down the range and the rounding error for each, and find one concrete case where fp16 overflows or underflows in a training step. Then note which ops PyTorch autocast keeps in fp32 and why, since that list is where the numerical pitfalls actually sit. [[obsidian:Mixed Precision Notes]]

title: Do a subscription cleanup across every mailbox and channel
body: Three mailboxes and two messaging apps are each collecting their own pile of newsletters and promo texts nobody reads. *The unsubscribe pass has to happen in one sitting or it never happens at all*, so block an hour and go through each account in turn.

title: Decide what counts as irreplaceable and where it goes offsite
body: Everything is backed up somewhere, which is not the same as everything important being safe from one bad week. Family photos, scanned passports and certificates, the tax archive, and my own writing — that's maybe forty gigabytes total, and it deserves a rule of its own rather than riding along with whatever else happens to sync. Define that subset explicitly, put it in a dedicated folder, and keep a copy of it offsite that isn't just 'in the cloud somewhere' — a drive at a relative's house, updated quarterly, counts; a forgotten storage tier does not. *The irreplaceable subset needs its own explicit rule, not the general backup's leftovers.*

body: We ran about thirty metric comparisons on one experiment and celebrated the two that came out under 0.05, which is close to what chance alone would hand us. Take the actual p-values and apply all three corrections, then see which results survive each. The choice should follow the cost of errors: for a launch decision where a false win is expensive, use Holm and control family-wise error; for exploratory metrics that only generate follow-up ideas, false discovery rate is fine. title: Understand the agent loop and what makes it stop
body: Before adding any more features, be able to explain the loop in my own words: model call, parse for tool use, execute, append result, repeat. The part I have been vague about is termination. A loop that ends only when the model says it is done will eventually run forever on a confusing task. Write down the /hard/ stops I want — max steps, a token or cost ceiling, a wall-clock limit, and detection of the same tool call repeated with the same arguments — and what the agent should report when one of them fires, so a stop looks like an honest failure instead of a silent hang.

title: Get a real grip on diffusion policy and cross-embodiment robot learning
body:
Robot learning is the part of this area where I know the vocabulary least and the headlines most. The plan is to read it in a sensible order rather than by whatever gets shared. Start with the diffusion policy paper: what is being denoised (a chunk of future actions, conditioned on observations), why that handles multimodal demonstrations better than a regression head, and what the action-chunking horizon does to smoothness and latency.

Then move to the cross-embodiment work: what it takes to train one policy on data from different arms and grippers, how action spaces are aligned or padded, and whether the reported transfer gains are large or just visible. After that read one survey or blog post on sim-to-real, focusing on domain randomisation versus system identification, and write down which failures each approach actually fixes.

Output: a two-page note comparing the three ideas, with one open question per paper that I could reasonably test on a toy environment later. If a paper's results depend on a proprietary robot fleet, mark it as something to read for ideas only, not for reproduction.

title: Read up on personalized PageRank and where it beats plain PageRank
body: I used it for related-item candidates years ago and never formalized why it worked. Read the standard treatment, then implement it with a restart vector on a small graph, and note **when the restart probability matters most** for locality of the scores. Write a half page of conclusions.

title: Apply rate-distortion intuition to decide how far to compress embeddings
body:
I have been treating embedding compression as a search for the smallest size that still works, which hides that this is a curve and not a threshold. Rate-distortion theory says that for a given amount of tolerated distortion there is a minimum number of bits, and that each extra bit buys less than the one before. If that holds for my vectors, the first halving of memory should be nearly free and the last one should hurt badly, and I should be able to see the knee.

Test that on a real set. Take a sample of a hundred thousand embeddings, compress them at 32, 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1 bits per dimension, and for each compute two things: mean squared reconstruction error, and recall at 10 against exact search on the originals. Plot both against bits per dimension. The interesting question is whether reconstruction error and recall agree about where the knee is, because I suspect recall is far more forgiving, since it only needs the ranking preserved rather than the vectors. Also try a dimension-truncated version at equal total bits, to see whether spending bits on fewer dimensions or fewer bits on all dimensions gives the better trade. Finish with a paragraph saying which operating point I would pick and why.

title: Check the LLM judge against forty hand-labelled answers before trusting it
body: The judge prompt has been giving confident scores for weeks and I have never compared a single one to my own reading. Label forty answers by hand, pass/fail only, then run the judge on the same set and compute Cohen's kappa alongside raw agreement. *Raw agreement alone is misleading here* because most answers pass, so a judge that says yes to everything already looks decent. Keep the confusion matrix in the file, not just the headline number.

title: Work out when ML is the wrong tool and rules would do

title: Learn to read learning curves before I blame the model again

Collect four examples of each pattern: train loss falling while validation climbs, both plateauing high, validation noisier than train because the split is tiny, and a suspicious gap that appears from epoch one which usually means leakage or a label problem. Plot my own past runs next to them and write one line per run on what I should have checked first. Keep the page short enough that I will actually open it mid-training.

title: Read up on deep CTR models and graph-based recommenders
body: Recommendation is where a lot of deployed deep learning lives, and I only know it through matrix factorization. Cover the CTR line first: Wide & Deep, DeepFM, and DCN with explicit feature crosses, noting what problem each solves that a plain MLP does not. Then look at graph-based recommenders, starting with NGCF and LightGCN, and write down why LightGCN drops the feature transforms and nonlinearities and still does better on collaborative filtering.

title: Move the basil pots out of the harsh afternoon sun
body: The leaves are scorching by =3pm=, so shift the pots to the shaded side of the balcony today.

title: Write down my personal *approach to system design* on one page
body: The order I clarify, estimate, sketch and stress-test in should be fixed, not improvised.

title: Make in-editor search return lexical and semantic hits together
body: Right now I run a text grep, and then a separate embedding search over my notes when the grep fails. One action that merges both lists would save the second guess. Prototype it with a reciprocal-rank fusion of the two result sets and see whether the top ten feels better.

title: Book a placement test before committing to the autumn class
body:
Last time I signed up for a class without checking my actual level first, and I spent six weeks either bored in the easy sections or lost whenever the teacher moved past basic tenses. That was a waste of both money and the two hours a week I could have spent doing something at the right difficulty, and it also killed my motivation for a month afterward because every session felt like proof I was behind.

Before enrolling in the autumn conversation class, book a proper placement test with the language school rather than guessing my level from how confident I feel in an app. Write down the result and the specific gaps the tester mentions, not just the grade, so I can tell the coordinator what I actually need practice with. Then compare two or three class times against my calendar and commit to the one I can realistically keep for the whole term, instead of the one that looked appealing on the sign-up page.

title: Order a second enclosure for the offsite backup drive
Plan the gift and card for the retirement lunch
body: Nobody has organised this yet, which usually means it falls on whoever notices first. The date is fixed for the =14th=, so the actual constraint is delivery time rather than choice: anything ordered after Friday risks arriving late, and a card bought at the last minute always looks like a card bought at the last minute. Sort the collection first, since the gift depends on how much comes in, then order something generic enough to survive being slightly wrong for the person - a decent bottle rather than anything more personal. Card gets signed properly, in ink, not passed round in a rush on the day itself.

title: Work through the Kubeflow Pipelines architecture and its core features
body: I keep using pipeline tools as black boxes and cannot say what the metadata store or the artifact layer actually does. Read the architecture overview, then run the =mnist= sample locally and trace one run from compiled spec to executed pod.

title: Pay the final gas bill from the old supplier
body: Owe them for the last three weeks before the switch went through; *pay it off* before it goes to a debt collector.

title: Work out why partial pooling helps the small-store sales model
body: Some stores have only a few weeks of data, and the per-store means swing wildly. Fit a varying-intercept model on the small stores, plot raw means against shrunk estimates, and note which stores move most and why.

title: Learn the basics of learning-to-rank: pointwise, pairwise, listwise
body: Read one survey and implement a pairwise loss on a toy set of queries.

title: Add a verb-conjugation reference tool to the language toolkit
body: Guessing endings mid-sentence breaks fluency more than any vocabulary gap does. Pick one conjugation reference that covers irregular verbs properly and bookmark it before the next lesson, details in [[obsidian:Language Reference Tools]].

title: Write scaled dot-product attention from scratch before touching any library
body:
Implement it in plain NumPy with the =sqrt(d_k)= scaling and a causal mask, then compare against the paper.
https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762

title: Finish the introductory chapters of the deep learning book
body: I skipped the maths chapters last time and paid for it later. Read the linear algebra and probability chapters as a refresher, one per week, and stop when the notation stops being familiar.

title: Read up on the C++ memory model before touching atomics again
body: Get acquire, release and sequentially consistent ordering straight in words before I write a single line of code.

title: Research which dictionary APIs are worth integrating first
body: Right now word lookups fall back to a single free API with patchy coverage for less common languages. The concrete step is to compare Wiktionary, Wordnik and a couple of open dictionary dumps, then pick whichever gives the *best coverage* for the top ten requested languages first.

title: Consolidate three photo libraries into one folder structure
body: Photos live in /three/ different apps now and none of them talk to each other.

title: Pick one glossary book and fix names for every figure
Understand task-based versus asset-based orchestration with Airflow and Dagster
body: Write one paragraph on what changes when the graph describes data rather than jobs.

title: Learn a short protocol for hyperparameter search that I would trust
body: Fix the budget first, use random search over grids, and *always report the spread across seeds*.

title: Write out a data exfiltration attempt step by step and then break it
body: I read about exfiltration through rendered markdown images and links, but never saw one work. In a sandbox with fake secrets, reproduce it against a small chat agent using the steps from the threat model, then add the mitigation that stops it, such as blocking outbound URLs in output, and record which step actually failed.

title: Work out why recurrent networks lost to transformers for language modelling
body: The sequential dependency was the obvious cost, but I want to know what else mattered, since state-space models are now retrying the same idea.

title: Practise PyTorch tensor indexing until gather and scatter stop confusing me
body:
Do the puzzles daily until advanced indexing feels boring. [[obsidian:PyTorch Indexing Cheatsheet]]
https://github.com/srush/Tensor-Puzzles

title: Draft a two-minute self-introduction for the new team standup
Practise explaining out loud why I rejected the AI's refactor suggestion
body: Pick a real diff from this week, say the reasoning to an empty room, and notice where it turns into hand-waving.

title: Unsubscribe from the newsletters clogging the personal inbox
body: Unsubscribed from everything opened in the last three months, no exceptions this time.

title: Work through altered dominants and common jazz substitutions
body: The ii-V-I sounds fine until a tritone sub or altered dominant shows up and I freeze mid-phrase. Pick five standard turnarounds, write out the substitution options for each, and play them slowly with a metronome until the shapes are automatic.

title: Read up on how PPO fixes the instability in vanilla policy gradient
Decide whether the sleep book earns a full read
body: A friend keeps recommending it, and I have already seen two of its main claims contradicted elsewhere, so I am not ready to give it a weekend. Get a chapter-by-chapter summary first. If the parts on sleep timing and napping are new to me, read only those, and check each claim against a second source before believing it. If the summary is mostly anecdotes and a sales pitch for a supplement, drop it and say so in a short note so I do not reconsider it in six months. Either way, the outcome should be one small change to my evenings that I can try for a fortnight.

title: Cancel the gym membership before it silently auto-renews again
body: Last year it renewed for another twelve months because I missed the thirty-day notice window by a week. This time send the cancellation email early, get written confirmation back, and mark the actual notice deadline in the calendar instead of the renewal date.

title: Learn why DQN needed target networks and replay in the first place
body: Write a short note on what /goes wrong/ when either one is removed, ideally with a tiny experiment.

title: Read the Mamba paper and note what it gives up
body:
Selective state spaces claim Transformer quality at linear cost; check which benchmarks back that up and at what scale.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00752

title: Learn what a good ML incident postmortem looks like versus a blame report
Draft a personal note on my goals and how I like to be helped
Pack the *donation boxes* for Saturday's clothing drive
body:
Sort what's left in the hallway before drop-off day.
- Coats and jackets into one box
- Kids' clothes separated by size
- Shoes paired and bagged
- Label each box with the drop-off address

title: Work out why TD(0) bootstraps and still converges
body: Rederive the TD(0) update on a five-state random walk before trusting it. [[obsidian:TD learning notes]]

title: Prepare the questions for the next one-to-one with my manager
body: I keep using the slot for status updates that could be a message. Write three questions that are actually /about me/ — scope, feedback I have not heard, and what promotion would need — and ask them first.

title: Look at a small travel air purifier for hotel rooms
body: Check whether a pocket-sized unit is *actually worth the weight* or just a gadget that fills a bag corner.

title: Learn how survey weighting changes an estimate and its variance
body: Unweighted survey means keep getting quoted as if the sample were the population. Work through post-stratification and inverse probability weights on a toy sample with a known skew, and compare the raw and weighted estimates. Also note how weights inflate variance through the design effect.

title: Drop off the winter coats bag at the donation bin
body: Three coats and a stack of scarves are ready to go this weekend.

title: Prepare the agenda and pre-reads for the offsite planning meeting
body:
The offsite always drifts into whoever talks loudest unless there's a written agenda circulated beforehand, and last time three people showed up having read nothing. Draft four topics with a fixed time box each, and attach the one document each topic actually depends on rather than a folder link nobody opens. Put the hardest, most contentious topic first while people are still fresh, not last when everyone just wants to wrap up.

Send the agenda and pre-reads five days out, not two, since half the value is people arriving with an opinion already formed rather than forming it in the room. Book the room with the whiteboard rather than the one with the broken projector, confirm dietary requirements for lunch this time instead of guessing, and print a couple of paper copies for the two people who never open attachments on their laptops.

title: Build a small computer-vision regression project with honest error bars
body: Pick something I can photograph myself, such as estimating the fill level of a water jug or the number of pages left in a notebook, and regress the value from a phone picture. The point is not accuracy but reporting it honestly. Split by session or lighting, not by random image, so near-duplicate shots do not leak between train and test. Report mean absolute error with a bootstrap interval, and a separate number for the worst lighting condition. **Split by session, not by image** is the rule that decides whether the error bar means anything. Compare against a dumb baseline that always predicts the mean, so the model has to earn its place.

title: Write a routine that predicts each company's likely design prompt
body: I keep walking into design rounds guessing blind instead of using the job description and engineering blog posts already sitting in front of me. Before the next loop, draft a one-page prediction per company: likely problem domain, scale, and two probable follow-up questions.

title: Read the =Learning to Rank= chapter of an IR textbook
body: Cover pointwise, pairwise and listwise losses and when each is used.

title: Set the regression tolerance for the classifier at =2 points= drop
body: Write down why two points, based on the run-to-run noise measured over five seeds.

title: Re-derive eigenvectors and say where they show up in ML
body: Redo the =Av = λv= derivation on a 2x2 matrix and list three places it appears.

title: Understand why exploration is hard to justify in a production ranker
body:
Most ranking systems only ever see feedback on items they already showed, so the training data quietly narrows the catalogue. I want a clear account of how this feedback loop works and what practical fixes look like: a small random slice of traffic, Thompson-style sampling on scores, or inverse propensity weighting on logged data.

Read one or two write-ups from teams that actually paid the cost of exploration, and note how they argued for it to stakeholders. The argument matters as much as the algorithm, because the lost clicks are visible and the gain is not. End with three bullet points I could say aloud in an interview. [[obsidian:Exploration in Ranking Systems]]

title: Polish the CV before applying to any new roles
body: The bullet points are three years stale and bury the one project that actually matters under formatting noise. Next step: rewrite the top third around outcomes, not duties, and check it against [[obsidian:CV master draft]].

title: Make retraining promote only when the candidate beats production
body: A nightly retrain that overwrites the live model unconditionally is a regression waiting for a quiet week. Build a scheduled job that trains a candidate, scores it on the frozen holdout set next to the current model, and registers it as the new version only if the metric improves by a margin. Otherwise log the numbers and exit cleanly. Test both branches by hand before scheduling anything.

title: Refresh what a CPU cache line and memory ordering mean today
body: My mental model of hardware is from a decade ago, single core, flat memory, and it shows whenever someone mentions false sharing or NUMA. Modern chips have deep cache hierarchies and weak memory models that change how concurrent code behaves. Read a current explainer on cache coherence and the C++ memory model, then write a small benchmark that shows false sharing on my own laptop.

title: Check whether the model I serve loses more accuracy on long inputs
body: Quantization error may compound over long contexts, and my eval only uses short prompts. Run the int8 and fp16 versions on a set of long documents and compare the scores, so I know whether the short-prompt numbers can be trusted.

title: Take the Duolingo-style ear-training quiz cold before buying the book
body: The music-theory book promises perfect-pitch shortcuts I doubt work in six weeks. Take an interval-recognition quiz cold first, record the baseline score, and only order the book if the claimed method beats guessing by a wide margin.

title: Write an RFC pattern note for design docs and reuse it
body: A design doc and an interview answer have almost the same bones, and I keep writing them as if they were unrelated. Capture the RFC pattern once: context, goals and non-goals, options considered, the chosen option with reasons, risks, and open questions. *The options-considered section is the part to get right*, because it is what shows judgement rather than just a solution. Add a short example about swapping a keyword retriever for a hybrid one, and link the note from the template library.

title: Read the spaced-repetition paper behind the flashcard algorithm
body: The flashcard app just says 'reviews due' without me understanding why the interval doubles some days and barely moves on others. Read the original SuperMemo SM-2 description and the Ebbinghaus forgetting-curve background behind it, since the algorithm is older and simpler than the app's UI suggests. The point is not to reimplement it, it's to understand *why intervals should depend on how wrong I was, not just whether I was right*, because right now my own manual review scheduling ignores that distinction and just repeats everything I got wrong yesterday.

title: Plan the bulk order of cleaning supplies for autumn
body: The cupboard under the sink is down to one bottle of everything, which is exactly the point where a small top-up turns into an emergency shop at whatever the corner shop happens to stock. Better to do this properly once: list what actually gets used monthly - washing tablets, the =Fairy= liquid, bin bags, descaler - rather than buying whatever looks low today. A single larger order usually undercuts three small ones anyway, and delivery is free above a certain threshold. Set a reminder for the same week next quarter instead of waiting for the cupboard to look bare again, since that is what keeps causing the panic buys in the first place.

title: Use the UX research methodology book only for interview bias
body: I don't need the whole book, just the chapter on leading-question traps before Thursday's user interviews. Skim the checklist, rewrite my three worst questions, and stop treating the *whole* thing as required reading.

title: Learn the Polars equivalents of my everyday Pandas moves
body: Write a two-column cheat sheet: groupby, merge, apply and pivot in Pandas next to the Polars expression.

title: Work out how the CLAUDE.md files stack across folders
body: I keep pasting the same rules into prompts because I do not know which file wins. Read the memory docs, then make a throwaway repo with =CLAUDE.md= at user, root and one subfolder level, and ask the assistant to list what it sees at each level.

title: Quantize a small classifier and measure what it actually costs
body: Take a small text model, export it at fp16, int8 and int4, and time each on the laptop CPU with the same fifty inputs. Record file size, median latency and accuracy on a held-out set in one table, so the trade-off is a set of numbers rather than a vague impression.

title: Add a retention rule to the nightly notes backup script
body: The backup script has been copying the notes folder every night for months and never deletes anything, so the target drive is now nearly full and I only noticed by accident. That is the wrong failure mode for a backup: it should keep itself tidy. Add a retention step that keeps the last seven daily archives, the last four weekly ones, and the last six monthly ones, and removes the rest. Before enabling deletion, run it in a dry-run mode that only prints what would be removed, and read that output carefully against the actual folder listing. Also make the script log how many archives it kept and deleted, so a silent misbehaviour shows up in the log rather than as an empty disk later.

title: Work through =ii-V-I= voicings until they come without thinking
body: Every jazz tune is mostly this cadence and I still rebuild it note by note each time. Start with shell voicings (3rd and 7th) in left hand, add the 9th on top, and run it through all twelve keys this week.

title: Merge the three overlapping question banks into one file
body: I keep three lists that overlap; merge them into =questions.org= today.

title: Prep the tutoring folders before Tuesday's after-school session
body: The kids' worksheets are still scattered across last month's folder, and I keep improvising each session instead of building on the last one. *Print a fresh packet for each reading level* tonight so tomorrow starts organized instead of scrambling.

title: Research a travel tripod that fits airline carry-on limits
body: Compare tripods under =500 g= that still hold a phone clamp steady.

title: Stop letting the flashcard deck grow past what I can review
body: Anki says 1200 cards are due, which is not a study session, it is a /debt collection notice/. The deck ballooned because I kept adding words from reading without ever pruning the ones I clearly know by now. Cap new cards at fifteen a day going forward, and before adding anything else spend one session doing nothing but suspending cards I have got right ten times running.

title: Work out how indirect prompt injection actually reaches the agent
body:
The version of prompt injection I keep picturing is a user typing something hostile into the chat box, and that is the easy case. The one that should worry me is indirect: the agent fetches a web page, reads a ticket, opens a PDF or gets a tool result, and somewhere in that text is a sentence addressed to the model rather than to me. The model has no reliable channel separating /data/ from /instructions/, so anything that lands in the context window is a candidate instruction, whoever wrote it.

Read the original indirect-injection paper and two or three recent write-ups, then take my own =support-triage-agent= and list every place untrusted text enters: search results, customer emails, attachment text, error messages returned by tools. For each entry point write down what the agent could do next that has side effects. The interesting question is not whether the model can be fooled, because assume it can, but which combinations of untrusted input plus a powerful tool make a fooled model expensive. Keep the output as a one-page table, entry point against reachable actions, and mark the cells where a human currently sees nothing before the action happens. That table should drive the permission work, not the other way round.

title: Understand codebook collapse in VQ-VAEs by breaking one on purpose
body: Train a tiny VQ-VAE on digits with a codebook of 512 entries and count how many are ever selected. Then try a dead-code restart and check =codebook_usage.png= before and after, so collapse is something I have seen and not just read about.

title: Reproduce the published MMLU numbers with lm-evaluation-harness and log the gaps
body: Pick one small open model with a reported MMLU score and run it through lm-evaluation-harness with the same few-shot setting the model card claims. Almost certainly the number will not match exactly, and the interesting part is why: prompt format, answer-extraction rule, batch size, or a harness version change. Change one thing at a time and write the score after each change, so the divergence gets attributed rather than guessed at. Keep the config files with the results so the run can be repeated. [[obsidian:LLM eval reproduction notes]]

title: Pick a daily language app and accept its flaw
body: Duolingo keeps me consistent even though its sentences never resemble real speech.

title: Read the DINO paper and note what self-distillation actually does
body: Focus on the teacher momentum update and centering, and why the model does not collapse.

title: Separate retrieval error from generation error in the RAG pipeline
body: Right now I only look at whether the final answer reads well, which tells me nothing about where it went wrong. Build a small labelled set of questions with the gold passage marked, then score retrieval on its own (recall@k, MRR) before the generator sees anything. Then feed the generator the gold passage directly and score the answers. *If the answer is wrong with the gold passage in hand, it is a generation problem; if the gold passage was never retrieved, it is a retrieval problem.* Tally both, and only then decide what to fix first.

title: Trace a latent video diffusion system from pixels to pixels
body: I can describe image latent diffusion from memory, but the moment video enters I lose the thread: where does time get handled, and what is actually different from the image model? Pick one open system, draw the whole pipeline on a single page, from the VAE that compresses frames, through the denoiser with its temporal attention or 3D convolutions, to the text conditioning and the sampler. Write down the tensor shapes at each hop, because shapes are what expose the parts I am hand-waving. Then note which pieces are inherited from the image model unchanged and which were added only for video. Finish with one paragraph on why temporal consistency is hard.

title: Work out how a Bloom filter's false positive rate really behaves
body: I can recite the formula but could not tell you why the optimal number of hash functions is what it is, or what happens to the error rate when the filter is overfilled by half again. Derive the false positive rate from bits per element, then check it numerically by building one in a short script with =mmh3= and inserting a million random keys. Compare the measured rate to the formula at three fill levels. After that, read about counting and cuckoo filters and note when each is worth the extra space or complexity.

title: Check the NAS drive health report before it's too late
body: The =smartctl= report on bay three has been showing reallocated sectors for weeks.

title: Write one precise spec-style prompt for a task I usually leave vague
body: Pick a real task, write the prompt as a spec with context, constraints and an example output, and compare it with my usual one-liner.

title: Set a reminder to review subscriptions every quarter
body: Cancelling things one at a time whenever I notice them is how a forgotten trial turns into eighteen months of charges. Add a recurring quarterly reminder to pull up the bank statement, list every recurring charge, and decide deliberately whether each one still earns its place.

title: Practise soloing over changes using a backing-track app
body: Scales without a target land nowhere, so pick one standard, load it into the app, and solo using only chord tones on beat one for a week. Slow the tempo down until every phrase resolves cleanly, then add passing tones once resolution stops being an accident.

title: Add example sentences to the vocabulary flashcard entries
body: Bare words without example sentences never stick past the second review.

title: Rearrange my prompts so the stable part comes first
body: Prefix caching only helps if the shared text is literally at the start. Audit the three prompt templates I use, move the system text and few-shot examples ahead of anything user-specific, and *put timestamps and IDs last*. Then compare cached-token counts before and after.

title: Pack the travel keyboard, stand and cable for the trip
Write annotation guidelines that two people could follow the same way
body:
The gold set is only as good as the labels, and at the moment the labelling rule is whatever I felt like on the day. Write a one-page guideline: what counts as supported, what counts as partially supported, what to do when the answer is correct but not in the notes, and three worked examples for each label including the ugly borderline ones. The borderline examples are the part that will actually settle arguments.

Then get one other person to label thirty items cold, with no discussion, and compare against my labels. Every disagreement goes in a list, and for each one decide whether the guideline was unclear or one of us simply erred. Rewrite the unclear rules, relabel, and only then freeze the set as the reference. Keep an adjudicated column next to the two raw labels so I can later see how often the first pass was wrong. Also record the guideline version in the file header, otherwise the judge calibration numbers will not be comparable a month from now.

title: Decide how to catch silent provider model updates
body: Pin the model version where possible and rerun the fixed probe set nightly to see if outputs shift.

title: Measure staleness in the *agent memory* store
body: Recall alone flatters the system, because an old fact can be retrieved confidently after it stopped being true. Pick twenty stored items, mark which are outdated by hand, and count how often retrieval returns the stale one over its replacement. That single rate tells me whether I need expiry or just better ranking.

title: Reserve the guesthouse before the festival weekend fills up
body: Rooms near the old town are already thinning out for that weekend.

title: Read one photographer's travel blog for location ideas
body: Start with the =Iceland= archive and note three places worth a second look.

title: Book an eye test to rule out early glaucoma
body: Book an eye test with a glaucoma screening, since it runs in the family and nothing hurts yet.

title: Finish the practical generative AI book chapters on diffusion
body: Do the diffusers chapters with the code actually run, not just read. [[obsidian:Hands-On Generative AI Notes]]

title: Try a Dask batch job on a small cluster and see where it helps
body: Pandas is fine until the feature build takes an hour, and I have not tested whether distributing it is worth the trouble. Run the same aggregation on a local Dask cluster with a few workers, compare timings against plain pandas, and check the dashboard. [[obsidian:Distributed Python experiments]]

title: Find a simulation environment for recommender systems worth trying
body: Compare two open simulators, such as /RecSim/ and one other, on how they model user behaviour and drift.

title: Read Designing Machine Learning Systems against my own pipelines
body: Go chapter by chapter and note where Huyen's advice matches what broke for me in production.

title: Compare the planned shot against what I actually got
body: The =sun angle= column in my scouting notes has been right nearly every time; the expected-shot column has been wrong almost as often. Go back through the last four outings and write down exactly where each guess failed and why.

title: Learn the quality, diversity and latency trade-offs in diffusion sampling
body: Guidance scale, step count and sampler choice all move the same three quantities and I only tune by feel. Read about classifier-free guidance, DDIM versus higher-order solvers, and distillation, then generate a small grid at fixed seeds. [[obsidian:Diffusion sampling trade-offs]]

title: Scan the project dependencies for known vulnerabilities
body: The lockfile has not been looked at since the first install and half the packages are transitive ones I never chose. Run =pip-audit= against the environment and note which findings are actually reachable from my code.

title: Track down the missing receipts for last year's home office
body: The home office deduction needs receipts for the desk, the chair, and a chunk of the electricity bill, and at least two of those receipts were never saved because the purchase happened on a card that got cancelled halfway through the year. Check the old statements from =Barclaycard= for the transaction dates, then request duplicate receipts directly from each retailer rather than trying to reconstruct amounts from memory, which is how the numbers went wrong last time.

title: Decide what the assistant's memory keeps and what goes to notes
body: Memory holds only stable preferences; plans live in =Projects.org=, and anything older than three months gets flagged for deletion.

title: Write an inverse propensity estimator for ranking from click logs
body: Implement plain IPS for position-based click data on a public ranking dataset and check it against the logged baseline.

title: Sort out the sources of bias in recommender training data
body: Position bias, popularity bias, selection bias and exposure bias all get lumped together as "the feedback loop" and I cannot say which fix belongs to which. Make a one-page table: source, how it shows up in logged clicks, and where it is mitigated, whether in data collection, the loss or re-ranking. Start with inverse propensity weighting.

title: Write a Python generator pipeline from scratch without any libraries
body: Build a three-stage pipeline with plain generators and see exactly where values get pulled and when cleanup runs.

title: Work out why word error rate flatters some ASR systems
body: WER counts every substitution the same, so "the" for "a" costs as much as dropping a drug name. Read up on the alternatives (semantic error rate, entity-level accuracy) and pick one to run beside WER on twenty of my own recordings.

title: Run a fuzzy-matching comparison on a messy company-names list
body: Compare edit distance, token-set ratio and character n-gram TF-IDF for deduplicating a public list of company names.

title: Compare offset pagination with cursor pagination on a large table
body: Time both at page 10 and page 100000 and note the difference.

title: Clear the password manager health report down to zero reused
body: Start with the reused passwords on banking and email, then work down to old shopping accounts I can simply delete.

title: Finally rewrite the *headline* on my LinkedIn profile
body: Five years out of date and it still lists the wrong city.

title: Compare *three* local dentists on price and reviews
body: The current dentist keeps upselling scans I don't need and the reviews back that up. Ring around three practices, ask for a price list and check-up-only quote, and cross-reference against the official ratings before booking anywhere for the overdue check-up.

title: Work through attribution graphs to trace what drives an answer
body:
Learn one interpretability method end to end rather than just reading the summaries.
- Read the Anthropic circuit tracing write-up on attribution graphs
- Run the open-source tooling on a small model with one short factual prompt
- Note which features are input-driven and which look like intermediate steps
- Write down one thing the graph cannot tell me about the output

title: Find cases where a plain difference in means beats a fancy learned model
body: Collect three examples where a randomized experiment or a *simple baseline* wins, so I stop reaching for complexity first.

title: Rewrite the pairwise distance loop with broadcasting
body: Do it on a 1000x3 array and check against the loop version. [[obsidian:Numpy broadcasting drills]]

title: Curate a scored QA set from an open corpus and show the lift
body: Take a large open QA or web-text corpus and score each example with a cheap quality signal: a small classifier, answer-length sanity checks, and deduplication against the test split. Keep the top slice, then fine-tune the same small model on the top slice and on a random slice of equal size. The deliverable is a single table with both runs on one held-out eval, with seeds repeated. If the *curated slice does not beat random by more than the seed noise*, the scoring is not doing anything and I should say so plainly.

title: Sort the shoebox of receipts before warranty claims expire
body: Two receipts already went missing exactly when I needed them for a return, and the box keeps growing without a system. /Today/: pull out everything from the last twelve months, photograph each one, and bin the paper once it's backed up.

title: Get straight what goodput means versus plain throughput in serving
body: Write one worked example where throughput looks great but *goodput under the latency target* is much lower.

title: Write manual data parallelism first, then swap in DDP and compare
body: Before trusting the wrapper I want to have written the thing it replaces: each rank runs forward and backward on its own shard, then I all_reduce every gradient by hand and divide by world size. Get that matching a single-process run to a few decimals, then swap in DistributedDataParallel and time both. Report scaling efficiency as throughput on N GPUs over N times throughput on one, and note where the bucketed overlap starts to matter. Keep the model small enough that communication, not compute, is what I end up looking at. [[obsidian:DDP Scaling Notes]]

title: Write down what a Fenwick tree does that a segment tree cannot
Read up on difference-in-differences and the parallel trends assumption

body: The architecture only makes sense to me on paper, and I cannot say what actually leaves each client. Simulate three clients with separate data folders, run a few rounds of federated averaging, and write down exactly which tensors get sent to the server and what could be inferred from them.

title: Prepare properly for next month's book club meeting
body: Last time I turned up having skimmed the last third that morning and said almost nothing useful for an hour. This time finish the book a full week early, then spend twenty minutes writing down three things that actually confused me and one passage worth reading aloud. Bring the physical copy with sticky notes on those pages instead of trying to remember where anything was during the discussion. The point of the meeting is the conversation, not proving I finished it, and I keep forgetting that under time pressure.

title: Extract the compute cost model from the Chinchilla scaling paper
body: I keep quoting 'twenty tokens per parameter' without being able to say where it comes from. Read the paper's three estimation approaches, write out the loss as a function of parameters and tokens under a fixed budget of roughly 6ND FLOPs, and note which fitted constants the rule depends on. Then judge how far it stretches to a small model trained with inference cost in mind, where overtraining past the optimum is deliberate.

title: Clean up the password manager's health report properly this time
body: The password manager has been flagging the same forty-odd weak and reused passwords for months, and I keep dismissing the warning instead of doing anything about it. Most of them are old accounts I don't even use anymore, which is its own problem — dead logins sitting around with reused passwords are just extra ways in. Go through the report properly: close the accounts that are dead weight, rotate the passwords that guard anything that matters, and generate fresh unique ones for what's left. Do it in batches of ten so it doesn't turn into another abandoned afternoon.

title: Read the RETRO or Self-RAG paper and pull out what applies
body: Read one grounded-generation paper properly, not just the abstract, and write down the three or four findings I could actually use in a small retrieval setup. Note how they measure whether an answer is supported by the retrieved text, since that is the part I usually gloss over. Then decide on a small experiment: a fixed set of questions, answers with and without retrieval, and a manual check of about fifty outputs. *The key output is a one-page summary of what to apply*, not a full reproduction. body: Every review I do is ad hoc: sometimes I read line by line, sometimes I skim the diff for the shape of the change and miss the null check hiding in =utils.py=. Write a short checklist — intent, edge cases, tests, naming — and force myself through it in order before commenting, so the feedback I give is about the code and not about whichever pass I happened to make first. title: Diagnose the recurring CUDA out-of-memory error on the fine-tune
body:
The run dies at a different step each time, which points at fragmentation or a growing tensor rather than a simple size problem. Things to check:
- Compare =memory_allocated= against =memory_reserved= at the failing step
- Dump =torch.cuda.memory_snapshot()= and look at the free block sizes
- Try =PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True= and see if the crash moves
- Check whether any list is accumulating tensors that still hold the graph
[[obsidian:CUDA OOM debugging notes]]

title: Survey audio generation models and their preference leaderboards

title: Redesign the settings dialog in the habit tracker app

title: Decide how much of diffusion sampling speed-up is worth learning
body: Sampling latency is the practical cost of diffusion models, and the literature on shortening it is wide: DDIM-style deterministic samplers, higher-order ODE solvers, distillation into few-step models, and consistency models. I want the shape of the trade-off, not every paper. Read the DDIM paper first and write down why fewer steps work at all, meaning what the deterministic reformulation buys. Then compare step counts against sample quality for two solvers on one small pretrained model, noting where =20 steps= starts to look noticeably worse than 50. Finish with a short note on when distillation is worth its training cost against just picking a better sampler.

title: Explain the *bias-variance decomposition* without looking at my notes

title: Read a book that bridges classical and neural retrieval

title: Collect concrete cases where simple randomized methods beat learned ones
body:
Every time a project drifts toward a large model I should first ask what a boring baseline would have done, and I have no list of cases where the boring option actually won. Start collecting them: random search matching or beating grid search and often Bayesian optimisation at equal budget, a simple linear model with a few good features against a tuned boosted ensemble on small tabular data, and a plain difference in means from a randomized experiment against any elaborate causal estimator.

For each case write down the reason it works, not just the result, because the reasons are what transfer: low effective dimension for random search, variance dominating bias on small samples, and randomization removing confounding by design. Finish with a one-page checklist of baselines to run before anything with more than a few thousand parameters.

title: Decide once whether a hardware display calibrator is worth buying
body:
Every print has come back slightly warmer than it looked on screen for two years running, and I keep fixing it by eye afterwards rather than at the source. The laptop panel has never been profiled, it was calibrated once by guesswork with an online chart and a squint, and that is not a colour-managed workflow, it is a colour-hoped-for workflow.

Before spending money, work out what the calibrator would actually fix. Borrow one if possible, or use a shop's, profile the display, then reprint the same test image that came back warm and compare it under the same light as before. If the mismatch disappears, the device pays for itself within a few prints a year at the local lab's prices; if it does not, the problem is downstream in the printer profile and no amount of screen calibration will touch it. Either way, write down the actual working distance and ambient light setup once it is dialled in, because I will not remember it in six months and will end up redoing this whole test. title: Chain a pipeline to transcribe piano recordings into sheet music
body:
The obvious chain is onset detection, then pitch tracking per note, then quantising the timing into a grid coarse enough to stay readable, then exporting to a format a notation program can open. Off-the-shelf models handle solo piano reasonably well on a single clean recording, so the plan is to run one full piece through the whole pipeline end to end before judging any single stage in isolation.

The likely failure points are polyphony, sustain-pedal blur, and dynamics that get quantised into a handful of arbitrary velocity buckets. Run the same passage through with and without pedal to see how much the pitch tracker actually degrades, and keep a short list of exactly where the output diverges from the score I already know by hand, bar by bar, rather than a vague sense that it sounds wrong somewhere in the middle.

title: Plan the load test for the inference endpoint before the launch date
body:
Launching without knowing where the endpoint falls over would be a bet I do not need to make, and a load test run carelessly is nearly as bad because it either proves nothing or takes the shared staging cluster down for everybody. So plan it on paper first.

Start from the traffic estimate: expected peak requests per second, the ratio of short to long prompts, and the latency target at the 95th and 99th percentile. Build the test from replayed real request shapes, not a uniform synthetic prompt, since token length drives GPU time far more than request count. Ramp in steps, hold each step long enough for queues to settle, and record where p99 bends upward, which is the number I actually want. Then work out the cost: instance hours for the test, the price per hour of the GPU type, and how long the run will take including warm-up and one rerun. Agree the window with whoever shares staging, and set a hard stop on spend so a runaway script cannot eat the month's budget. Finish with a one-paragraph capacity statement: replicas needed at peak with 30 percent headroom. [[obsidian:Load testing plan]]

title: Separate aleatoric from epistemic uncertainty with a small ensemble experiment
body:
I use the two words loosely and would not be able to say which one a given model output is capturing. Fix that with a tiny regression problem where the noise level changes across the input range and there is a gap in the middle with no training data at all.

Train a five-member ensemble where each member predicts a mean and a variance. Average predicted variances to get the aleatoric part, and take the variance of the member means as the epistemic part. What I expect: aleatoric follows the noise pattern everywhere, while *epistemic blows up only inside the gap* and shrinks with more data. If the two are tangled, that is the interesting result and the thing to understand.

Then repeat with a single network trained by plain MSE and note what it cannot tell me. Save the plots and a paragraph in the notebook, and try explaining the distinction to myself without using the word reducible.

title: Build a mask-based image editing tool as a learning project
body:
The goal is to understand how the pieces fit together, not to make a better Photoshop. Start with a segmentation model that gives a mask from a click on the image; Segment Anything is the obvious choice and has a friendly demo to compare against. Get the mask out as a plain black and white PNG and display it over the picture at half opacity so I can see what it thinks the object is.

Then do the smallest useful edit with that mask: blur the background, or desaturate everything outside it. Only after that works, try object removal by feeding the masked image to an inpainting model, and compare the result against simple blur-fill so I can see what the heavy model actually buys. Style transfer can wait for a separate task, since it has different inputs and would blur the lesson. Keep everything in one notebook, with one cell per stage, so the flow from click to mask to edit stays visible. Save inputs and outputs side by side in a folder so I can look back at failures, because the failures, such as ragged edges and ghost shadows, are where most of the learning will be.

title: Decide whether daily sunscreen earns a permanent place in the routine
body:
Three years of longer weekend rides means three years of extra UV exposure on the forearms and the back of the neck, and the base tan I used to treat as protection is not actually doing much once you look at the actual absorption numbers. The skin cancer risk in cyclists and outdoor workers is well documented, and the evidence for daily broad-spectrum SPF as prevention rather than just sunburn avoidance is about as solid as anything in dermatology gets — it is one of the few habit changes with genuinely good trial data behind it rather than just plausible mechanism.

The resistance so far has been purely logistical: forgetting it before an early start, the greasy feel under gloves, and not wanting another bottle cluttering the bathroom shelf. None of that is a reason not to do it, just a reason to make it frictionless — a travel-size tube left in the kit bag itself rather than the bathroom, applied at the same point as putting on the gloves so it becomes part of the same motion rather than a separate decision each morning. Try it for a month before deciding whether it earns a permanent slot. [[obsidian:Skin and sun exposure]]

body: My prompts read like notes to myself: "clean this up", "make it better". *State the goal, the audience, the constraints and one example of good output* every time. Take five recent vague prompts, rewrite them properly, run both versions, and keep the pairs for comparison.

title: Compare linear attention variants against softmax attention on paper
body: Write out the kernel-feature view and the recurrent form for each variant, side by side. [[obsidian:Sequence Model Cheatsheet]]

title: Read the Sutton and Barto chapter on exploration again, slowly
Work through the from-scratch LLM book chapter by chapter
body: I keep using transformer libraries without being able to explain what happens between the token IDs and the logits, and that gap shows up every time a training run misbehaves. Go through the build-an-LLM-from-scratch book in order: tokenizer, attention, the GPT block, pretraining loop, then the fine-tuning chapters. Type the code out instead of pasting it, and after each chapter write three sentences on what I would have got wrong before. title: Turn the conflicting advice on morning caffeine into one protocol

title: Write down the family medical history before the next check-up
body: Doctors weigh screening ages by family history, and mine currently lives in my head as vague impressions. Ask my mother and my aunt about cancers, heart events and diabetes, note ages at diagnosis, and save it in one place before I book anything. [[obsidian:Family Medical History]]

body: The last mock answer drifted into infra trivia and never got to the ranking model tradeoffs. Time-box thirty minutes, force myself through requirements, then scale, then model, and note the gaps in [[obsidian:ML System Design Practice Log]].

title: Plot regression to the mean with repeated noisy measurements
Read Thinking, Fast and Slow and mark which claims still hold
body:
Everyone quotes it and I have absorbed most of it second-hand, which is exactly the problem: I cannot say which parts I have actually checked. Several of the priming studies in the early chapters got caught up in the replication trouble, while loss aversion and the planning fallacy seem to have fared much better. Get a summary first, then read only the chapters on anchoring, the planning fallacy and the two-systems framing, and skip the long middle on prospect theory unless the summary says it earns the time.

While reading, keep a two-column list: claims with solid replications, and claims that rest on one small study. *The point is a sorted list of what still holds, not a book report.* Then look up the replication status of the three shakiest ones before writing anything down, and finish with one paragraph on what I would change in how I make estimates at work.

title: Break down model usage stats by day week and month
body: Right now it is one lifetime counter, nowhere near granular enough to spot patterns.
