body: I always say I prefer landscapes, but nobody's ever actually in a photo I took.

title: Write down which classical RL failure modes reappear in RLHF runs
body: Reward hacking is the obvious one, but the list should be longer: distribution shift between the policy and the reward model as training moves off the data it was fit on, credit assignment over long sequences with a single terminal reward, exploration collapse when entropy drops early, and off-policy staleness when rollouts lag the learner. For each, put one sentence on how it looks in a training curve, so I can recognise it rather than just name it. Keep the note short enough to reread before starting a new run.

title: Check tetanus and typhoid status before the trekking trip
body: It's been over a decade since the last tetanus booster and I have no record of ever having typhoid coverage. Look up the current travel vaccination guidance for the region, then book the travel clinic appointment at least six weeks before departure to allow for a full course rather than a single dose.

title: Set up TransformerLens and open the public sparse autoencoder releases
body: Get a notebook loading GPT-2 small with activation caching working.

title: Buy a small foldable daypack for the next trip
body: The gym backpack I've been using doubles as an overnight bag but weighs almost a kilo empty, which defeats the point on a trip where every gram in the carry-on counts. The Matador-style packable daypacks fold into their own pocket and *weigh under 200 grams*, small enough to live in the bottom of the main bag until there's a day trip or extra shopping to carry back. Check reviews for seam durability before ordering, since the ultralight fabric is the usual trade-off on these.

title: Read up on reward hacking before designing the next reward
body: Every reward I've hand-written so far has been gamed in some way I didn't predict.

body: Ask the surgery for my vaccine record and check whether a tetanus booster or the shingles jab is due.

title: Make window functions and CTEs automatic instead of looked-up
body:
Every time a query needs a running total or a latest-row-per-group, I still open a tab and search. That is fine for a job, but in an interview the hesitation reads as not knowing, and it eats the minutes I need for the actual problem. The fix is repetition on a small set of shapes, not reading more documentation.

Pick six patterns and write each from a blank editor until I can do it without peeking: running sum with an explicit frame, top-N per group using row_number, gap between consecutive events using lag, rank versus dense_rank on ties, first and last value per partition, and a two-step CTE that filters after the window is computed (since a window cannot go in WHERE). Use one small made-up orders table so the data stops being a distraction and only the syntax is being tested.

The part I usually get wrong is the default frame when there is an ORDER BY inside OVER, which quietly changes what last_value returns. Write a query that demonstrates it, so it is remembered as a bug I have seen rather than a rule I have read. Time each pattern; anything over three minutes goes back on the list for tomorrow. Stop when all six are clean twice in a row on different days.

title: Learn how git bisect finds the commit that broke things
Decide how synonym and antonym fields attach to entries
body: Each word entry needs optional synonym, antonym and related-word slots before I add more languages.

title: Compare Welch, Student and Mann-Whitney on ugly data
body: I default to the plain t-test and could not say when that is the wrong call. Generate groups with unequal variances, unequal sizes, and heavily skewed data, run Student, Welch and Mann-Whitney on each, and record false positive rate and power under the null and a small shift. Use =5000= replicates per cell so the differences are not noise. Finish with a short table of which test to reach for in which situation, in my own words.

body: Read the "rethinking generalization" result on fitting random labels and note which bounds it breaks.

body: Two contractors' hours are still flagged for review and payroll cuts off Friday. Open the approval queue this afternoon instead of leaving it for the last minute again.

title: Plan the =locust= load test before touching the staging cluster
body:
A load test run blind either proves nothing or knocks over a shared environment, so the plan should exist on paper first.

body: Keep one screen for reading, one for tools, and drop everything I have not opened this year.

title: Learn how survey weights change what a proportion actually means
body: An unweighted average of survey responses describes the people who answered, not the population, and I keep forgetting that. Work through post-stratification and inverse probability weights on a small made-up sample where one age group is badly over-represented. Compute the weighted and unweighted estimate, then the design effect and effective sample size, since weighting widens the confidence interval. Note down what to ask about any survey before believing its headline figure: who was sampled, who responded, and how they were reweighted.

title: Track the recurring headaches and medication use for a month
body:
The headaches are frequent enough now that guessing the pattern from memory isn't working anymore.
- Log time, intensity, and any trigger foods or sleep the night before
- Note every painkiller taken and the dose, since overuse itself can cause more headaches
- Track whether screen breaks or hydration make any measurable difference
Four weeks of this before the GP appointment, details in [[obsidian:Headache diary]].

body: Every prompt tweak so far ships on vibes, and the last one quietly broke date handling. Curate 60 real inputs with expected outputs, run them in CI on each prompt change, and block the merge if the pass rate drops below the last release.

body: Consolidate the sticky-note chaos into one page. [[obsidian:Planning meeting notes]]

body: The chain's been squeaking since the last rainy commute, and dry rust starts a rot that's expensive to fix later. Degrease it, apply =GT85=, wipe the excess, and check the gears shift cleanly before the ride to work tomorrow.

body: Every editor I use treats Escape as a mode switch and Caps Lock sits right under my pinky doing nothing useful. title: Plan the dinner menu for guests visiting next weekend

Pick a main that can be made a day ahead and only needs reheating, a side that can sit at room temperature, and a dessert that does not need the oven at the same time as everything else. Write the shopping list on Thursday so there is a spare day if something is out of stock, and confirm numbers with everyone by Wednesday at the latest.

title: Trace the Stable Video Diffusion pipeline from pixels to pixels

title: Build a retraining job that only promotes a better model
body:
Right now retraining is a notebook I run when I remember, and whatever comes out overwrites the previous model. That is backwards. *The job must promote a new model only if it beats the current one on the held-out set*, and otherwise leave production alone and log why.

Smallest version that counts: a script that trains, evaluates against the model currently marked as production in the registry, and compares one metric with a small margin so noise does not cause flip-flopping. If it wins, register it and move the alias; if not, exit cleanly. Then run it from a Kubernetes CronJob or a scheduled cloud pipeline on a tiny dataset so a full run takes minutes, not hours.

Things to decide up front: which metric, what margin, and what happens when the evaluation data itself changes. Run it three times, once with a deliberately worse model, to see the rejection path actually work. Turn the schedule off when done so it does not keep spending money.

title: Understand two-stage retrieval and what each stage is allowed to cost
body: Every search system I read about splits cheap candidate generation from an expensive reranker, and I can recite that without explaining why. title: Write next week's language goal before Monday morning
Derive logistic regression from the likelihood and read the odds ratios
body:
I keep quoting odds ratios from model output without being able to say where they come from, which is a bad habit when a colleague asks whether a coefficient of 0.4 is big. Start from the Bernoulli likelihood, write the log-likelihood, take the gradient and show it reduces to X^T(y - p). Note why there is no closed form and that Newton's method turns into iteratively reweighted least squares.

Then the practical half: exponentiate a coefficient, say what it means holding the other predictors fixed, and why it is not a change in probability. Work one example by hand with a binary predictor such as a customer being on a discount plan, then check it against a fitted model on a toy dataset. Finish by writing down what happens to the estimates under perfect separation, because that is the failure I have actually hit and could not explain.
[[obsidian:Logistic Regression Derivation and Odds Ratios]]

title: Learn how to test a system whose outputs change every run
body: Ordinary assertions break the moment the output is a sampled sentence or a model retrained on fresh data. I need a working vocabulary for this: fixed seeds and their limits, property-based checks, tolerance bands on metrics, golden sets with graded rather than exact matches, and using a second model as a judge with its own known biases. Also work out what belongs in CI versus a nightly run, since the expensive evals cannot gate every commit. Write a short note on one concrete test strategy for an LLM summariser: what is checked deterministically, what statistically, and what only a human reviews.

title: Consolidate the scattered photo and video library into one tree
body:
The photo library is currently four separate things pretending to be one: the old iPhoto library nobody opens anymore, a Lightroom catalog on the NAS that only covers 2019 onward, whatever the phone has auto-uploaded to cloud storage, and a folder of scanned prints from before any of this existed. Finding a specific photo means guessing which of the four it's in, and duplicates have crept in every time I've tried to consolidate before and given up halfway.

This time the plan is a single folder tree organised by year and month, filenames normalised to a consistent date-based scheme, and one pass of a deduplication tool before anything gets merged rather than after. The old iPhoto and Lightroom catalogs get exported to plain files first — I don't want the archive depending on either application still existing in ten years. Videos follow the same tree rather than living separately by device. Once the merge is done, the four old locations get archived read-only rather than deleted, in case the dedupe missed something. Refs: [[obsidian:Photo Library Reorganisation]].

title: Build a regression gate for the retriever before touching chunking again

title: Explain why a well-calibrated model can still be a poor classifier
body: Calibration and discrimination keep getting merged in my head. A model that predicts the base rate for everyone is perfectly calibrated and useless, and a sharp model with an overconfident tail can rank well and still be miscalibrated. Fit logistic regression and a small gradient-boosted model on one tabular dataset, draw reliability diagrams for both, and put AUC and expected calibration error side by side. Then try temperature scaling on the held-out fold and see which number moves and which does not. The goal is a paragraph I could say aloud without notes.

title: Set up a CI release gate for the RAG assistant using the golden set
body:
Right now a prompt or retriever change goes out on the strength of me trying five questions and thinking it looks fine. That is how a quiet regression gets in, and I only find out when someone reports a wrong answer weeks later. The fix is to make the check automatic and boring, so it runs whether or not I feel careful that day.

Plan: keep the golden set in the repo as a versioned file with question, expected key facts and the source passage it should cite. On every pull request, run the whole set through the candidate pipeline at temperature zero, score with a mix of cheap deterministic checks (citation present, key facts contained, no forbidden phrases) and a small judge-model rubric for the rest, and compare against the last released baseline instead of an absolute number. *Fail the build on any drop in the must-pass subset, and on a drop beyond the noise band for the rest.* Measure that noise band first by running the unchanged system ten times, since judge scores wobble. Also decide who is allowed to update expected answers, because a gate that anyone can quietly edit protects nothing.

title: Collect behavioral stories into a bank tagged by competency
body: Right now every loop I reach for the same two stories and stretch them to fit questions they don't answer. Write down ten distinct stories, tag each by competency, and *always keep one metric per story* so the answer stays concrete.

title: Work out GPU autoscaling and what a cold start really costs
body:
Scaling a GPU pool up on demand sounds like a solved problem until you count what happens between a pod being pending and the first token being served. The node has to be provisioned, the driver and device plugin have to come up, the image has to be pulled, and the weights have to be loaded into memory. For a large model that chain can take many minutes, and that is the number that decides whether scaling from zero is acceptable or just embarrassing.

Start by reading how the cluster autoscaler and a queue-based or request-based autoscaler differ, and what signal each one scales on. CPU utilization is a poor signal for GPU work, so look at queue depth or requests in flight instead. Then time a real cold start on the test cluster, broken into node ready, image pulled, weights loaded and first response, so I can see which stage dominates.

After that list the trade-offs plainly: keep one warm replica and pay for idle hours, scale from zero and accept the delay, or pre-pull images and cache weights on local disk to shrink the gap. Decide which fits a bursty workload with a tolerable wait of about a minute, and write down the cost of the warm option per day so the choice is a number instead of a preference.

title: Put a real kernel on the roofline plot for once
body: Take one matmul and one layernorm, compute FLOPs per byte, and mark both against the card's ridge point.

title: Plan the shard and replica layout for the main index
body: Right now the whole corpus sits on one node and a rebuild means downtime. Sketch a layout with shard count, replica count and a blue-green rebuild into a fresh alias, using the current =40 GB= index as the sizing baseline, and note what breaks if one shard is lost.

title: Find out what QK-norm does to attention logit growth
body: Read one paper on attention-logit blowup and note the fix it proposes.

title: Buy a small rechargeable headlamp for camping trips
body: The current torch runs out mid-hike and charging cables never make the pack.

title: Compare MHA, MQA and GQA by how much KV cache each one costs
body: The cache size per token is what decides batch size at long context, so I want the arithmetic straight.

title: Clean the career notes folder and turn the stub into a *prep hub*
body: Move the loose files into subfolders and make the stub link out to everything.

title: Audit which third-party apps have access to the main email account
body: Over the years plenty of apps and services have asked for permission to read or send from the main email account, and most of those integrations were one-off tasks finished long ago. Open the connected apps page, go through the full list, and revoke anything that is not actively used today. A handful of these still have full read and send access from services I stopped using entirely, which is a bigger risk than any password would be on its own. Do this before setting up the password manager, since a compromised email account undermines everything else downstream.

title: Compare response-level, on-policy and self-distillation and note where each wins
body: The word distillation covers at least four different things, and the differences decide which one to reach for. Response-level is the cheap one: sample from a big teacher, fine-tune the student on the outputs, and it copies style more than reasoning. On-policy distillation has the student generate and the teacher score each token, which closes the gap between the training data and what the student actually produces. Self-distillation and few-step distillation are further variants. Write one row per variant: signal, cost, failure mode.

title: Swap =ReLU= for GELU in a small MLP and compare gradients
body: Log per-layer gradient norms for both over the first few hundred steps and plot them on one axis.

title: Try the two-minute rule from Getting Things Done for two weeks
body: Small chores pile up because I defer anything that takes a minute. Run the rule for a fortnight and note in =trial-log.org= each evening how many things I closed on the spot.

title: Try spaced repetition on interview stories instead of cramming
body:
Every time an interview comes up I rewrite the same five stories from scratch the night before, and the details drift depending on my mood. Cramming just re-derives the same material under pressure, which is the opposite of a rehearsed answer. The stories that come out smoothly are the ones told out loud enough times to be automatic, not the ones read the night before.

Write five core stories once, each as bullet points for situation, action and result, not full prose. Review them on a spaced schedule - day one, three, seven, then fourteen - saying each aloud from memory rather than reading it, noting which one is still shaky. By the time an actual interview is scheduled, the review should just confirm what is already fluent, not build it from nothing under pressure.

title: Skim the WebRTC overview before touching audio transport
body:
Good map of the moving parts: ICE, STUN/TURN, RTP and codecs.
https://webrtc.org/getting-started/overview

title: Make the payment-calling agent safe to retry without double charging
body:
The agent calls an API that has real side effects, and at the moment a timeout means I cannot tell whether the call happened. If the loop just retries, I will eventually create a duplicate. Learn how idempotency keys work properly: who generates them, how long the server remembers them, and what happens when the same key arrives with a different payload.

Then the retry side. Exponential backoff with full jitter, a cap on attempts per call, and a global retry budget so that a bad hour downstream does not turn into a retry storm from my side. Start with a budget of roughly =10%= of request volume and see whether that is sensible. Write the key derivation as a small function that hashes task id plus step number, so a resumed run reuses the same key instead of minting a new one. Finish with a test that kills the process mid-call and checks that only one side effect lands.

title: Check the law of large numbers with a running mean plot
body: Plot the running mean of =100000= fair coin flips and see how slowly it settles.

title: Pull flashcard review stats into the vocabulary app database
body: I study words in the flashcard app but the vocabulary tool has no idea what I know. *Import the exported review history into a table* keyed by word, with last-reviewed date and ease, so the tool can highlight weak words. Start with a CSV export.

body: Ordered list of what to delete and in what order, so nothing keeps billing. [[obsidian:K8s Teardown Runbook]]

title: Compare He and Xavier init on a =20-layer= plain net
body: Log activation std per layer at step zero and after =100= steps, then see where the signal dies.

title: Check what the autumn trip needs in vaccines and malaria advice

Consider a spare of the merino base layer that fits
Settle on a default architecture for agents after reading the published designs
body: I have read pieces of several agent-design articles and come away with a vague feeling rather than a decision. Pick three of the well-known ones, read them properly in one sitting, and write down what each says about who holds authority and what tools the model can reach. Then commit to a default: *the model proposes, deterministic code decides*, and every tool is scoped to the narrowest thing the task needs. Note where each article disagrees with that default and whether the disagreement is worth caring about. One page in the notes, not an essay, and revisit only if a real project breaks it.

title: Learn the convergence rate of gradient descent on smooth convex functions
body: Every learning-rate argument I hear rests on this and I have only ever nodded at it. Prove the O(1/t) bound under L-smoothness with step size 1/L, then see what strong convexity changes and why the rate becomes linear. Keep it to one page of proof, not a textbook chapter. title: Rehearse the conflict-story answer until it fits ninety seconds
body: Every time this question comes up I ramble for three minutes and lose the point. Time a tight answer to ninety seconds, write the beats down, and rehearse aloud twice this week. [[obsidian:Interview story bank]]

body: Run both variants across a few clipping thresholds and plot bias against variance.

title: Build a nightly job that fetches new preprints and mails a digest
body: I keep meaning to follow a handful of arXiv categories and instead scroll the listing page once a month and lose an evening. Write a small script that pulls yesterday's submissions from the API, filters on a keyword list, stores hits in SQLite keyed by arXiv id, and mails a plain-text digest. *Dedupe on the id before anything else*, because a digest that repeats last week's items gets muted by the third day. Cron on the home server is enough; no framework.

title: Sketch a side project ranking financial news headlines by relevance
body: Start with a small labelled set of earnings-related text and compare a simple baseline against an embedding model.

title: Add Stanford CS224N to the queue and start with lecture one
body: Word vectors, attention and the transformer lectures are the part of NLP I keep half-knowing from blog posts. Course page is web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n. Watch the first two lectures on YouTube and look at assignment one before deciding on pace.

title: Compare DPO and its variants by the instability each one targets
body:
I keep lumping DPO, IPO, KTO and SimPO together as one thing, and I could not say why any of them exist beyond the original. Make a small table with one row per method and three columns: what the loss looks like, what failure it addresses, and what it costs.
Start from DPO and the implicit reward derived from the KL-regularised objective, then note the known problem that both chosen and rejected log-probabilities can drop together, and that the method can overfit when preferences are near-deterministic. IPO is meant to address that with a squared loss. KTO works from unpaired good and bad labels. SimPO removes the reference model and uses length-normalised log-probability. For each, find one sentence in the original paper that states the motivation, and copy it into the table so I am not paraphrasing from memory.
Then decide which of the four I would try first on a small model with a noisy preference set, and why. If there is time, run the cheapest one on a tiny dataset and watch the reward margin during training.

title: Work out which ZeRO stage fits a 1B model on 24GB
body: Tabulate per-GPU memory for stages 1, 2 and 3 and note that *stage 3 buys memory by paying in extra all-gathers* every step.

title: Build a query-decomposition RAG loop for multi-hop questions
body: Single-shot retrieval keeps failing on questions that need two documents joined, and I only have a hunch about why. Take HotpotQA's dev set, split each question into sub-queries with a small model, retrieve per sub-query, and write up exact-match against the plain single-query baseline with a few failure cases.

title: Set a realistic weekly page target for the memoir
body: Twenty pages a week sounded fine back in spring and now the book is three months behind my own schedule. Cut the target to something I will actually hit on a bad week and track it weekly. [[obsidian:Reading goals 2026]]

title: Study prefix caching and lay prompts out so the cache actually hits
body:
Most of my prompts start with a system block, then some retrieved documents, then the user question, and I have never checked whether the front of that is byte-identical between calls. Prefix caching only pays when the shared part comes first and does not change, so a timestamp or a per-user name near the top quietly kills every hit. Read how vLLM's automatic prefix caching hashes blocks and how the hosted providers describe cached-token pricing, then take one real prompt template and move the stable parts up and the volatile parts down.

Then measure it rather than believing it: send the same template fifty times before and after the reshuffle and compare time-to-first-token and the cached-token count in the usage field. Also write down where semantic caching differs, since it matches on meaning and can return a wrong answer with confidence, which prefix caching never does. Keep the before and after numbers in the note so the layout rule has evidence behind it. [[obsidian:LLM prompt layout and caching]]

title: Compare my reading list with a maintained curated recsys list
body: Note which gaps matter. [[obsidian:Recommender Systems Reading List]]

body: Film the screen with slow-motion phone video at three brightness levels and note any banding in the frames.

title: Find out what grokking actually claims and what is still disputed
body: The phrase gets used for any delayed generalization curve. Read the original modular arithmetic paper and one later explanation about weight decay and circuit formation, then write a short note separating what was shown from what is speculation.

title: Write down when a rules engine beats a model
body: Half the proposals I hear are ML for problems with six stable conditions and no labelled data. Build a checklist: label availability, rate of change, cost of a wrong answer, need for explanation. Then apply it to two past projects and see which should have been rules.

title: Work out what embedding dimension actually buys me
body: I default to 768 or 1024 dimensions without knowing what is lost at 256. Read up on Matryoshka-style /truncatable/ embeddings, then take one model that supports them and plot retrieval recall against truncated dimension on my own small corpus. Note where the curve flattens.

title: Renew the health insurance before the current policy lapses
body: The policy renews automatically next month at a higher premium unless I compare alternatives first. Spend an hour on a comparison site, check the dental cover specifically, and either switch or confirm the current one is still the best deal.

title: Compare Welch, Student and Mann-Whitney on skewed data with unequal variances
body: I default to whichever t-test the library picks and could not defend the choice. Simulate three setups: equal variances and normal data, unequal variances with unequal group sizes, and heavily skewed lognormal data. For each, run Student, Welch and Mann-Whitney ten thousand times and record the false positive rate under the null and the power under a modest shift. The point to pin down is that *Welch loses almost nothing when variances are equal and saves you when they are not*, so it should be the default. Write the result as a small table in the stats notes, with one line on when rank tests answer a different question rather than a robust version of the same one.

Submit the conference travel expense report before it expires

The finance portal gives sixty days from the trip end date, and this is week five already. Sort receipts by category — flights, hotel, meals — convert the two cash ones manually since the card feed missed them, attach the boarding pass as proof of dates, and submit before the window closes and it turns into an exception request nobody wants to process.

title: Get multiple comparisons straight before reading another results table
body: Every paper with twenty metrics and a few bolded wins makes me wonder how many of those wins are noise. Work through the arithmetic of familywise error, then Bonferroni, Holm and Benjamini-Hochberg, and simulate a hundred null comparisons to watch about five come out significant. *The key thing to internalise is that the number of comparisons made counts, not just the ones reported.* Write down a rule for what I do when I compare several model variants on my own data.

title: Learn why =Arc<Mutex<T>>= keeps appearing in the Rust tools
body: I use ripgrep and a few other Rust tools daily and could not read a single source file in them without stalling. The goal is modest: not to write Rust fluently, only to follow ownership, borrowing, traits and the common smart pointer types well enough to understand what the code is doing. Work through the ownership and smart pointer chapters of the official book, then open a small file from a tool I already use and annotate it line by line. title: Read Sutton and Barto's RL book, introductory chapters only
body: Every reinforcement learning tutorial I have followed leans on vocabulary I only half own: value functions, bootstrapping, the difference between on-policy and off-policy. The canonical textbook is free and written to be read in order, so start at the beginning and stop once the tabular methods are solid, roughly the first eight chapters. Skip the function approximation maths on the first pass. Do the small examples like the gridworld and the bandit by hand or in a short script instead of nodding along, because reading the update rule is not the same as being able to write it. title: Write a tiny async task scheduler to understand Python's event loop
body: I use =async/await= daily without knowing what the loop actually does between awaits. Build a toy scheduler from generators: a ready queue, a =sleep= primitive and a timer heap. *Once it runs three interleaved tasks correctly, the event loop stops being magic.*

title: Draft a real career goal instead of vague drifting
body: For the last year the plan has basically been *keep applying and see what sticks*, which isn't a plan at all. Pick one direction — technical lead or product-adjacent — and name the specific skill gap for each: system design depth for one, stakeholder communication for the other. Write down what a good outcome looks like twelve months out, then check it against actual applications instead of whatever job posting catches my eye that week. The point isn't to lock in forever, just to stop reacting.

title: Review the reading-tracker project area by area before new features

Take a tiny sequence, work through both forms by hand, and see where the kernel trick removes the quadratic term and what gets lost. Then read one paper that tries to recover the lost quality.

body: Expert choice flips the question so each expert picks its tokens, which fixes imbalance by construction but breaks down for autoregressive decoding. Read the Google expert-choice paper and note *what it does to per-token compute variability* in a short table.

title: Read up on double descent and summarize it precisely, not loosely

I want to know exactly what the claim is: test error peaking near the interpolation threshold, then falling again as parameters keep growing, and the version that shows up in epoch-wise and sample-wise curves too. Read the original paper and one clear follow-up, then write half a page covering the setup, what the classical bias-variance picture gets wrong, and which conditions are needed. Also do the tiny min-norm least-squares experiment with random features to see the peak myself instead of taking it on trust.

title: Try the "reverse brainstorm" technique on the flaky deploy problem

Take the flaky deploy pipeline, spend fifteen minutes listing ways to make it *fail on purpose*, then invert each one into a fix. Note afterwards whether it produced anything I would not have thought of by just staring at it.

body: Replace the nested loops in =pairwise.py= with one broadcast subtraction and time both versions.

body: The word agent covers everything from a chat loop with tools to long-running planners, and I cannot place the interoperability protocols against those types. Sort agents into four or five kinds, then read the public specs for Model Context Protocol and Agent2Agent and write down which layer each one covers and where they overlap.

body: Loading a /pickle/ checkpoint runs arbitrary code, so check whether safetensors covers my cases.

Try the Pomodoro technique for two weeks before judging it

title: Learn what CUPED actually assumes before trusting the variance reduction
Review how a ranker corrects for position bias inside the model
body:
There are two broad ways to deal with position bias in a tree ranker, and I have only ever used the cheap one. The cheap one is to add position as a feature at training time and set it to a constant at serving time, which works surprisingly often but quietly assumes the position effect is separable from relevance. The other is to learn propensities and reweight the loss, as in the inverse propensity scoring papers, or to learn relevance and examination jointly with a two-tower or regression-EM setup.

Pick the ranker we already have and write down which of these it does, if any. *The key question is whether the position feature leaks into the relevance score at serving time*, because if it does then every offline gain I have seen is partly the bias feeding itself. Then check what the library gives me: LightGBM has =lambdarank= with position debiasing arguments, and I should read what those actually do rather than trusting the parameter name. Finish with a short list of the propensity estimation options that fit our logs, and which would need randomisation we do not have.

title: Score the anomaly detector with almost no labels
body: Hand-label the top fifty alerts and a random fifty from the rest, then estimate precision and rough recall from those.

title: Pull word frequency data to rank the German list
body: Grab a frequency corpus and reorder the =German.csv= list by real usage rank.

title: Learn how to actually run on-call for a model serving stack
body:
Most of what I know about on-call is from web services, and ML adds failure modes that do not page anyone: silent drift, a stale feature table, an upstream schema change that keeps returning plausible-looking numbers. The first task is to list which of those would actually trigger an alert today and which would only be found by a customer.

Then read a few public runbooks and postmortem templates, and work out what a runbook for a model incident needs that a service runbook does not. My guess: how to roll back to the previous model version, how to switch to a fallback rule, who can decide that a degraded model is better than no model, and how to tell a data problem from a model problem in the first ten minutes.

End with a draft one-page runbook for a single made-up ranking service and a blameless postmortem outline with a section for what the monitoring failed to notice. The goal is to discuss severity levels and escalation paths for ML systems without borrowing vocabulary that does not fit.

title: Find out where gensim and older word2vec code stands today
body: Check whether gensim is still maintained and what people use now instead for embeddings.

title: Reproduce the classic t-SNE pitfalls on a dataset I know well
body: Everyone warns that cluster sizes and distances in t-SNE and UMAP plots mean little, but I have never seen it break myself. Run both on =MNIST= subsets at perplexity 5, 30 and 100, vary the seeds, and save the plots side by side so I can point at exactly what changes and what does not.

title: Build a written position on sparse autoencoders and what they show
body: I keep nodding along to SAE feature results without being able to say what would count as evidence against them. Read the dead-latent and feature-splitting critiques, look at the cases where the learned features fail to beat simple baselines on downstream probing, and write down in my own words what I believe and what would change my mind. The goal is a one-page position I could defend in a conversation with someone who works on this, not a survey of everything published. Start from the reconstruction-versus-interpretability tradeoff and go from there. [[obsidian:SAE critiques reading notes]]

title: Update the vaccination record before the trip clinic visit
body: The travel clinic wants proof of what I've already had before they'll advise on anything new, and my own record is a mix of a paper booklet from years ago and half-remembered dates. Dig out the booklet, cross-check it against what the surgery has on file, and note anything that's missing before the appointment so I'm not guessing in the room. Bring both the booklet and the printed surgery summary along, since they occasionally disagree on the tetanus booster date.

title: Learn paired tests for comparing two models on one test set
body: McNemar for classifiers, paired bootstrap for everything else, and know when each applies.

title: Study reward model formulations and where RL post-training goes wrong
body:
I use the words reward model and reward hacking as if they were settled, and they are not. Start with the Bradley-Terry formulation, where a scalar reward is trained on pairwise preferences, and compare it against pointwise scoring models and generative judges that output a verdict in text. Write down what each one assumes about the preference data and what it cannot represent, such as ties, intransitive preferences or annotator disagreement.

Then the pathologies: length bias, over-optimisation against a proxy reward, KL drift from the reference policy, and reward models that are confidently wrong out of distribution. For each, find one paper or blog post that demonstrates it and note the mitigation proposed, such as ensembles, length penalties or early stopping on a gold reward. The goal is a one-page map from formulation to failure mode that I can check against when a training curve looks too good. [[obsidian:Reward models and RLHF notes]]

title: Compute KV cache size for the chatbot workload I have in mind
body:
I keep quoting KV cache numbers from memory and they are always off by some factor I cannot explain. Do it properly once for a concrete case: a 32-layer model with 8 KV heads under grouped-query attention, head dimension 128, fp16, and then a workload of 20 concurrent users with 6k tokens of context each. The formula is two tensors (K and V) times layers times KV heads times head dim times bytes times tokens, so write it out symbolically first and only then plug in numbers.

After that, vary one thing at a time. What happens with full multi-head attention instead of GQA, with an 8-bit cache, with context doubled to 12k? Put the results in a small table and note how many concurrent sessions fit on a 24 GB card once the weights are subtracted. The point is to be able to answer, in under a minute and without a calculator app, whether a given model and traffic pattern is memory-limited by weights or by cache. Also check what paged allocation changes: it does not shrink the cache, it reduces waste from over-reserved contiguous blocks, and I should be able to say roughly how much waste that is.

title: Implement REINFORCE with a baseline in one readable file
body: Single file, under about 200 lines, CartPole first with no framework beyond torch and gymnasium. Then run it against a reference curve from a well-known implementation over five seeds and see where mine is worse. If the gap is large, the bug is probably in the return normalisation, so check that first.

title: Replace the expired first aid kit and the dead whistle
Explore a hiking and travel blog for trip ideas
body: I keep saying I want a proper trip with a camera but never get further than a vague region. Find one hiking and travel blog with honest trip reports, read five posts end to end, and write down two routes that seem doable in a long weekend, with the reason each one appeals.

title: Choose the alert threshold by cost of errors, not by round numbers
body:
The current fraud-score cutoff of 0.5 was never chosen; it was the default and nobody questioned it. A missed case and a false alarm do not cost the same, and the reviewer queue can only absorb so many alerts a day, so the threshold is a budget decision as much as a statistical one.

Write down three numbers first: what a missed positive costs, what a wasted review costs in analyst minutes, and how many reviews per day the team can actually do. Then plot expected cost against threshold on the validation set and mark where the alert volume crosses capacity. *If the cost-optimal threshold produces more alerts than the team can review, the capacity limit wins and the cutoff moves up*, however unpleasant the missed-case number looks.

After that, check how stable the choice is: bootstrap the validation set and see how far the optimum wanders. If it wanders a lot, pick the flatter region of the curve rather than the exact minimum, and re-run the whole exercise each quarter when base rates shift.

title: Write down a decision rule for tabular deep learning versus GBDT
body: One paragraph I can reuse: dataset size, feature types, latency, and when I would even try a neural net.

title: Build a verifier and measure best-of-N against a plateau

title: Decide the randomization unit for the checkout-page test and defend it in writing
body: User-level randomization looks obvious, but people share accounts and switch devices, and if the change affects inventory or shipping promises, treated and control users are competing for the same stock. Write a one-page argument comparing user, session and region-level assignment: what each protects against, what it costs in power, and which interference I can live with. Add a note on stratifying by past order frequency so the heavy buyers do not land unevenly in one arm. The point is to have the choice on paper before the data exists, so I cannot rationalize it afterwards. See [[obsidian:Experiment design checklist]]

title: Restart the daily experiment log and keep it going

body: I keep picking a framework by whichever README I read last. Make a short list of two or three options, and write down what each one actually solves: transport, turn detection, tool calling, interruptions. Then run the hello-world example of each.

title: Clear out apps that have been quietly running in the background
body: The battery has been draining faster than it should, and half the apps on the home screen I cannot remember installing. Go through settings and check which ones actually have background refresh or location access enabled, and remove anything unused for six months. One in particular, called =TrackFit=, has apparently been pinging location every few minutes despite never being opened. title: Tidy the keyboard layout file and comment every odd remap
body: Half the entries in my layout config have no explanation and I already forgot why the right thumb key does what it does. Go through it line by line, add a short comment to each non-obvious remap, and remove the two layers I never use.

title: Draft a safety checklist before evaluating the next image model
body: The last eval run skipped anything adversarial and I only noticed because a colleague asked about it afterward. Before the next model lands, write a short checklist covering unsafe content, memorised faces, and watermark robustness, and run it before any quality numbers get reported.

title: Collect the freelance invoices before the filing deadline creeps closer
body: Every year the same panic: half the invoices are in email, half in a folder that stopped being updated in spring. Go through each client thread now and save PDFs into one folder, because doing it in /one/ sitting is faster than three scattered ones later.

title: Add a statistics page with graphs to the food tracker
body: The tracker has months of meals in it and I have never once looked at them in aggregate, which defeats most of the point of logging. Start with three graphs only: daily calories against target, weekly average protein, and body weight as a rolling seven-day mean rather than the raw noisy points. Use whatever charting library is already in the project instead of adding a new dependency. Put it on its own route so the main screen stays fast. The rule for scope is that every graph must answer a question I have actually asked myself, otherwise it does not go in.

title: Run k-means on toy data and find where it breaks

k-means is the default I reach for, and I have never deliberately fed it data it should fail on. Generate a few shapes with scikit-learn and look at what comes out:

- Blobs with very different variances and sizes

- Silhouette score for each, and whether it warned me at all

Search for *unsubscribe* in each inbox, sort by sender, and drop anything I have not opened in months. Do the same for the muted channels I never read. title: Explain partial pooling with a small-data shop-sales example
body: Take eight shops with between five and thirty weeks of sales each and fit a hierarchical model for the mean weekly uplift from a promotion. Compare three versions: complete pooling, no pooling and partial pooling. Plot the estimates so the shrinkage is visible, and note that the shops with the least data move furthest toward the group mean. Write a short paragraph on how the group-level standard deviation controls how much shrinkage there is, and what happens to the estimates if it is given a very wide prior.

body: Been going back and forth between the =Peak Design Everyday Sling 6L= and a cheaper Amazon sling for a month without deciding, and the trip is in three weeks. Read two more real-use reviews focused on airport security lines, then just order one before the price changes again.

Find out whether the flashcard app exports its review history, write a small import script for it, and add an ease or lapse count to each word row so hard words can be sorted to the top.

title: Prepare for the one-to-one about scope and the next promotion step
body: The last two one-to-ones drifted into status updates and I left without an answer to the only question I cared about, which is what would make the next level a realistic conversation. Go in with three written questions: what does the manager see as the gap, who else needs to see the evidence, and what is a fair time frame. Ask them in that order, write down the answers during the meeting rather than afterwards, and end by restating what I heard so any misunderstanding shows up while we are still in the room. Do not start by defending the past year.
